#4392. Tesla FSD v15 is AI4’s last shot as Musk reveals how little compute is left

Tesla’s FSD v15 is its last real shot at delivering unsupervised self-driving on the AI4 computer in millions of customer cars. Elon Musk spent the weekend explaining on X how the new software uses the hardware, and there isn’t much room left.

He also confirmed that cars won’t get the next-gen AI5 chip, and that the mid-cycle AI4.5 upgrade just had its RAM cut from 32GB to 24GB.

The most visible part of FSD v15 is Tesla Reality View, a live, video-game-like rendering of the car’s surroundings with chevrons floating in the sky for upcoming turns. Musk called it “real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator.”

The fan accounts ran with that as a flex. But Musk’s follow-up posts tell a different story.

He explained that after Tesla moved a decoder into SRAM, “we only have half a TRIP out of three on SoC B, for this reality visualizer, so spent the compute as best we could.” In other words, half a TRIP is what was left over. He added that TRIP, Tesla’s neural accelerator, “basically only handles 8-bit int and has to run softmax in emulation mode in 28 steps.”

In another post, Musk described Reality View as a roughly 1-billion-parameter diffusion model running off the same vision encoder features “that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions.” He admitted the visualization’s latency is “a bit high due to compute constraints.”

That 3B figure is worth noting. Tesla talked up a 10x jump in FSD model size for over a year, first for v14 and then for v15. Musk didn’t say whether 3B covers the entire driving stack, but it’s nowhere near 10x.

And Tesla’s own engineers aren’t describing a chip with lots of headroom. Dilreet Raju, who works on Tesla’s AI silicon, wrote that the hardest work of his life was co-designing the v15 vision encoder “to squeeze out the last few percents of MFU from AI4.” MFU is model FLOPs utilization, a measure of how much of the chip’s theoretical compute the model actually uses. Musk replied with a target emoji.

When Tesla unveiled its FSD computer in 2019, the selling point was redundancy: two independent chips on one board, each with its own power and memory, so one could take over if the other failed. As we noted when Tesla started shipping the AI4.5 computer in Model Y in January, Tesla’s FSD computers have historically used two identical chips for exactly that reason.

That’s what an unsupervised, Level 4 system needs. With nobody in the driver’s seat, a hardware fault can’t simply hand control back to a human. The car needs enough healthy compute left to keep seeing the road and pull over safely.

But Musk’s own description shows SoC B running the decoder and the Reality View model, not sitting idle as a mirror of SoC A. Tesla hackers, including greentheonly, have reported for years that Tesla started splitting its FSD workload across both chips back in the HW3 days.

Tesla has never explained how much of AI4 it reserves for failover, or whether a single SoC can run enough of the stack to bring a car to a safe stop on its own. The more of the board v15 needs, the harder that question gets.

Waymo has answered it publicly. The company says both of its onboard computing systems run full workloads in parallel and that a secondary computer can bring the vehicle to a safe stop if the primary fails, backed by redundant braking, steering and power. Its new custom chip is rated at more than 1,000 TOPS. By our own comparison of AI4 and Nvidia’s Drive Thor, AI4 is estimated at roughly 100 to 150 TOPS across both chips.

Tesla started rolling out FSD v15 on Saturday, claiming “25x better handling of safety critical cases” without any baseline. So far, the people posting videos are mostly the usual crowd of Tesla-focused accounts that get early builds. Just hours before the rollout started, Musk wrote that v15 “goes to wide release next month.”

The early clips are almost all about Reality View, the new parking spot selection, and the floating arrows. Those are UI features. They say very little about how many miles v15 can drive between critical interventions, which is the only number that matters for unsupervised driving.

That brings us to AI4.5. On Tesla’s Q1 2026 earnings call, Musk announced an “AI4 Plus” with RAM doubled from 16GB to 32GB per chip, which raised the question of whether HW4 would follow HW3.

This weekend, Musk said “AI4.5 is a relatively small performance improvement that is mostly due to needing to upgrade RAM to LPDDR5X.” Hours later, he added: “RAM is super expensive, so we reduced AI4.5 from 32GB to 24GB. That will be fine. It’s hard to use 32GB anyway, given memory bandwidth constraints.”

He also said that AI4 “costs twice as much now due to memory and storage price hikes.”

So the mid-cycle refresh exists mainly because Tesla needs a newer memory type it can actually buy, not to unlock bigger models. If memory bandwidth is the bottleneck, as Musk keeps repeating, adding capacity doesn’t change much.

Asked by an owner on Sunday whether to wait for AI5 before upgrading from HW3, Musk answered: “It’s going to Optimus. Cars will remain at AI4. That’s enough to solve superhuman driving.”

An interesting comment, as it destroys one thing that HW3 owners were holding to: Tesla was delaying HW3 upgrades until it had AI5. Now, it’s clearly not the case and Tesla has no excuse not to upgrade HW3 cars.

He described AI5 as “a gigantic improvement. Roughly 12X more compute,” and later as “roughly an order of magnitude hardware performance improvement, all things considered. Memory bandwidth is a constraint.” Last year, he said that by some metrics AI5 would be 40 times better than AI4.

AI5 is also moving around. In October, Musk said Tesla cut AI5’s RAM in half to 72GB to get enough volume for Optimus, then nudged it back up to 96GB a day later. AI6 was cut by a third, to 144GB of LPDDR6. When asked about AI6 this weekend, Musk replied with a chef’s kiss meme.

As we reported in July, Samsung’s Texas fab won’t reach AI5 volume production until the second half of 2027, nearly two years behind Musk’s original timeline. And that volume is now headed to robots and data centers, not cars.

This is the situation for AI4 owners: v15 has to be the one. And we heard Elon Musk calling every FSD update “the one” for the last decade.

Tesla’s own engineers are talking about squeezing the last few percent of utilization out of AI4. Musk describes a half-accelerator scrap of compute left for the visualizer. The AI4.5 refresh is a RAM swap that just got downsized, and AI5 isn’t coming to cars. If v15 can’t get to unsupervised driving on AI4, there’s no hardware escape hatch for the fleet.

The simple truth is that Musk doesn't know how much hardware capacity is needed for autonomous driving. Partly because Musk doesn't actually have much AI expertise. But even Tesla's engineers don't know. And they won't know until they've solved the problem. What we can say with some certainty is that as unsupervised driving is rolled out, there will be all kinds of failure modes discovered, and there's likely to be several years of continual updates the model to try to address those. Even Waymo runs into this with regularity, and they're several years ahead of Tesla on autonomy. If they're so close to exhausting AI4's capability, and their current approach is bigger and more complex models, then it seems unlikely that AI4 is going to cut it. There could always be some AI research breakthrough that enables distilling models down to smaller numbers of parameters while maintaining functionality. But Tesla doesn't really engage in that kind of pure research, so they're dependent upon someone else making the breakthrough and publishing it.

We’ve seen this movie before. Tesla said HW3 was enough for unsupervised self-driving until it wasn’t, and those owners are still waiting on an answer about upgrades. AI4 owners paid for the same promise.

And even if v15 drives well, I want to know how Tesla handles a chip failure with nobody behind the wheel. That’s not optional for Level 4. If the stack needs both SoCs to drive, what brings the car to a safe stop when one of them crashes?

As for v15 itself, I’m not drawing conclusions from influencer clips. Reality View looks great, but it’s also visibly laggy, and Musk admits it’s compute-limited. A great visual update is nice. Driving performance is what matters. I’ll wait until I get it in my own car to see how big the improvement actually is.

#4390. Melissa Joan Hart Explains It All: Hot Flashes, Menopause, and Turning 50

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Actor Melissa Joan Hart has a vivid memory of her mother standing in front of their open freezer to cool off. As a child, she didn’t understand why. Now, as a 50-year-old woman, Hart knows that her mom was experiencing hot flashes.

“[She’s] only 20 years older than me, so maybe I missed the part where she was going through [menopause], but there was no conversation about it,” Hart told Healthline. “I feel like it’s just becoming a hot topic with women, where…the taboo is going away from it now.”

Her own perimenopausal symptoms started with night sweats.

“[It] was really jarring, and the first few times, you’re not really sure what that was…do I need to turn the air down or what’s going on here?” Hart said.

Over time, she learned that she was experiencing moderate to severe hot flashes, which affect up to 80% of women during the menopause transition and can persist for 7 to 10 years.

Doctors categorize hot flashes as mild, moderate, or severe, said Diana Bitner, MD, OB-GYN, at Corewell Health.

“[So] if they’re mild, it’s a sense of warmth (maybe in the chest, or the neck, or the face). A moderate hot flash is where there’s associated sweating, and a severe hot flash is something that stops you in your tracks, wakes you up from the middle of the night,” Bitner told Healthline.

Hart has mostly experienced hot flashes while home or at her three sons’ activities, and they have yet to interfere with her work. However, according to research, one in three women report moderate to severe challenges in managing their work due to symptoms related to menopause.

“It’s just so sad that about 10% of women leave the workforce due to menopause,” said Bitner. “And so it can really affect our ability to perform at these key years of not only institutional memory, but also of earning power, and it can really affect the whole community.”

Bitner said women should feel empowered to bring up their menopausal symptoms or questions with their doctor.

“[This] is something that was taboo for so long…women didn’t really talk about this, whether it was because of embarrassment, or [they] weren’t sure if anyone was experiencing it,” she said. “[There’s] no reason, in this day and age, we need to suffer through it…it’s something that there are treatment options for.”

In fact, Bitner said providing specific details about their symptoms, such as how many mild, moderate, or severe hot flashes they’ve experienced over the past week, can help doctors better assess patients’ needs.

Hart plans to discuss treatment options for her hot flashes with her doctor soon. In the last few years, she said she has put emphasis on her midlife health.

“I just was sick of waking up with aches and pains in general [thinking], ‘is this the rest of my life?’” she said.

She started listening to self-help books in the car while driving her kids around and found ways to put herself first.

“My kids are a little bit older, so I kind of have that freedom to be able to do that,” she said. “[But] along with getting older, comes the menopause, comes that different time in life. And I think it’s a good time to reevaluate [how] our bodies can’t handle what [they] used to handle, and let’s figure it out.”

Hart has partnered with pharmaceutical company Bayer on its “Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash” campaign, which encourages women to discuss menopause symptoms with their doctors and promotes Lynkuet, a hormone-free prescription medication for moderate to severe hot flashes associated with menopause.

“It’s called ‘Life Doesn’t Stop for a Hot Flash’ campaign because it shouldn’t, because we should be able to push through, and this should be a time in our lives when our kids are getting older, and we’re able to kind of reinvent ourselves,” said Hart. “And I think it’s an exciting time, and it shouldn’t be something that we’re afraid of.”

She is embracing speaking openly about midlife health.

“I hit 50 this year, and it was, like, a huge milestone, and I think that’s something to be proud of, and not something to shy away from,” she said.

Hart also hopes to challenge the longstanding barriers women face in Hollywood as they age, including fewer opportunities for leading roles.

“[I] think we’re seeing that the generation before, and my generation, it feels like we’re pushing those boundaries…and we’re saying, you know, that women at this age have a lot to give, have a lot of information to share, have a lot of stories to tell and experiences and adventures still ahead of us, and, you know, we’re not ready to stop,” Hart said.

In everyday life, Bitner said that while some patients avoid talking about midlife issues like menopause with their doctors, she is seeing more patients who are confident being forthcoming.

As more women talk openly about menopause, she hopes to include men in the conversation, too. In fact, she invites her patients to bring their partners to appointments, so they can gain an understanding of menopause and the experiences their partners face, such as hot flashes, sleep issues, vaginal dryness, and discomfort or pain during intercourse.

“[Often], there’s, you know, comments that come up [from men who] say, ‘How do I talk about this without getting in trouble?’” said Bitner. “[We] want everyone to join this conversation…it doesn’t have to be just her issue because we know it’s not.”

#4389. Honda Recalling Thousands of S2000s for Potential Fuel Leak

Examples of the high-revving convertible from the 2004–2005 model years are being asked to come back for a check-up.

It’s not too often we get new recalls for older cars like the Honda S2000, but today is one of those days. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Honda is recalling 16,387 S2000 roadsters from the 2004–20005 model years, the first two years of the AP2 refresh. A quick look at the sales figures for those years seems to suggest that means all (or close to all) S2000s from those years are part of the recall population.

The reason for the recall is that the “fuel flange joint assembly may have been improperly manufactured.” As a consequence, Honda says this could allow the fuel line connection to loosen and separate, ultimately resulting in a fuel leak and engine stall. The problem with manufacturing relates to whether or not it was built with brazing material at the joint-to-flange connection. With the part being a push-to-fit part, Honda says this lack of material could cause the connection to become loose and separate.

Honda says that when part production shifted locations, 67 replacement parts were produced without brazing material. These parts were shipped and potentially installed in S2000s. Honda estimates the percentage of cars with the defect is 1 percent. There won’t be many warning signs before it’s too late to continue driving, but Honda says stalling, a misfire, fuel odor and an inability to start the engine are all symptoms.

As of now, Honda says there are no injuries or deaths related to this issue. Those with cars in the recall range will have to bring their convertibles into the Honda dealer for the remedy. Once there, it will receive a new and improved fuel flange joint assembly free of charge.

#4388. NASA spacecraft created stadium-sized crater after slamming into asteroid

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 25, 2026 12:30 PM EST

After over four years of years of anticipation, the European Space Agency has obtained images detailing the aftermath of NASA’s head-on collision with the asteroid Dimorphos. The photos and scans from ESA’s Hera spacecraft highlight the results of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test’s (DART) intentional run-in with Didymos’ 500-foot-wide moonlet Dimorphos in 2022, revealing a stadium-sized crater, cloud of boulders, and a new, erratic orbital path.

“Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape, or stayed the same,” Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement. “Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once!”

Michel explained that while DART flattened one side of Dimorphos into a massive crater, the rest of the space rock isn’t much different. Fields of boulders largely remain where they could be seen in DART’s photos from 2022, although the event did drastically change the binary system’s surroundings.

“Another big surprise is that Hera is showing that the asteroids are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders, just a few meters in size,” added mission scientist Michael Kueppers.

Hera employed three instruments during its first observations—a thermal infrared imager to measure surface temperature, a 25-color multispectral imager, and a monochrome camera.

The car-sized probe’s work is only just getting started, too. In December, Hera will ultimately travel to barely eight miles from the asteroids, while obtaining increasingly higher-resolution photos. The spacecraft will then deploy a pair of CubeSats to get even closer to the binary system in January 2027. If all goes as planned, one of those devices will even attempt to land on the surface of Dimorphos. The combined measurements from this phase will help researchers understand the impact’s efficiency and improve future deflection strategies.

Hera’s first images were debuted at the dinosaur hall of the Berlin Natural History Museum—an intentional choice on the team’s part.

“Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid impact changed the course of life on Earth,” said Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. “Today, for the first time in history, humanity is validating how to prevent such an event from happening again.”

#4387. ‘Ferritin Face’: What Low Iron Actually Does (and Doesn't Do) to Your Appearance

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Social media influencers claim that having a “ferritin face” may indicate you’re low in iron.

Ferritin is a protein that helps your body store iron. You need iron in order to make healthy red blood cells, which carry oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. Iron is also important for bone marrow, organs, healthy muscles, and brain development.

As “ferritin face” makes its way across social media platforms, users are describing several tell-tale signs, including:

Users have also shared images of their face before and after taking iron supplements or getting an iron infusion. Videos about “ferritin face” have garnered millions of views on various platforms.

However, medical professionals state that your appearance alone is not enough to diagnose iron deficiency.

“It’s important to understand that ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis, nor is it a confirmed symptom of iron deficiency. While some people with iron deficiency can appear pale due to low hemoglobin levels in their red blood cells, there are many other symptoms to consider,” said Daniel Atkinson, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and clinical lead at Treated.

“Notably, these symptoms are also present in many different conditions, and their presence does not necessarily mean iron deficiency anemia or even low ferritin levels. Similar features are seen in people with iron processing and absorption issues, such as gluten intolerance, or in urgent sudden blood loss scenarios,” added Jonathan Jennings, MD, board certified internist at Medical Offices of Manhattan.

Iron deficiency can affect your skin and appearance. These signs are often subtle, but may include:

In some ways, the social media videos are correct. Your skin and face can change when your iron levels are low.

“The facial signs people point to, like pale skin and a washed-out look, mostly come from anaemia, when your haemoglobin has dropped. But iron deficiency and anaemia aren’t the same thing,” said Thom Phillips, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and Chief Medical Officer at Forth. “By the time low iron shows on your face, your stores are usually close to empty.”

It is important to speak with a healthcare professional, who will run blood tests such as a complete blood count and ferritin levels.

It is also important not to take iron supplements without first checking with your healthcare professional, because having too much iron in your body can also cause negative effects.

Too little and too much iron could raise your risk of infection, which is why it’s important not to take supplements without medical supervision.

The signs and symptoms of iron deficiency can depend on whether you are anemic or not. Some of the early signs may include:

“These symptoms typically occur because your body produces fewer red blood cells, which results in less oxygen being delivered throughout your body, making you feel tired and weak,” said Atkinson.

While your facial appearance can be a sign that something isn’t right, healthcare professionals consider other symptoms and how you feel overall.

They also rely on blood tests to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

“The misinformation is the idea that you can spot it yourself. That leads to two problems: people with low iron who look fine assume they’re OK, and people who look tired start taking iron supplements they don’t need,” said Phillips.

Atkinson also noted that factors such as different settings and environmental conditions can affect how your face appears.

That being said, the “ferritin face” trend may help bring awareness to certain symptoms and when to get them checked.

“[This] trend may raise some awareness about iron deficiency anemia and how low iron levels can impact daily life,” said Atkinson.

“Fatigue and lightheadedness are common side effects of low iron, but it manifests in other ways too, such as paler skin or increased hair shedding, which can be concerning for many people. If you experience these symptoms, you should let your doctor know so they can help treat the condition appropriately,” he said.

#4386. The 61 Best New Shows of 2026 (and 1 More We Can't Wait For)

We've got murder mysteries, stories of love and lust, and lots and lots of Yellowstone. And that's just the beginning.

THE IDEA OF "new" television shows is a little bit of a tricky one these days. Sure, we do still get a fair share of truly new, exciting, unique ideas each year—just look at shows like Severance a couple years ago and Pluribus last year. Shows like last year's The Lowdown—rich, well-written, character-focused stories—still draw major stars like Ethan Hawke and still hit in a big way for audiences that watch it. If someone was being dramatic and wanted to say original TV was dead, dying, or on life support, there's plenty of evidence out there to throw in their face.

But at the same time, they aren't entirely wrong. For one reason or another, so much of the TV landscape—even shows we're really excited for—are based around something that in one way or another already exists.

Look, we can't beat too much around the bush: People love nostalgia, people love things they recognize and remember, and it can be pretty hard to get anyone to even attempt to give their attention to something new, let alone get really into it in the way we all like to with the very best of TV. Which is why we kind of have two different options here—people need to be really trusting of word of mouth and really aware when something is a really good new, original show (because no one likes to waste their time with a piece of junk), and we just need to really hope that all the remakes, reboots, reimaginings, and re-whatevers are good.

And they should be! HBO's Lanterns is modeled after True Detective, stars Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre as the titular Green Lanterns, and counts Watchmen genius Damon Lindelof as a producer. Of course it’s good. Below, we're going to keep track all year. We're charting the shows we already know are good. We're charting the shows we think might be good. And we're charting the shows that may not even come out this year, but if they do... they still might not be good. But, again, say it with us: We're choosing to be hopeful.

Netflix has been really good of late at the pulpy, potboiler, limited series, and His & Hers is the latest in that winning streak. The show follows a detective (Jon Bernthal) and his estranged journalist wife (Tessa Thompson) as they both hunt for answers when a local woman—whom they both have a close connection to—winds up dead. Based on Alice Feeney's book of the same name, His & Hers is exactly how this kind of show should be: Juicy, fun, easy to watch, and filled with really good actors.

In shrinking its story down to a more intimate one that takes place between the margins of major universe events, Game of Thrones takes a page out of the Andor handbook with A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms (based on George R.R. Martin's Dunk and Egg novellas). This short series, which follows a big, humble, anxious hedge knight (former professional rugby playerPeter Claffey)and his little friend/squire (Dexter Sol Ansell) is a true breath of fresh air for Thrones fans on both a story and character level. It's a delight.

Doesn't the premise of Ponies just sound fun? This spy series set in '70s Moscow follows a pair of women working with the CIA who find themselves at the midst of a vast conspiracy when their husbands both die under mysterious circumstances. And those women are played by The White Lotus's Haley Lu Richardson and Game of Thrones queen Emilia Clarke. Sometimes something that sounds like a winner just turns out to be one.

The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins (NBC/Peacock)

This show about a disgraced former football player (Tracy Morgan) and a documentary filmmaker following him (Daniel Radcliffe) comes from the team behind 30 Rock, so you know you're going to get several jokes per minute. Plus, Morgan and Radcliffe are no slouches themselves. The show had a special debut in January and will continue on a regular schedule later in February.

At the very least, Wonder Man is among the best shows Marvel ever made—and you could make a case that it's at the top of the list. Yahya Abdul Mateen II plays the titular hero (aka actor Simon Williams) as the kind of guy we love to love in this sort of story: humble, well-meaning, charismatic, and ambitious. But when he meets fellow actor (and former fake terrorist) Trevor Slattery (Ben Kingsley) and learns that his favorite movie from childhood is being remade by an acclaimed director, everything changes. Wonder Man isn't just a good Marvel show, but a good show about people, movies, and friendship period. Let's hope the MCU takes notes from what worked so well here and keeps the streak going in the future.

One of America's great cultural institutions made its grand return in 2026: The Muppet Show! This version—coming from executive producers Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg—is directly modeled on the original Muppet Show, which means special guests, musical performances, comedy sketches, and lots of fun. The first episode, which featured special guest star Sabrina Carpenter, was an absolute delight for anyone who likes Kermit, Miss Piggy, and friends (or who just likes laughing and having a good time). For now, it's just this one episode, but if the reaction is strong enough (and it seems like it might be), the show will come back in full.

The latest entry in producer Ryan Murphy's American Story universe is called Love Story, and follows the romance and life between Carolyn Bessette Kennedy and John F. Kennedy Jr. The show is, however, much better than that tabloid-y description sounds; Sarah Pidgeon, who plays Carolyn, is a star, coming off her Tony-nominated role in the Fleetwood Mac-inspired play Stereophonic. But Paul Anthony Kelly, who plays JFK Jr., is a real discovery—it's his first role (he was previously a model), and he truly feels like a reincarnation of the late attorney/magazine publisher/dashing public figure. Of course, this is a story that ends in an extreme tragedy—so if you get invested, be sure to have your tissues ready.

This wild documentary series looks at different disputes between neighbors, telling compelling and often escalating true stories that will truly floor you in the depiction of their very-real truth. Think about this less as a story about the legalities of these disputes, and more a look into some larger-than-life characters through an often trippy, absurd lens. The series is produced by Josh Safdie and Ronald Bronstein, coming off of their recent success on the Oscar-nominated Marty Supreme.

The new season of Scrubs brings back almost all of the original cast, including Zach Braff, Donald Faison, and Sarah Chalke. And audiences who love and/or remember that trio and most of the show's original dramedy premise should be pleased with this new version of the beloved aughts sitcom. The last season aired in 2010, so we're OK with calling this 16-years-later revival a 'new' show.

DTF St. Louis follows trio of languishing adults—played by the electric trio of Jason Bateman, Linda Cardellini, and David Harbour—who get involved in a love triangle and general madness that results in one of them winding up dead. You may think you have an idea of what you're getting into with this show based on the cast and that premise, but believe us—all of your expectations will be upended. DTF St. Louis is a tonal balancing act, a show that bounces between hilarious dark comedy, compelling mystery, and gutting, relatable drama. It's one of the best shows of the year.

The second age of Yellowstone begins in earnest with Marshals, a 13-episode drama that airs on CBS (and streams on Parmaount+ either simultaneously or a day later, depending on which tier of subscription you have). The series focuses on Luke Grimes's character Kayce, and how an old SEAL Team leader (Logan Marshall-Green) recruits him into his Marshal squad. There's at least one more Yellowstone spinoff coming in 2026—Dutton Ranch—and so this is the one leading the charge.

One of the busiest men in show business these days—on both the big and small screen—is Guy Ritchie, and his newest endeavor takes him back to a world he's inhabited a couple times before. Young Sherlock follows, well, a Young Sherlock Holmes. And as you can imagine, it follows Arthur Conan Doyle's famous detective as he solves a mystery. Hero Fiennes Tiffin plays the titular character, and Colin Firth is also part of the show's cast. If you're into that, you'll have a fun time! It's an enjoyable show.

The erotic thriller is back! Or, well, juicy erotic character study dramedy? Whatever we want to call it, Netflix's Vladimir is one of the year's most exciting new shows. Based on the novel of the same name, this show follows a longtime literature professor at a college (Rachel Weisz, constantly breaking the fourth wall) who finds herself in the midst of controversy when her fellow professor husband (John Slattery) gets caught sleeping with students. She takes this as an opportunity to switch things up a bit, and so she becomes smitten with her very sexy new colleague (Leo Woodall). It's a fun, zippy, juicy time—and kind of like if Deadpool was actually about a smart woman in academia who's spinning her wheels and maybe just a little bit horny.

From the mold of Ted Lasso and Shrinking comes Rooster, which stars Steve Carell and counts Lasso and Shrinking co-creator Bill Lawrence (who also made Scrubs and Cougar Town) as its showrunner. Carell plays an author who heads to help his professor daughter on a college campus... and becomes enamored with life there. Imagine Back to School but with some middle-age soul-searching and academia at play? Sure! HBO's got another winner on their hands with this one—and maybe Carell can get the Emmy that he somehow never got for The Office.

There are 29 books in the Scarpetta series, and, now, one TV show on Prime Video starring Nicole Kidman and Jamie Lee Curtis. The series follows forensic pathologist Dr. Kay Scarpetta (Kidman) as she solves a crime—but the show is so much more than just that. In a way, Scarpetta is destined to fit into Prime Video's roster of rock-solid procedural murder mysteries, which also includes Reacher, Cross, Bosch, and plenty more. But it's got a little bit of an extra chaotic oomph—helped out by the star-studded cast that also includes Bobby Cannavale and Simon Baker—that make it worth your while and a unique, fun show.

Sunny Nights, which aired in Australia last year, now makes its U.S. debut on Hulu. The premise is simple: A pair of siblings (played by the very funny Will Forte and D'Arcy Carden) want to start a spray tan business, but wind up entrenched in the criminal underworld. Whoops! Forte and Carden have been two of our finest comedic actors for a while—with ability to play depth in addition to that humor—and the show thrives when they're at their strongest. A solid watch for anyone looking for something light but compelling.

This series—from Yellowstone super writer/producer Taylor Sheridan—follows Stacy Clyburn (Michelle Pfeiffer) and her family, as they move from the busy, stressful world of New York City to a more rustic setting out in beautiful Montana after a totally unforseen tragedy. Kurt Russellplays her husband, Preston, with his usual endless charisma, while the supporting cast includes the likes of Matthew Fox and Suits star Patrick J. Adams. Sheridan does his usual zigging and zagging in The Madison—the tone can sometimes shift from very sad to zany and comedic, and, as usual, there's a bit of social commentary speechifying buried in almost every scene. But if you're on board with the writing style he uses in shows like Yellowstone and Landman, you'll probably be OK with it here, especially if you're ready for a heavier and more contemplative tone. This show was originally planned to be part of the Yellowstone connected universe, but those plans have since been changed; It's now a new story, but with that Montana setting, you still get to look at all sorts of beautiful landscapes.

After striking gold a couple years ago with Jury Duty, Prime Video gives its grand Truman Show-esque experiment another try with a second season called Company Retreat. This time around, we follow a regular guy who thinks he’s working as a temp for a hot sauce company and joining them on their annual company bonding retreat. Of course, everyone around him is actually an actor in a scripted, engineered situation. It’s a little goofier than the first season, but seeing how everything plays out is compelling, often very funny television nonetheless. A worthy follow-up, and, honestly, we might just watch these as long as they feel like making them.

Riz Ahmed is the creator and star of Bait, a show about an actor who thinks he's about to get offered the role of a lifetime—James Bond!—and the madness that spirals out of such a revelation. If you're a fan of Ahmed's (and why wouldn't you be?) this will be a fun ride.

Something Very Bad Is Going To Happen (Netflix)

Camila Morrone (Daisy Jones and the Six) and Adam DiMarco(The White Lotus) are set to get married in this horror series from showrunner Haley Z. Boston (who worked on the very underrated Brand New Cherry Flavor) and producers The Duffer Brothers. And not to oversell, but Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen is the best horror show I've seen in quite some time. While the show plays with familiar settings and tropes—you may think of Ready or Not or Midsommar during the show's eight episodes—it's so filled with Ari Aster-esque dread and stunning, striking camera work that it doesn't even matter. Horror fans are in for an absolute treat with this one.

#4385. Toyota is giving the Corolla a radical makeover, including its first 100% electric version

Toyota is overhauling its best-selling vehicle of all time, which will include the first fully electric Corolla.

The Toyota Corolla is one of the most recognized and best-selling automotive nameplates of all time.

Since its debut in 1966, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla thanks to its reliability, low cost of ownership, efficiency, and affordable price tag.

Toyota sells the Corolla in more than 150 countries and has expanded the lineup over the past 50 years from sedans and hatchbacks to coupes, wagons, a sporty GR Corolla, and the Corolla Cross compact SUV.

For its 13th generation, Toyota is planning a major overhaul that’s expected to be its biggest transformation yet.

The next-gen Toyota Corolla will be based on a new “multipathway” platform that will support gas, hybrid, plug-in hybrid, and, for the first time, fully electric powertrains.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle ― whatever the power source ― let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive!” Toyota’s former president and current CEO Koji Sato said after unveiling the Corolla Concept at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Toyota has kept most details a secret, including battery and powertrain specs. However, the new version is expected to adopt a similar design to the concept.

“When we created the concept, we wanted to give the Corolla name a new twist,” Norihiko Kobayashi, who has led the Corolla program since 2011, told Motor.es during a recent interview.

The Corolla has undergone several minor updates over the past 60 years, but the next-gen model will look nothing like its predecessors.

“It wasn’t simply about following in the footsteps of the past,” Kobayashi explained, “we wanted to delve into the future while still maintaining the Corolla identity.”

Developing the next-gen Corolla “wasn’t just about making a new car, but about redefining the future without looking back,” he added.

Like the current version, the new Toyota Corolla will come in several different body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and a GR variant.

If they can deliver a Corolla cross EV for $30k sticker that dealers sell for $27k. That could be a large market a win for everyone . They appear to be doing what they did with hybrid and what KHG did with some models for a few years. Just starting with hybrid then going shades to pure bev.

Details have yet to be confirmed, but the Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations and offer a pure electric driving range of at least 250 miles.

The hybrid will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the hybrid system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota’s next-gen Corolla is expected to debut sometime in 2027 as a 2028 model year. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

Earlier this month, the next-gen Toyota Corolla Cross was spotted testing for the first time (see the images here).

#4384. Spyker's CEO Wants You to ‘Drive the Hell’ Out of His $1.8 Million Supercars

Victor Muller discusses plans for an endurance racing comeback and explains why he'd rather see his cars on the road than locked away.

When people spend nearly $2 million on a two-seat, mid-engine car, you can safely assume it is not the only car in their garage. It makes sense that it will not be driven every day; however, often times cars like this are not really driven at all. They spend their entire lives in climate-controlled garages, tucked beneath soft covers. And when the car in question is something like a one-of-25 C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, the temptation to preserve it as a collectible is understandable.

But Spyker CEO Victor Muller has a different idea. He wants his customers to get behind the wheel and drive. "We prefer to sell our cars to people that actually use them," Muller told me during an interview at Retromobile New York. "Because that's what I made them for. To drive the hell out of them."

That's a refreshing philosophy from someone selling a car this pricey. Particularly when that car is the new C8 Preliator XXV Coupé, which looks as much like a piece of fine jewelry as an 800-horsepower road rocket. Unfortunately, Muller admits that many of Spyker's previous creations haven't enjoyed particularly active lives.

"Many of our cars, of the 252 we made so far, have just ended up in dungeons, in vaults, in spaces where nobody will ever see them," Muller said. He's hoping to change that by organizing more owner events and encouraging customers to spend time enjoying their cars; Spyker has joined the Supercar Owners Circle, a global network of car collectors, and is planning gatherings in Europe and the United States.

The company is also in a position where it can be selective about who gets its cars. According to Muller, all 25 Preliator XXV Coupés sold during their debut at The Quail, a Motorsports Gathering in August. Every single one was snapped up in a day. "I've never seen anything like that in my entire life," he said. Spyker plans to build 25 Spyders and 25 Sedancas in 2028, he added, once production of the Coupés is complete next year.

Who is buying these cars has changed dramatically over the last quarter century. "In 2000, my typical customer was a fifty-five to sixty-year-old industrialist—old money, car collector, very astute buyer," Muller explained. "Fast forward twenty five years. Your average age is thirty-five years. Tech investor. Huge collection. Knows his cars completely. But nobody asks how much it is."

Muller says approximately 40 percent of his new buyers are existing or former Spyker owners, and roughly 80 percent of the new cars are expected to go to the United States. But no matter how old the buyer is or where they live, Muller wants them to drive the cars. This makes sense when you understand his approach to engineering; The new car has no massive infotainment screens or hybrid systems, and electronic intervention is largely limited to essential safety features like ABS and stability control.

“If you mis-shift in a Spyker and you drive two hundred miles an hour and you shift to second gear, you blow up the engine," Muller said. "And I think it has to be that way in Spyker world." For Spyker, the connection between driver and machine is more important than chasing lap records, acceleration figures and electronic nannies. "If you don't like that, buy something else," he added. "If not, man up—drive a Spyker."

Another way to demonstrate that these cars are meant to be driven is to get the brand back into racing. Muller revealed that Spyker is taking steps toward returning to professional endurance competition. The company competed in the 24 Hours of Le Mans eight times, most recently in 2010. Naturally, I asked whether another trip to Le Mans might be in Spyker's future.

"Absolutely," Muller said. "We'd love to go back in racing." Muller says Spyker is preparing to re-enter endurance racing, although he stopped short of announcing a timeline, championship, or confirmed race entry. He certainly likes the idea of seeing his latest creation on the track. More importantly, he's already started putting people in place to make it happen.

"I actually hired my former GT2 race director again," Muller said. "He started a week ago today."

#4383. Mammograms May Offer Early Insight Into Cardiovascular Disease

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.

The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.

On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.

While BAC is harmless to the breasts, it is associated with a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular disease. A 2022 study found women with BAC were 51% more likely to develop heart disease or experience a stroke than those without it.

Laxmi Mehta, MD, a cardiologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, said BAC is associated with cardiovascular risk factors, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Additionally, BAC has been connected to:

“The reasons for BAC resulting in higher risks for cardiovascular disease are not definitely determined; however, there are some potential mechanisms, one being that they share similar risk factors that result in vascular injury or metabolic stress that result in vascular calcification and atherosclerosis,” Mehta told Healthline.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center, added that because BAC and heart disease share many of the same risk factors, “calcium in breast arteries therefore suggests disease in the heart (coronary) and brain arteries as well,” he told Healthline.

While 1 in 39 females in the United States dies from breast cancer each year, cardiovascular disease causes one out of every three deaths, resulting in 1 death per minute.

“Cardiovascular disease is still the most common cause of death in premenopausal women,” Richard Reitherman, MD, PhD, a radiologist and medical director of breast imaging at MemorialCare Breast Center at Orange Coast Medical Center, told Healthline.

“The presentation of cardiovascular disease in premenopausal women is notoriously different than in postmenopausal women, primarily [because] there are no typical symptoms such as chest pain.”

Reitherman said that a prevalent and common health screening procedure such as a mammogram can lead to the early identification of women with silent cardiovascular disease.

“Cardiovascular outcome studies that have included breast arterial calcifications as a risk factor are increasingly reported in the medical literature,” he said.

“The hope is that identifying younger women with silent cardiovascular risks [like BAC along with] appropriate integrated risk identification, analysis, and interventions can significantly reduce mortality in this age group.”

Mehta said there are several reasons BAC has been overlooked as a risk factor for heart disease.

“Mammograms are completed for assessment of breast cancer, and BAC has been historically an ‘incidental’ finding, which is not clinically relevant from an oncologic standpoint,” she said.

Additionally, there is no standardization on quantification of BAC severity, nor is it a required component of mammogram reports, said Mehta.

However, routine reporting of BAC on mammograms is an urgent goal of the American College of Radiology, Society of Breast Imaging, and Medicare, said Reitherman.

In fact, it is gaining traction in the United States. A new Maryland law, passed on October 1, requires mammography centers to notify women when a BAC is detected on their mammogram.

“Automated identification and reporting of these calcifications detected on screening mammograms will become increasingly prevalent in the coming months [and] years,” said Reitherman.

The next step is to identify this group of women to primary care physicians so that appropriate risk evaluation can take place, Reitherman added.

In addition to doctors routinely screening for conditions related to heart disease, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, he hopes BAC will also be routinely considered.

“Under current development are protocols to identify patients needing a cardiologist’s training and expertise to appropriately stratify this group of patients,” said Reitherman.

“The common healthcare behavior [of] having regular mammograms not only reduces risk of morbidity and mortality from breast cancer but will hopefully contribute to the reduction of morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease in younger women.”

He said this type of integrated healthcare approach demonstrates cross-specialty integration and coordination among women, radiologists, and their healthcare providers to improve women’s lives.

“This is an amazing game-changing opportunity,” Reitherman said.

Mehta said it’s reasonable for women to ask if BAC is present on their mammogram report.

“But if it is not uniformly reported by the radiologist, the individual clinician may not have the answer,” she said.

More research is needed before BAC on mammograms can be used routinely to predict heart disease.

Finding out your BAC could provide additional information to help you and your doctors decide how aggressively to address your cardiovascular risk factors, Chen said.

Reitherman agreed. “The goal of reducing morbidity and mortality from any cause such as cardiovascular disease is based on recognition of risk factors, followed by appropriate lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions,” he said.

#4382. These Are the 46 Best Action Movies Ever Made

AS LONG AS there are movies, there will be action movies. Why? Because no young girl or boy grows up pretending to be a damsel in distress or a sidekick. They all want to punch, draw swords, and run toward the danger. They are the heroes and the future directors, choreographers, and performers who bring these imaginations to life.

And to the incredulity of your father (who insists no movie will ever top First Blood) the action genre hasn’t slipped on it’s roundhouse kick. If anything, we are now experiencing another golden age of ass-kicking cinema. While there are obvious developments in VFX technology, which have allowed for larger set pieces and more realistic thrills, much of what makes a great acton film a great action film hasn’t changed: painstaking choreography, fearless stunt performers/actors, and clear cinematography (and not that Taken fence jumping bullshit.)

The only thing that’s changed are the names and faces. Legend action directors like Ang Lee, John Woo, Robert Clouse, and Zhang Yimou (still going strong) have given way to newer arrivals like Gareth Evans, Chad Stahelski, and Christopher Nolan. And performers like Bruce Lee, Jean-Claude Van Damme, and Arnold have changed to Tony Jaa, Iko Uwais, and Charlize Theron.

If anything, the fights are becoming more brutal, more carefully choreographed, and more ambitious. And international actors and directors are finally getting increased attention (and direction) in a Hollywood overly-saturated with slapstick cinematography and post-production punches.

Here’s hoping for more John Wicks, more Raids, and more Atomic Blondes in the future. Until then, here is, in no particular order, the 36 best action movies ever made.

John Rambo would become increasingly cartoonish as the sequels went on, but in the original, he was just a scared veteran trying to survive out in the real world.

The Raid was more frenzied, but the sequel (also written and directed by Gareth Evans) got grand, introducing an intricate crime-drama plot. Didn’t matter: Redemption is brilliantly violent, a ballet of broken bones, perfect punches and crazy car chases.

The film marked the breakout moment for Muy Thai martial artist Tony Jaa and the beginning of one of the best action franchises ever. There’s not a lot of fakery in Jaa’s fight scenes. Dudes are getting punched for real.

The second film is more dialogue-heavy, but the first half is essentially nonstop action … and it’s a good thing the Crazy 88 fight is in black and white, because it’d almost be too bloody to watch otherwise.

What should have been Jason Bourne’s final adventure is a thrilling, satisfying conclusion to this kinetic trilogy. Director Paul Greengrass and star Matt Damon permanently reshaped how we think of the globetrotting espionage thriller. James Bond is still playing catch-up.

Mission: Impossible – Rogue Nation (2015)

You can’t go wrong with any in this series – though it has only gotten better as the years have gone along – but the introduction of Rebecca Ferguson to this series just amped up the emotional stakes.

Keanu Reeves’ first of two masterful franchises on this list, John Wick gave us a mournful 21st-century assassin who won’t let his grief get in the way of shooting every bad guy in the head at point-blank range.

Bruce Lee was popular before this film, but this is what sent him into the stratosphere. Well-made from start to finish, and absolutely unrelenting. The best part about it is that there isn’t a gun to be found in the whole film.

Ong-Bak gave us Tony Jaa and Muy Thai, and Ip Man gave us Donnie Yen and Wing Chun. While Yen had been in many other great action films previously (check out Kill Zone — S.P.L.), its the Ip Man films that will define his legacy, the character forever his—the semi-biographical person of Ip Man, Bruce Lee’s trainer. Though the films can feel a bit jingoistic at times (they’re basically Hong Kong’s Rambo), the fight scenes are femur-breaking legendary.

Zhang Yimou’s magnum opus, Daggers is maybe more love story than a martial arts film—and so the most action-packed love story of all time—but “love story” is no cinematic pejorative. The film features the most colorful and vibrant cinematography of any film on this list. Action is a visual genre. And no film here is more pleasing to the eyes.

John Woo’s Hollywood career wasn’t as sparkling or consistent as fans would have hoped, but this late-‘80s peak remains a glorious salute to melodramatic plotting and poetic shootouts. Chow Yun-fat made for a fierce, soulful assassin — and, never forget, The Killer is where Woo began his obsession with dove-filled action scenes, which have been parodied everywhere from 21 Jump Street to Scary Movie 2.

Oh, don’t dare not think of this as an action movie. The existential dread of Ridley Scott’s original is replaced by James Cameron’s trademark intensity, and even though this has aliens and spaceship, this is as concentrated a dose of thriller mania as you will find. You’re gripping your chair just thinking about it, aren’t you?

George Miller had been mulling a new Mad Max film for years, and clearly, he spent that time coming up with every possible permutation of a chase sequence. This movie remains thrilling, almost insane, four years later.

Because of Ang Lee’s prestige and the glamorous international cast, there is sometimes a sense that this film is bland, good-for-you Important Filmmaking. But watch it again today. This movie is iconic for a reason: it's a blast, and a euphoric ride.

If the first installment was more of a gritty thriller, then T2 is where director James Cameron cranked up the action spectacle. (That’s the kind of thing that happens when you have a much bigger budget.) Harnessing the power of then-new CG technology, this sequel threw down a challenge at the start of the ‘90s that other blockbuster filmmakers struggled to answer.

Men in Black is that perfect mix of boot-chasing, gun-firing acton with so much outer-wordly originality, Hollywood is still trying to suck every last ounce of life-force out of the 1997 original. Can we just leave the classics alone?

Yes, the car chases are as amazing as you’ve heard, but what’s striking today is how well this holds up as a cop procedural. Steve McQueen was an incredible movie star, and he was never better than he was here.

Popeye Doyle is the perfect action star for the ‘70s: grizzled, cranky, morally compromised, not the least bit likable, but absolutely tenacious about getting the bad guy, even if it’s for reasons he can’t even necessarily comprehend. Gene Hackman was at the absolute peak of his powers at this point.

Hollywood remade Akira Kurosawa’s masterpiece as The Magnificent Seven. It couldn’t compare: Not only is Seven Samurai an epic of scope and scale, it’s one of the most emotionally nuanced of action movies, featuring a slew of characters you come to care deeply about.

Michael Mann’s epic is the culmination of everything he’d been working toward his entire career; the years since still feel like his own response to it. Everybody remembers the diner scene, but the bank heist sequence feels like a magic trick even more today.

#4381. 25 Years of ‘Fast & Furious’ Movies, Illustrated

We revisit the story beats that turned a street-racing film into a $7 billion blockbuster machine.

If the Fast & Furious franchise taught us anything, it’s that there’s always another gear, and there’s no such thing as a bad plot­line. (Also: family.) To honor its silver anniversary, here’s a recap of the F&F universe, as it expanded from the L.A. street-racing scene to encompass every action-film trope, device, and format ever scrawled on a Hollywood studio whiteboard.

Cop Brian O’Connor infiltrates the L.A. import-car scene to bust hijackers who steal DVD players and at least one sweet 13-inch TV/VCR combo. He bonds with bald kingpin Dominic Toretto, then lets him go. Executives smell a sequel. Toretto has other plans: The Chronicles of Riddick. Danger to manifold: 10/10

Now a fugitive with a Nissan Skyline but no visible means of support, Brian joins the feds to catch a drug lord who tortures a corrupt cop with the ol’ rat-in-the-ice-bucket trick. Roman Pearce replaces Dom as the bald guy at the emotional core. Camaro jumps onto yacht. Danger to manifold: 5/10

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006)

The Fast and the Furious: Tokyo Drift (2006)

Brian who? Now it’s Sean, a high schooler who looks like he’s 35. Busted for street racing, he’s sent to Tokyo, the capital of street racing. He crosses the yakuza-­connected Drift King and falls in with Han Seoul-­Oh, who can’t stop snacking. Dom cameo as sequel bait. Danger to manifold: 七/10

Dom’s back, and the crew now executes road-train robberies in the Dominican Republic. Brian, now FBI, infiltrates a heroin pipeline. Letty dies. Dom seeks vengeance. A Road Warrior–style chase ends in a killer wheelie, literally. Dom is busted, but a sequel is nigh. Danger to manifold: 3/10

Street racing? Nah. We’re a heist franchise, dog. Dom’s crew, now fully Hollywood four-quadrant tested, steals a crime lord’s fortune in Brazil. A former wrestler shows up as DSS agent Luke Hobbs. Bald jokes and legal ambiguity ensue. Everybody walks with $100 million. Danger to manifold: 1.5/10

Hobbs is back, and we meet British scoundrel number one, Owen Shaw, an ex-SAS mercenary who drives a ramp car that flips police cruisers like a spatula. Letty is alive (huh?), with amnesia, and on Shaw’s payroll. Gisele dies. (Who’s Gisele again?) Danger to manifold: –10/10

Jason Statham (really?) is Deckard Shaw, Owen’s scoundrel brother, who fireballs Dom’s family home. The crew parachutes into Azerbaijan in their cars. A Lykan HyperSport jumps between three Abu Dhabi office towers. Han’s dead (like we believe that). The saddest ending imaginable. Danger to manifold: N/A.

Roll call: John Cena. Dame Helen Mirren. Charlize Theron. Jason Momoa. Sir Idris Elba. Old villains are in the crew now. #4380. BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design

A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight. BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.

The preliminary relief judge at the District Court of The Hague issued the ruling on Friday, November 20, in summary proceedings JLR brought against 11 BYD companies.

JLR put six registered EU designs in front of the court. The judge only needed one of them: design 005248580-0004, registered in April 2018 and covering the current Defender 110, known internally as the L663.

According to the ruling, the elements that dominate that design are the rounded “shoulders,” the rounded corners, the signature panel on the C-pillar, the rounded wheel-arch cutouts, the continuous window line, and the overall silhouette. The court found every one of them on the Ti7.

Here’s how the two SUVs compare from the same angles, using official press images from BYD and JLR:

BYD argued that the headlights, grille, bumpers, hood and side profile are all different. Not enough, said the judge, who ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression. The court also found the Ti7 sits closer to the Defender than to older boxy SUVs like the Ford Flex, Jeep Wrangler and Mercedes G-Class.

BYD doesn’t sell the Ti7 in the EU. It told the court it has “no concrete plans” to launch it there and that the SUV can only be ordered in the UK.

The judge didn’t buy that as a defense. By BYD’s own account, it developed the seven-seat layout for the UK and Europe, a promotional video called the Ti7 the first seven-seat SUV “in Europe,” and BYD wouldn’t commit to keeping it out of the EU. That was enough for the court to find a threat of infringement.

So BYD’s EU entities can no longer import, produce, offer, sell, store or supply the Ti7. The order kicks in one week after the ruling is formally served, and it even covers BYD’s Hungarian unit, since the judge considered it conceivable the Ti7 could come out of the new Szeged factory.

The UK is a different story. The court said it has no jurisdiction over BYD UK and threw out JLR’s UK design claims, so British deliveries are still on for January 2027. That’s the one European market where BYD actually opened orders, pricing the Ti7 at £47,995, about £24,000 below the £71,840 plug-in Defender 110.

BYD said it “strongly disagrees” with the judgment and will appeal, adding that the Ti7 “is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights.” JLR told AFP it protects its intellectual property and takes legal action when necessary.

BYD has four weeks to appeal, but the injunction stays in force while it does. JLR, for its part, has six months to file a full case on the merits, or BYD can get the injunction lifted.

There’s more coming. JLR also has a separate case in Rotterdam over copyright and “slavish imitation,” with a hearing scheduled for Wednesday.

This whole thing started in August, when JLR had bailiffs raid BYD’s Dutch offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. The court later ordered JLR to destroy everything it seized, saying it didn’t need BYD’s internal files to make its design case. And it didn’t. JLR won on the design registration alone.

The Ti7 looks like a Defender. We said so when BYD first brought it to the UK, and so did pretty much everyone else. Chinese automakers have been building Defender lookalikes for years, but most of them stayed in China.

BYD brought one to the Defender’s home turf at a £24,000 discount, so a fight with JLR was always coming.

"...ruled that those differences, on their own or combined, don’t give an informed user a different overall impression."

Really? I feel like anyone who pays even a little attention to car designs isn't going to mistake the two. The thing most people see as differentiating within the same category is the headlights, tail lights, grill - which are all significantly different.

The only real similarity is the proportions, there are a ton of similarly proportioned SUVs but that's a result of the form factor.

But honestly, all these boxy SUVs look the same to me.

Nobody owns “boxy.” JLR even failed to trademark the classic Defender’s shape in the UK, a fight it lost in its legal battle with the Ineos Grenadier. But it registered the new Defender’s design in 2018, and that specific combination of shoulders, C-pillar panel and wheel arches is exactly what the court protected. That’s how design rights are supposed to work.

The actual business damage is small for now. The Ti7 sells roughly 30,000 units a month, almost all in China, and the UK launch goes ahead. The stock dip was about headlines more than lost Ti7 sales.

#4379. Plant-Based Milk Alternatives May Not Give You Enough Iodine. Here’s Why That Matters

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

The United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine. This compares with 61% for calcium and 46% for vitamin B12.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.

The study found that replacing as little as 20% of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives could increase the risk of inadequate iodine intake, particularly among adolescent girls and women of reproductive age.

“People often worry about a decline in calcium intake when they replace some of their dairy with plant-based alternatives. As a result, iodine is frequently overlooked. This study serves as a valuable reminder of iodine’s significance as a nutrient,” said Victoria Finn, MD, board certified endocrinologist at Medical Offices of Manhattan, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included analysis of UK plant-based milk, cheese, and yogurt products, as well as dietary data from 3,500 people.

The researchers used statistical modeling to predict how swapping dairy for PBAs might affect iodine and other nutrients.

The people who are most vulnerable to iodine inadequacy are adolescent females and people at reproductive age, especially those who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant.

The researchers estimated that replacing 20% to 35% of dairy intake with PBAs would increase the proportion of people with inadequate iodine intake:

When the researchers modeled the replacement of all dairy products with PBAs, the proportion of adolescent females with inadequate iodine intake rose to 80%. Among females ages 19 to 49, that proportion remained relatively stable as replacement rates increased.

It is important to keep in mind that the study used dietary modeling rather than direct measurement of iodine status.

Iodine is important for thyroid hormone production, metabolism, and both fetal and child brain development.

“Your thyroid gland requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and supporting normal growth and development,” said Finn.

She added that if you consistently consume too little iodine over an extended period, the thyroid gland may enlarge and eventually struggle to produce enough hormones. This condition is known as hypothyroidism, which can lead to various symptoms such as lethargy, sleepiness, weight gain, dry skin, and more.

“Hypothyroidism can be particularly dangerous during pregnancy, as the baby’s brain, nervous system, and organs rely heavily on the mother’s thyroid hormone during the early stages of development,” Finn added.

In the United Kingdom, dairy is a major iodine source due to cattle feed supplementation, not because dairy is naturally high in iodine.

In the United States, dairy is also an important source of iodine for the same reasons.

However, the risk profile for iodine deficiency in the U.S. may differ from the U.K., as iodized salt is also a significant source of iodine and is widely available in the U.S., but not in the U.K.

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the recommended daily intake of iodine depends on your age.

Plant-based or plant-forward diets have grown in popularity, in part due to the health benefits they offer. For example, consuming less meat can reduce your risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol.

However, as this study suggests, it may be possible to reduce your iodine intake when transitioning to a plant-based diet. There are ways you can protect your iodine intake when choosing a more plant-forward diet, though.

Check the labels on plant-based dairy alternatives to find those fortified with iodine. You can also read the nutrition label. Iodine may be listed as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.

Seafood, eggs, and iodized salt are all good sources of iodine.

You can also discuss iodine supplements with your healthcare professional.

“Iodine supplements should be taken with caution, especially without checking your thyroid levels,” said Finn. “Additionally, be cautious with kelp supplements, as their iodine content can vary, and excessive iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function.”
