#4342. New Zealand’s Twin-Engine Toyota Celica Is Essentially Unstoppable

A fairly conventional overlanding Celica build quickly spiraled into a monster with two engines, dual gearboxes, and semi-amphibious capability.

The art of modifying cars is gleefully rule-free. Sure, there are never-ending hoops to jump through for street legality, but actually building your perfect vehicle is merely a matter of dreams. For Kiwi Gareth Wadsworth, who goes by @garethcars on social media, those dreams meant stuffing two engines and two transmissions into a single sixth-generation Toyota Celica. Seems easy enough, right?

Wadsworth’s twin-engine Toyota Celica has made literal waves on social video in the past few weeks, as the Christchurch resident demonstrated its remarkable wading abilities in a series of viral videos. The basic recipe is a pair of Toyota’s 2.0-liter 3S-GE engines—one mounted in the front and one mounted in the rear—mated to a pair of manual transmissions and fed to individual differentials.

With so many moving parts, Wadsworth went analog with the controls; a pulley system attached to the original clutch pedal also operates the clutch for the rear transmission, and the throttle pedal is divided into an upper portion for the front engine and a lower portion for the rear engine. If you press directly in the middle of the accelerator, both engines will rev up (somewhat) in sync. Wadsworth emphasized that it is two completely separate drivetrains that require two of everything (two batteries, two fuel tanks, two ECUs, two radiators) and can be driven separately or simultaneously.

But this Celica build wasn’t always this extreme. In fact, the initial version was supposed to be a simple overlanding setup for a university off-road club trip in 2020. He initially off-roaded the Celica with a simple four-inch lift kit and 31-inch tires, but Wadsworth wanted to try something more extreme—and he didn’t want to abandon the existing platform.

“I had this Celica that I bought crashed, and I didn't have anything to do with it. I was a student. I didn't have the money for a four-wheel-drive, so I ended up building it into a four-wheel-drive,” Wadsworth said to Road & Track. “I paid $800 for the car, and then I sold the wheels and tires that were on it. So it was effectively a free car just sitting around, and I got some suspension left over from other projects that I threw in it, and the engine came from a crashed car I found upside down off the side of the road.”

After a year of mud-slinging fun, Wadsworth decided to go all-in on the dual-engine swap. The rear engine transplant only took two weeks, with most of the work happening after school and during a series of all-nighters. A day or two after the build was complete, Wadsworth and friends trailered the dual-engine Celica to an off-road area and began testing its abilities. Some limitations were quickly revealed.

“It was just the stock intakes for a few trips. It did have a snorkel on the outside for the front engine. Once it was twin-engine, it had enough power that we could hit the water faster, and that meant that the bow wave would keep going over the roof and filling the front engine's snorkel. We had one trip on the White Bear River that was in flood, and we hydrolocked the front engine twenty-three times, and we got sick of having to pull the spark plugs out, blasting the water out, and trying to get it running again. And so that's why I moved the intake to the glove box,” Wadsworth said.

Wading is one of the twin-engine Celica’s best tricks, as it is fast enough to glide onto the water and light enough to float through. The Celica has floated through currents that have sunk heavier 4x4 trucks, Wadsworth said. But the twin-engine Celica doesn’t just excel at water crossings, either. Because the gearboxes run independently, Wadsworth can tune the gear ratios of either end to suit his needs.

“There's no weird handling from the differences between the front and rear. It's just whichever engine's got the least load on it speeds up to catch up with the other one. They're effectively a fifty-fifty split,” Wadsworth said. “Because of the biasing, I quite often run almost exclusively rear-wheel-drive, and I only add front when I need it for traction. It's quite a unique feeling. It's so much fun, and probably the main reason I've still got it is being able to dynamically shift between front, rear, or four-wheel-drive and throttle biasing on the fly. In a mud pit, I can sit around doing donuts with the front in neutral, and then I can put the front-end gear in and let the clutch out slowly on the front to transition from donuts to power slides.”

And it isn’t even too hard to drive—relatively speaking. Wadsworth said that his mates can hop in and romp it with minimal coaching, at least in this configuration. Shifting the two gearboxes can get awkward, but the rear transmission shifter is placed near the traditional shifter, so you don’t have to reach far. Before the pulley clutch system, Wadsworth wired the rear clutch through the parking brake, which required a gentle touch to keep from stalling.

But it wasn’t always so accommodating. “On the original build, we didn't have time to connect any of the controls, so it had two drivers back then. And we didn't have a throttle, so the strap for tightening the hood was tied onto the rearview mirror and back to the rear throttle body, and you pulled it like a train horn,” Wadsworth said. “We certainly had a lot of difficulty driving it when we first built it, because it required two people to communicate—but it didn't have any exhaust, so we couldn't hear each other, and we had no total control on the rear; it was either fully on or fully off. And you had to get up out of your seat, turn around, and put it in gear for the rear engine.”

Even after six years of ownership and five years with two engines, Wadsworth plans to continue driving the twin-engine Celica as long as possible. Initially, he considered adding four-wheel steering using a power steering motor from a Nissan Leaf, but he said the time under the knife wouldn’t be worth it. The more time spent off-road, the better.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4341. World’s fastest animal may gain habitat by 2080

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 26, 2026 12:00 AM EST

While climate change represents a threat to most animal populations, the reality isn’t quite as straight forward. As the landscape reacts to a shifting climate, some species might actually see their habitat expand.

That could be the case for peregrine falcons (Falco peregrinus), the fastest animal on the planet, living in the United Kingdom. That’s what Connor Panter, a researcher at the University of Nottingham’s School of Geography, found in a study published today in the journal Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.

Panter analyzed how various future climate change scenarios might make different parts of the country more or less appropriate for 16 species of breeding birds of prey.

“We know that climate change is altering where wildlife is found across the world, but scientists’ understanding of how different birds of prey may respond to these changes is still relatively limited,” Panter tells Popular Science. “Raptors play important ecological roles as predators, and understanding how their distributions might change is important for informing future conservation efforts.”

Panter investigated a “middle-of-the-road” climate-change scenario and a “worst-case” climate-change scenario in the U.K. Today, there are 42,570 square miles of suitable habitat for peregrine falcons. Under the middle-of-the-road scenario, that could increase by 40.6 percent by 2060, and under the worst-case scenario, it could increase by 73.5 percent by 2080.

Hen harriers (Circus cyaneus), golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos), little owls (Athene noctua), long-eared owls (Asio otus), western barn owls (Tyto alba), and western marsh harriers (Circus aeruginosus) could also see increases. Suitable habitats for common buzzards (Buteo buteo), European sparrowhawks (Accipiter nisus), and tawny owls (Strix aluco), aren’t predicted to change much in any scenario. But British short-eared owls (Asio flammeus), red kites (Milvus milvus), merlins (Falco columbarius), and Eurasian goshawks (Astur gentilis) will likely lose significant amounts of suitable land.

Ultimately, Panter’s work emphasizes that climate change will probably not impact all birds of prey in the same way, even if they live in the same areas. This could represent a significant problem for conservation, because future efforts aiming to safeguard these species will have to take these differences into consideration, according to Panter.

“It is also important to recognise that an increase in the area suitable for a species does not necessarily mean that its population will grow or that it will become more widespread,” Panter says. For example, “whether peregrine falcons can occupy newly suitable areas will depend on numerous other factors, including the availability of prey, nesting opportunities, threats from humans and interactions with other species.”

#4338. Meteorites fascinated ancient Egyptians—just look at King Tut’s ‘space dagger’

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 26, 2026 9:01 AM EST

In August 2026, an analysis of iron from ancient Greek tombs revealed surprising results. The objects surveyed included weapons and jewelry from around 3,000 to 4,000 years ago. Most of them were fashioned from regular old iron ore, but around 10 rings were made of iron from outer space—aka from meteorites that crash-landed on Earth.

It seems that, among the upper classes of Bronze Age Greece, rings fashioned from this out-of-this-world metal were all the rage. Before people learned how to extract iron from ore by melting it at super-high temperatures—a process called smelting—the only source of metallic iron was the occasional space rock. This material, known as meteoric iron, is rare worldwide, but especially in Greece, where approaching meteors usually disappear into the sea rather than make landfall.

Researchers believe that the Greek meteoric rings were actually imported from Egypt: a land with a special relationship to this metal from the skies.

Meteoric iron can be identified because it’s purer than the iron ore that naturally occurs on Earth, with a higher proportion of nickel mixed into it. Because meteoric iron “already arrives on Earth in metallic form,” says Victoria Almansa-Villatoro, a professor of Egyptology at Yale University, “it’s very malleable” and can be shaped more easily than unrefined ore.

The Egyptians started working with this rare material early. “The oldest meteoric iron objects in the world come from Egypt,” says Almansa-Villatoro: Nine small beads, excavated from a site called Gerzeh along the bank of the Nile about 20 miles south of Cairo, are the oldest artifacts discovered made from space rocks. They are dated to around 3,200 BCE, more than a thousand years older than the 10 meteoric iron rings found in Greece.

Not only are the Gerzeh beads older than any other meteoric iron objects, they are much, much older than widespread iron smelting in Egypt. Almansa-Villatoro explains that “Egypt was relatively late in comparison with other Near Eastern civilizations to start smelting iron.” By the time the Egyptians were producing iron on a large scale in the 500s BCE, ancient people in Anatolia and other regions had been doing it for about five hundred years.

A major reason for this late adoption was Egypt’s natural resources. Iron smelting forges burned a lot of wood charcoal, and Egypt had no large forests. For centuries, the Egyptians relied on bronze, which cost less fuel to produce. It wasn’t until major changes in political and trade networks, including pressure to match the iron arsenals of foreign enemies like the Assyrians, that the Egyptians finally made the shift.

While early iron weapons and armor were not automatically better than bronze ones, iron proved easier to repair, and could be strengthened through further reworking. But objects like the Gerzeh beads show that the ancient Egyptians shaped small amounts of meteoric iron long before they knew how to extract it from ore.

The Gerzeh iron beads were incorporated into jewelry with gems and gold, hinting at their perceived value. All of the other Egyptian objects believed to be made of meteoric iron are similarly small and mostly decorative. The largest and most spectacular is a dagger with a meteoric iron blade more than eight inches long. It was found in the tomb of Egypt’s famous pharaoh, Tutankhamun, who died around 1,323 BCE.

Government records from the reign of Tutankhamun’s grandfather, Amenhotep III, mention an Anatolian king gifting a dagger to the Pharaoh. “People have speculated that this was the same dagger,” says Almansa-Villatoro. “Because, why would they make such a big deal about this king receiving a dagger from a foreign leader, unless it’s made of a very important or very rare material?” As seen with the recent findings from Greece, demand for meteoric iron in the ancient Mediterranean was international.

As of 2013, archaeologists had discovered 28 objects in Egypt believed to be made of meteoric iron. This accounts for about half of the 55 known ancient meteoric iron artifacts found across Europe, Asia, and Africa as of 2023.

The prevalence of meteoric iron in Egypt is difficult to determine, as the composition of many iron objects has never been evaluated. Additionally, says Almansa-Villatoro, “we find more things in Egypt in general from this time period than in other regions,” due to the long history of archaeology there.

Analysis has shown that some of the Egyptian meteoric iron objects are made from several small meteorites combined. This might suggest that the Egyptians were “harvesting” and “actively looking” for this rare material, says Almansa-Villatoro, rather than just using it at random when a meteorite happened to land nearby.

Almansa-Villatoro believes that meteoric iron “was valuable because it was recognized to be material that came from the sky,” not just because it was more pure than other iron. Ancient Egyptian religious texts link iron with the heavens and the spiritual realm of the gods, who were sometimes described as having iron bones. One Egyptian term for iron literally translates to “the iron of the sky.“

“Some tools made of meteoric iron were used in a very important funerary ritual known as ‘the Opening of the Mouth,’” says Almansa-Villatoro. These include small iron blades found in Tutankhamun’s tomb (though not the famous dagger). The purpose of this ritual was “to give the deceased back their senses,” Almansa-Villatoro explains, allowing them to speak, breathe, and eat in the afterlife. Meteoric iron might have been particularly prized for crafting these ritual objects.

By the time of Tutankhamun’s reign, the Egyptians might have encountered smelted iron produced in other lands, but they were still using meteoric iron in rituals and reverently placing it in tombs.

“It is possible that they still saw meteoric iron as something different” from smelted iron, says Almansa-Villatoro, though it’s hard to say for sure.

Ancient Greece’s most famous oracle was just high on gas fumes

In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution

Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy

At Scotland’s ancient Cladh Hallan, homes were full of human bones

For ancient Romans, pooping was a group activity

Some Egyptian texts describe a dome of water with an iron shell enclosing the Earth. Meteoric iron might have been explained as fragments of this cosmic shell breaking off and falling to the Earth.

It’s clear that the Egyptians considered meteoric iron to be a special material, but what exactly they knew or didn’t know about it is not always easy to figure out. The Egyptians understood and interpreted the world around them using very different methods from our own. While we rely on experimental data documented in writing, ancient Egypt “was very much an oral society, where knowledge was transmitted through ritual and through recitation of texts,” says Almansa-Villatoro.

In ancient Egypt, “things that we wouldn’t consider science nowadays, like myth, could have fulfilled the same function” as science does today, says Almansa-Villatoro. The Egyptians used narrative myths to describe the physical universe. The iron shell surrounding the Earth appears in accounts of the soul’s journey to the afterlife, as a barrier that the spirits of the dead must sail across to reach the skies.

With our modern knowledge, it’s easy to explain how a space rock might land on Earth. But what if all you knew of outer space was what you could see with your eyes from our planet’s surface? Egyptian myths may not have the structure of a modern scientific paper, but they offer a glimpse into how ancient people made sense of awe-inspiring natural phenomena like metal falling from the skies.

#4337. How to Plan Your Holiday Meals in a Year of Unprecedented Recalls

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Following a series of high-profile food recalls and outbreaks this year, many Americans may be concerned about keeping their families safe from foodborne illness during the holidays.

In fact, according to a recent national survey by Orlando Health, around 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years.

Although several major foodborne illness outbreaks have ended and their associated recalls are no longer active, food safety remains an important concern. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 48 million people in the United States experience foodborne illness each year.

However, there are simple steps you can take to reduce the risk of foodborne illness when preparing holiday meals and storing leftovers.

While there were several food recalls in the United States over the summer, two of the largest involved Salmonella linked to jalapeños and Cyclospora linked to lettuce.

These outbreaks prompted widespread recalls and raised concerns about the safety of certain foods, particularly fresh produce.

Although health officials have since declared the major outbreaks over, some consumers may still be hesitant to purchase foods associated with previous recalls.

Even with this declaration, you may still feel nervous about purchasing certain foods, but experts say you don’t need to worry.

“Here in the United States, we have the safest food supply in the world. The recent recalls show that our food safety system is working,” said William Schaffner, MD, Professor, Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University.

Michelle Routhenstein, preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, told Healthline that past recalls do not mean entire food categories need to be avoided. The important thing is whether the specific product you have matches a current recall, based on details such as brand, lot number, package size, and expiration date.

“You should enjoy familiar foods, including properly cooked poultry, washed fruits and vegetables, and pasteurized dairy products,” she said. “The key is checking relevant recalls and practicing safe food handling.”

“Before shopping or cooking, review FDA and USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) recall information and compare any relevant notices with the labels on your ingredients,” said Routhenstein.

Check the pantry and freezer, too: something purchased months ago may still be affected.

“Stay alert to any news reports about food recalls and use good food preparation practices. Those simple actions should keep your holidays happy and safe,” said Schaffner.

Consumers can sign up for food recall alerts through the FDA or visit FoodSafety.gov for recall information from both the FDA and USDA.

Schaffner emphasized the importance of following safe food-handling practices when preparing everyday meals and holiday gatherings.

“Remember the longstanding advice: keep food hot or cold. Avoid long times at room temperature,” he said.

Routhenstein advised focusing on four basics: clean, separate, cook, and chill.

Schaffner noted the importance of refrigerating leftovers promptly rather than leaving them at room temperature for extended periods. He recommends clearing the table and refrigerating leftovers soon after the meal ends.

Routhenstein reiterated that you should refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours rather than leaving them out to cool.

Divide turkey into smaller portions and transfer sides and gravy into shallow containers to help them cool quickly, she advised.

Leftovers can typically be stored in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. If you don’t plan to eat them within that time, consider freezing them.

The important thing is to keep an eye out for any new recalls, practice food safety, and enjoy your holiday meals!

#4334. Here’s How the Porsche 718 Boxster EV’s Fake Flat-Six and PDK Work

Porsche chose the 981-generation Boxster GTS model as its sound reference.

The upcoming Porsche 718 Boxster EV hops on board the growing simulated-internal-combustion-engine-and-transmission electric car trend. We just drove a prototype, and while there’s a lot to discuss about the car in general, it’s also worth honing in on the sound aspect. As you might expect, it’s rather pivotal to the experience behind the wheel.

The system that debuted in the Taycan is still called “E-Shift” here in the Boxster, and you can turn it on or off via a button on the steering wheel. Porsche chose the 3.4-liter naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster as its muse. It’s a good choice, but also a bit of a surprise considering the spectacular sound out of the 4.0-liter flat-six found in the previous 718 Boxsters. But Porsche has its reasons, as Dr.-Ing. Sebastian Lefevre, team lead advanced driver assistance systems 718, tells us.

“It was a big discussion in our company,” Lefevre said. “From our point of view, the 4.0 engine is a little bit too soft in the sound. In our company, the 981 GTS sound, six-cylinder, was a little bit louder, and it would also feel more popular and familiar with our old customers.”

Once you hear the sound, there’s a good chance you’ll end up agreeing with Porsche. Lefevre mentioned the possibility of using the four-cylinder from the previous 718, but just as quickly shot the idea down referencing critique of the flat-four’s sound. How it reproduced the engine and exhaust via speakers is similar to how other OEMs with simulated internal combustion engines in EVs do it.

“A lot of microphones outside, inside,” Lefevre said. “And then we measured it all over the complete rpm range. And then we put it here, in this car, and measure it again. With the speakers, which are installed here. We have two.”

The most controversial speaker is bound to be the exterior-positioned one. More than anything, however, this exterior speaker exists as a sound maker for occupants to enjoy when the roof is off. It tries to emulate a mid-engine powertrain arrangement by way of the sound emanating from behind the driver and passenger; Porsche increases the volume inside the car with the roof removed, too. That’s a neat idea, but one that struggles to work in practice; I could hear some faint backfires on “downshifts” like Porsche’s ICE cars produce, but the experience is far from that of a real exhaust and engine echoing and reverberating off mountainsides or buildings.

Mercedes-AMG has the best ICE simulation around right now, with its AMG GT 4-Door Coupe going so far as to induce proper NVH characteristics by using exciters in the seats. The Boxster EV Prototype we drove relies entirely on the speakers to induce its hypnosis. But E-Shift brings a few theatrics to the table.

When lining up for a launch control start, Porsche pulses the torque of the electric motor to give a sense of an impending launch. It also lets you run the car into “redline,” tossing you forward with brake torque, just as it would in a manually-shifted gas-powered car. That said, Porsche took some liberties with the 8000-rpm redline depicted in this prototype; the 981 Boxster GTS instrument cluster shows a redline of 7600 rpm, so you have an extra 400 fake revs to play with in the EV.

Not as though this extra headroom matters, however, as Porsche chose to not simulate the torque curve of the flat-six. Instead, peak performance from the single electric motor is always available, and the car shuffles through its fake seven gears as speeds rise and fall. How it shifts is dependent on drive mode per usual with Porsche PDKs, and you can choose between manual or automatic shifting. You’ll even hear a tone difference in the engine noise over the speakers depending on whether you’re on- or off-throttle, just as you would were the real 3.4-liter be gulping in air behind your head.

For our full first impressions from behind the wheel of the 718 Boxster EV, make sure you read our prototype drive review.

BYD held a launch event for its new flagship five-seat electric SUV on Tuesday. The third-gen Tang is available in three variants: standard Premium, Laser Premium, and Laser Flagship.

All versions come standard with rear-wheel drive (RWD), but buyers can upgrade the Laser Flagship model with an optional all-wheel-drive (AWD) steer-by-wire package for an extra 20,000 yuan ($3,000).

The Laser Premium and Laser Flagship models start at 207,900 yuan and 219,900 yuan, respectively, also well below the pre-sale price.

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade LFP Batteries. RWD models use a single 402 hp (300kW) electric motor, delivering CLTC ranges of 453 miles (730 km) for the base Premium model and 528 miles (850 km) for the Laser Premium and Laser Flagship versions.

Upgrading to the dual-motor AWD powertrain bumps power to 690 hp (515 kW) and delivers a CLTC range of up to 478 miles (770 km).

The flagship electric SUV is equipped with BYD’s latest tech and other features, including its God’s Eye B laser-assisted driving system with DiPilot300 and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

BYD’s God’s Eye B uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to support ADAS features such as city navigation assist, high-speed navigation assist, and all-scenario parking assist.

The third-gen Tang also has BYD’s new high-speed tire blowout stability system, which can keep the vehicle stable and in its lane at up to 112 mph (180 km/h).

Measuring 5,045 mm long, 1,980 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, with a 2,950 mm wheelbase, BYD’s new Tang SUV is about the size of a Tesla Model X or BMW iX.

The third-gen Tang will join the larger Great Tang as BYD expands its flagship SUV lineup. The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

#4331. Planning to Stop Taking a GLP-1? Here’s How to Maintain Weight Loss

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Switching GLP-1 medications or undergoing bariatric surgery may help people maintain greater weight loss than stopping treatment entirely, according to a new study presented at ObesityWeek and published in eClinicalMedicine on November 14.

The Cleveland Clinic study compared five strategies for managing weight after treatment with GLP-1 medications, analyzing data from 20,486 adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes.

People who stop taking GLP-1 medications often regain weight. Researchers examined whether continuing treatment, switching medications, or undergoing bariatric surgery could help limit weight regain or support further weight loss.

The findings showed that people who underwent bariatric surgery or switched between semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) experienced the greatest overall weight loss.

The study participants had an average age of 56.7 years, an average weight of 109 kg (240.3 lbs), and an average body mass index (BMI) of 38. All had been taking either semaglutide or tirzepatide for at least 90 days.

The researchers categorized the participants into five groups:

After 2 years, those who underwent bariatric surgery saw an average loss of 28.2% of their body weight or about 31.5 kg (69.4 lbs).

“We increasingly view medications and surgery as complementary tools rather than competing ones,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“For patients with severe obesity (typically a BMI of 35 or higher, or 30+ with metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes), bariatric surgery remains the most durable, cost-effective intervention available,” he added. “Using a GLP-1 beforehand can safely reduce liver volume and lower surgical risk, while surgery provides the permanent anatomical and hormonal reset needed to maintain that weight loss long-term without relying indefinitely on weekly injections.”

During the same period, those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide lost 16% of their body weight, or about 18 kg (39.6 lbs).

Participants who switched from semaglutide to tirzepatide lost 3 kg (6.6 lbs) more than those who continued taking semaglutide. However, participants already taking tirzepatide lost 4.5 kg (9.9 lbs) more by continuing treatment rather than switching to semaglutide.

The other groups experienced lower amounts of weight loss:

After one year, participants with type 2 diabetes experienced HbA1c reductions of 1.76% following bariatric surgery, 1.43% after switching GLP-1 medications, and 1.32% after continuing their original medication, compared with 0.48% among those who discontinued treatment entirely.

After one year, participants with hypertension (high blood pressure) also experienced greater reductions in blood pressure following surgery or switching GLP-1 medications than those who discontinued treatment entirely.

“[This study] reinforces the need for a long term, multi-modal continuum of care rather than treating GLP-1s as a temporary fix,” said Ali.

Ali also recommended the following strategies to help maintain weight loss after stopping a GLP-1 medication:

The findings highlight the importance of having a long-term weight management plan in place before stopping a GLP-1 medication.

Before stopping a GLP-1 medication, talk with a healthcare professional. They can help you explore your options and determine which strategies may be most appropriate for your health needs.

Ali told Healthline that identifying the reason for stopping treatment is an important first step. He noted that people often discontinue GLP-1 medications because of gastrointestinal side effects, supply issues, or loss of insurance coverage rather than because they no longer need treatment.

He said that if side effects are the issue, adjusting the dose or switching to a different agent often solves the problem.

Ali also emphasized that stopping a GLP-1 medication shouldn’t be viewed as a test of willpower. Increased hunger after discontinuing treatment is a biological response, not a personal failure.

“Have a concrete ‘off-ramp’ plan in place with your doctor before taking your last dose, so you have medical, nutritional, or surgical support ready to protect the health gains you worked hard to achieve,” advised Ali.

Wickens will make his 24 Hours of Daytona debut this upcoming January.

Eight years after a harrowing crash at Pocono Raceway paralyzed the then-IndyCar star, Robert Wickens has made his way to the grid of the biggest sports car race in the United States. He will contest the 2027 installment of the 24 Hours of Daytona in a Hanley Motorsports Inc.-run BMW M4 GT3, part of his first-ever full season of IMSA racing.

Wickens will pair with Mason Filippi in a full-season effort in the GTD class. Both drivers are champions in the IMSA Pilot Challenge TCR class; Wickens won the title in 2023, while Filippi scored his own championship in 2026. The pairing reunites two drivers that shared a DXDT Racing Corvette during the sprint races last season, the second such schedule for Wickens in the past two years. Their 2026 season was briefly interrupted when the team’s hauler caught fire on its way to the round at Laguna Seca.

Since those were all sprint races, Wickens would only have to get into or out of the car one time per race event. Endurance races are a new challenge, one that will mean more driver changes complicated by his paralysis. It will also mean more chances to win, and opportunities to win his class in the country’s oldest and most prestigious sports car events. That opportunity is an exciting one, the biggest step yet what Wickens hopes is a long road back to the top.

“I’ve worked incredibly hard for a long time to reach this point in my career,” Wickens says, “and I’m filled with gratitude for everyone who has helped me achieve my goal of returning to the highest levels of motorsports... I couldn’t be more excited to get to work and compete in my first full season in the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship.”

#4328. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: Why One Big Meal Isn’t the Real Holiday Health Problem

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In the classic Thanksgiving comedy Planes, Trains and Automobiles, hapless hero Del Griffith (played by the late, great John Candy) delivers an emotional riposte to Steve Martin’s uptight ad man Neal Page that stands as a beautifully dignified defense of kindness, empathy and self-love in the face of his own perceived shortcomings.

“You want to hurt me? Go right ahead if it makes you feel any better…I could be a cold, hard cynic like you. But I don’t like to hurt people’s feelings. You think what you want about me, I’m not changing. I… I like me. My wife likes me…because I’m the real article. What you see is what you get.”

For many of us around the holidays, particularly after a night of excess, Del and Neal’s exchange could read as our internal monologue – your kinder inner voice battling the internal bully who judges your every overindulgence. The jury’s out on whether the kind voice is ever as potent as Del’s is in that moment. But it should be, because when it comes to your health around the holidays, the bully has usually got it wrong.

The truth is, for most of us, one day of immoderation during Thanksgiving is unlikely to matter in the grand scheme. As such, you would do well to avoid the litany of holiday season health myths out there, many of which seem hell-bent on punishing you for taking a day off:

Like all misinformation, these kinds of medical myths are loud and tend to die hard, but they almost always trade on quick fixes that target the wrong thing.

A 2020 review of 23 observational studies found that most showed significant weight gain during festive periods, averaging roughly a pound and a half. One of the original studies, a landmark NIH study from 2000, found that much of that weight tends to stick around. So the question is not what you ate on Thanksgiving Thursday and how quickly you can “undo the damage,” but rather whether the extended holiday season becomes a two-month period where your healthy routine goes out the window. Some things to look out for on that front:

None of this is a free pass for everyone. If you manage a health condition, you likely have less margin for error, even when talking about a single meal or a drink. Critical factors include timing, sodium intake, alcohol intake, and missed medication. A few non-exhaustive examples:

Whatever condition you’re managing, the move for all of them remains the same – be prepared. Check your plan with your care team before the holiday, not after, and call them if something feels off afterward.

Technically, feeling good on Black Friday starts on Thursday. A short and light walk after a feast can help smooth out post-meal blood sugar – the earlier the better, ideally within an hour of eating. Staying upright for a couple of hours to help with digestion, particularly if you’re prone to reflux, is also a great idea. If you’re on medication, remember to take it on time. And, at the risk of sounding prudish, and this goes for everyone: try to get to bed at a sensible hour.

Above all else, Thanksgiving is a holiday built around gratitude and kindness, so channel your inner Del Griffith and remember to be both grateful and kind, to yourself and to those around you – evidence suggests that’s also good for your health.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4325. New York Just Made It Harder for Automakers to Put Car Features Behind a Paywall

A new law takes aim at subscription fees for features already built into your vehicle, but automakers can still charge for certain services.

These days, the average new car payment in America is over $800 a month. With a payment like that, the last thing you want is to pay even more to access all of your car’s features. The state of New York is now taking steps to ensure that won’t happen; however, like most things in life, there are exceptions.

On Monday, November 23, New York governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation restricting automakers and dealers from charging consumers subscription fees to access certain features already installed in their vehicles. Essentially, if the hardware necessary to operate a feature is already installed in the vehicle, and activating that feature doesn't require continued support or expense on the part of the automaker, dealer, or third-party service provider, it cannot be put behind a subscription paywall.

A few years ago, BMW faced backlash in Europe for charging a monthly fee in order to enjoy heated seats. BMW has since backed away from that plan, and under this new legislation, that subscription approach would no longer be legal. According to a report by the New York Post, companies that violate this new law will face a $250 fine per subscription.

However, this doesn’t mean that New Yorkers can wave goodbye to all automotive-related subscription services; automakers can still charge for navigation updates, satellite radio, infotainment services, in-car Wi-Fi, roadside assistance, and certain connected vehicle services. Also, software-dependent driver-assistance and automated driving features like Tesla’s Full Self-Driving and General Motors’s Super Cruise are also exempt, meaning motorists shouldn't expect their hands-free highway driving subscriptions to suddenly become cost-free too.

Automakers and third-party companies have about 90 days to get into compliance before the law takes effect on February 27, 2027. It will be interesting to see if other states will follow New York’s lead, but the bigger question is if automakers will simply begin charging more for optional equipment at the time of purchase.

#4324. Two-Thirds of Dementia Content On TikTok Is Misleading, Researchers Say

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new survey suggests that about two-thirds of dementia advice videos on TikTok are misleading

Of the videos examined, the analysis shows that nearly half contained inaccurate and potentially damaging information.

The researchers say that approximately 44% of TikTok creators who share dementia content lack credibility and appropriate qualifications.

Although misleading dementia content may appear on other social media platforms, this research examined only TikTok content, warranting further investigation.

The survey was commissioned by Homewatch Caregivers and has not been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

A spokesperson for TikTok told Healthline that if health-related content is potentially harmful, it is flagged for removal. The spokesperson added that 99.6% of misinformation deemed violative was proactively removed from the platform in 2026.

The spokesperson added that TikTok relies on fact-checking and guidance from public health authorities to help assess the accuracy of content. The platform may also apply warning labels to content that cannot be verified as accurate.

Looking to social media for health information is not uncommon. A recent poll reports that 31% of adults in the United States use social media at least once a month to look for health information and advice.

Experts advise seeking information about dementia from trusted sources, such as a primary care doctor and organizations like the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and the Alzheimer’s Association, rather than social media, where content creators who share advice often lack expertise.

“It’s normal to want answers quickly when you’re caring for someone living with dementia, and a short video from someone who seems to know what they’re talking about can be really convincing,” said lead researcher Jennifer Winarski, senior manager of care operations and quality for Homewatch CareGivers.

“Despite there being some genuinely helpful information out there, you don’t always know whether it’s backed by medical evidence, so we wanted to bring our own expertise to uncover whether popular TikToks can be trusted,” she told Healthline. “We hope our report will encourage people to be a bit more careful about what they act on.”

For the survey, researchers selected a sample of 500 of the most-watched dementia-related videos on TikTok with hashtags such as:

Researchers then transcribed the video data to assess its accuracy.

The researchers found that two-thirds (66.4%) of the popular TikTok videos contained misleading information. Of those videos, about half (47.6%) contained potentially damaging misleading dementia information.

“It’s clear that many of the creators mean well, but much of what we saw was personal opinion rather than proven information, and in a few cases, general good health tips were presented as if they were specifically helpful for individuals living with dementia,” Winarski said.

“If families act on that, they could end up spending time and money on things that won’t help — and in the worst of cases, it could delay getting the support their loved one really needs,” she added.

Dung Trinh, MD, an internist for MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of the Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, said it’s important to be aware of the volume of misleading dementia information on social media. Trinh was not involved in this survey.

Some people may be making decisions about their health based on incomplete, misleading, or incorrect information, he said.

“For example, someone might see a video claiming that a particular supplement can reverse Alzheimer’s disease or that certain memory problems automatically mean someone has dementia,” Trinh said.

“These messages can lead to unnecessary fear, false reassurance, wasted money, or delays in getting a proper diagnosis.”

“We are entering an exciting era in Alzheimer’s care, with advances in blood-based biomarkers, earlier detection, and treatments that may slow disease progression in appropriately selected patients,” Trinh continued.

“Getting an accurate diagnosis and receiving timely medical guidance are becoming increasingly important.”

The researchers examined the content creators behind the TikTok videos included in their analysis. They found that 44% of video creators behind the misleading videos had no relevant qualifications.

Rehan Aziz, MD, vice chair of education in the Department of Psychiatry at Hackensack Meridian Jersey Shore University Medical Center and associate professor of psychiatry and neurology at the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine in New Jersey, said that content creators offering dementia advice should have relevant qualifications. Aziz wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Start by looking at the creator’s profile for a full name and a specific credential, such as MD, DO, PhD, or RN, along with a specialty,” Aziz told Healthline.

“For dementia, the most relevant experts include neurologists, geriatric psychiatrists, geriatricians, neuropsychologists, and nurses, including advanced practice nurses, or social workers who specialize in dementia care.”

“You can confirm a doctor’s license through your state’s licensing board website and check board certification at certificationmatters.org,” Aziz said.

As of 2020, more than 55 million people worldwide were living with dementia — a neurological condition that negatively affects the brain. Researchers predict this number will hit 78 million by 2030.

The increase in the number of people seeking dementia content online is a reflection of this trend.

When looking for accurate dementia information and guidance, Nestor Beltre, MD, a neurologist with Baptist Health Kenneth C. Griffin Neuroscience Institute, part of Baptist Health South Florida, said a great first step is to speak with their primary care physician. Beltre wasn’t involved in the survey.

“Memory changes can occur for many different reasons, and some causes, including vitamin deficiencies, depression, and certain medical conditions, may be treatable,” he told Healthline.

“Early evaluation can help identify what may be contributing to these changes and determine the most appropriate next steps. Depending on the individual’s symptoms, a neurologist, psychiatrist, or neuropsychologist can provide further evaluation and guidance,” Belter continued.

Beltre advised turning to trusted resources such as the Alzheimer’s Association and the National Institute on Aging, which can increase public understanding of memory-related conditions and available treatment options.

“The most important message is that patients and families have resources available to help them better understand and manage cognitive health,” he said.

#4322. Stellantis Is Ending Factory WEC Racing, While Promising More Performance Cars

Stellantis is also withdrawing from Formula E as part of efforts to redirect racing expertise toward the likes of Alfa Romeo and Maserati.

Alfa Romeo and Maserati each have plenty of history they can leverage. Getting American buyers excited to snap up what's current or excited about what’s next has proven much harder, though. Now, a retreat by Stellantis from motorsport could give both brands the engineering attention they need.

On November 23, Stellantis announced that it was ending its participation in the World Endurance Championship at the end of this year; next year, it'll end its efforts in Formula E once the season is over. Its new priorities are customer racing and high-performance vehicle development. Alfa Romeo and Maserati are explicitly named as beneficiaries of that expertise.

Perhaps most notably, Stellantis intends to retain and redeploy affected employees, including into performance-car development. That could put people accustomed to solving problems at the highest end of motorsport into roles where they help customers enjoy their cars on public roads.

There's certainly plenty for these brands to do on that front. Alfa Romeo sold just 2316 vehicles in the United States through September, down 52 percent from the same period last year. Its third-quarter total was 569 cars across the Giulia, Stelvio, and Tonale. Whatever affection Americans might have for the badge, it isn’t translating into much showroom traffic.

Maserati, meanwhile, has fresh material to work with; its updated North American lineup includes a 385-hp Grecale V-6, and 582-hp Trofeo versions of the GranTurismo and GranCabrio. Those are solid offerings, but when it comes to marketing, there's plenty of room for the brand to grow.

Of course, there’s a sizable financial caveat: Stellantis hasn’t disclosed expected savings from the withdrawals or promised an accompanying increase in, for example, American marketing spending. It reported a €453 million ($497 million) net loss and negative industrial free cash flow of roughly €4 billion ($4.4 billion) in the third quarter. Any freed-up cash will have plenty of competing demands. That said, it's great to see that Stellantis directly emphasizing that the end of the WEC and Formula E programs will mean more resources go to Alfa and Maserati production cars—and “high-performance models” at that.

#4321. GLP-1s Like Ozempic May Boost Brain Health, But Can They Lower Dementia Risk?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 medications have transformed obesity and type 2 diabetes treatment. Now, researchers are investigating whether the effects of this blockbuster class of drugs extend beyond weight loss and affect brain health.

A comprehensive new review published on November 5 in the journal Science evaluated the current evidence on how GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide may affect the brain across aging, cardiometabolic disease, and Alzheimer’s disease.

The authors of the review suggested that GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Zepbound may offer brain health benefits. However, they were also left with the question of whether the medications act directly on the brain or whether better brain health is actually a consequence of improved cardiometabolic health.

Sheena Aurora, MD, vice president, Medical Affairs, Alzheimer’s Association, who wasn’t involved in the review, told Healthline that more research is needed to better understand the effects of GLP-1 drugs on the brain.

“While research suggests GLP-1s could reduce brain inflammation, improve blood vessel health, and even protect neurons, much broader, randomized clinical trials on GLP-1s and brain health, including in people with Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, are needed,” she said.

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, mimic the GLP-1 hormone. Tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro and Zepbound, also targets a second hormone pathway called GIP.

These medications have been shown to produce significant weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic health.

This is important for brain health because obesity, type 2 diabetes, and vascular dysfunction are all linked with cognitive impairment and dementia. Insulin resistance and chronic inflammation may also link metabolic and brain health.

Analyses of large outcome trials and observational cohorts have suggested that GLP-1 medications may be associated with a reduced risk of cognitive impairment and dementia. However, randomized trials in diseases like Alzheimer’s disease have yet to demonstrate clinical benefits.

Around 200 preclinical and mechanistic studies have shown benefits for learning, memory, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal resilience, though results are heterogeneous in design and direction, so a clear consensus on magnitude and mechanism remains lacking.

It is also unclear how well GLP-1 medications reach the brain. They appear to reach certain areas, such as the hypothalamus, brainstem, and circumventricular organs, more readily than regions protected by the blood-brain barrier.

The report authors noted that some studies have shown that GLP-1 receptor agonists may reduce the risk of cognitive impairment and dementia in people with type 2 diabetes. This may be due to cognitive issues being linked to factors such as blood sugar, blood pressure, vascular health, and sleep.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline, “These findings are interesting, but like many of the other benefits associated with GLP-1 medications, a direct causal relationship has not yet been proven.”

“Rather, the benefits appear to be more closely tied to the reduction in obesity and better control of diabetes,” he said.

Aurora noted that growing evidence supports the heart-brain connection.

She cited new findings from the Alzheimer’s Association’s landmark U.S. POINTER study presented at the Clinical Trials in Alzheimer’s Disease (CTAD) conference November 16–19 in Boston, MA.

The research showed that the structured lifestyle intervention program also improved heart health risk factors, such as:

“U.S. POINTER can change those risk factors within 24 months, and better heart health risk-factor control was linked with better cognition,” Aurora said. “We’re also interested to see whether adding a drug like a GLP-1 to a U.S. POINTER-style lifestyle program improves cognition in at-risk older adults more than the program alone.”

To find out, the Alzheimer’s Association is funding the Prevention of Risk for Cognitive Decline through Combined Therapy (PROTECT-Cog) global phase 3 clinical trial.

PROTECT-Cog is a first-of-its-kind trial designed to evaluate whether combining a proven multidomain lifestyle intervention with a metabolism-targeting drug, like a GLP-1, can further reduce the risk of cognitive decline, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia in at-risk older adults.

Dung Trinh, MD, internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the review, told Healthline, “I often remind my patients that what’s good for the heart is generally good for the brain.”

“The brain depends on a healthy cardiovascular system to deliver a constant supply of oxygen, glucose, and other nutrients. Conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol can damage blood vessels, promote chronic inflammation, and increase the risk of stroke and vascular cognitive impairment,” he said.

“Over time, these changes can also contribute to the development or progression of dementia.”

Trinh added that while GLP-1 medications can improve several cardiometabolic risk factors, these improvements do not automatically translate into proven dementia prevention.

“Regular physical activity, a heart-healthy diet, adequate sleep, and management of cardiovascular risk factors remain essential strategies for maintaining brain health as we age,” he said.

When the report authors turned their attention to more stringent tests on semaglutide in people already living with early Alzheimer’s disease, the picture began to change.

Novo Nordisk’s EVOKE and EVOKE + Phase 3 Trials examined the efficacy of semaglutide in people with early stage Alzheimer’s disease.

The studies showed that while semaglutide produced changes in several disease-related biomarkers, it didn’t slow the progression of Alzheimer’s disease.

This emphasizes that fixing metabolic issues might prevent cognitive decline in someone with obesity or diabetes. But it might not be enough to reverse the damage in someone with established Alzheimer’s disease, where profound synaptic loss and protein pathology have already occurred.

The review authors suggest that future research on obesity and diabetes should also include rigorous and specific cognitive testing.

#4320. Inside the Hot Wheels Design Center

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 26, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Excerpted from HOT WHEELS: THE CREATIVE DRIVE: Imagination and Innovation at the Hot Wheels Design Center by Dan Bova and Freddie Holmes. Copyright © 2026 Mattel. HOT WHEELS™ and associated trademarks and trade dress are owned by Mattel. Reprinted by permission of Mattel Press.

State-of-the-art car garage. Museum. Mad scientist’s lab. Stuntworks. The most incredible toy store on Earth—Mattel’s Handler Team Center, the company’s design hub tucked away on a nondescript stretch of road in El Segundo, California—is all these things and more.

From a giant mural, Mattel’s cofounders, Elliot and Ruth Handler, smile down on the building’s front lobby, where life-size Hot Wheels vehicles appear poised for action, and wall art displays iconic Mattel playsets and characters from the company’s inception through the present day. Down at the very far end of the lobby, the Epic Loop screams for attention. It is an eleven-foot-tall Hot Wheels duo racetrack with side-by-side loops. Visitors are encouraged to re-create a game played by millions of young Hot Wheels fans by climbing a flight of stairs and sending a die-cast car of their choice down the competing tracks in a race to launch their car into a bucket that marks the finish line.

There’s speed (the cars reach what would equate to 297 mph at full scale), experimentation (do you go with a weightier or sleeker car?), and crashes. Lots of crashes.

The message is clear: This place is a temple of wild design and outrageous fun.

Push deeper into the 200,000-square-foot building (which once housed an aerospace company), and you arrive at the beating heart of the world’s most famous brand on four wheels: the Hot Wheels Design Center.

Every inch of this place is filled with reminders of Hot Wheels’ storied past, as well as the schematics and prototypes that map out its high-tech future.

Oh, and there are toy cars. Everywhere. Toy cars on tables, toy cars in pristine display cases fit for the Louvre, smashed-up toy cars piled in cluttered cubicles. It’s every kid’s and every collector’s dream come true—as well as a dream come true for the people working inside these walls.

The Hot Wheels die-cast design team sits together in a ring, their cubicles surrounding long tables that serve as a communal space for collaboration, display, tinkering, and sharing the occasional Friday morning donut.

Black light-blocking hoods arch over each cubicle, giving them the feeling of a custom car garage or the messiest kid’s bedroom ever. Within the cubicles, toy cars in every stage of design are piled up against keyboards, and the interior cube walls are plastered with pinned-up artwork, schematics, and toy racks.

Underneath one of these hoods sits Dwayne Vance, a longtime Hot Wheels designer who is now manager of product design and steers the visual direction of every graphic in die-cast for Hot Wheels. Vance has worked for other huge brands like DC Comics, EA Games, and Texaco, and his passion for art and automotive extends well beyond the walls of this place, from his creation and curation of art shows to his own book series, Masters of Chicken Scratch, devoted to futuristic and fantasy hot-rod artwork and designs.

An oversize rendering he created in the early 2000s of the Hot Wheels classic car Bone Shaker, with the word Attitude boldly emblazoned across the top, hangs over his work area. Unlike many of his fellow designers, Vance’s cubicle is neatly arranged and organized. “It helps me creatively to sit down in a nice clean space,” he says. Some of his favorite cars fill his shelves, as does his Matty Award.

Every designer has particular strengths, so when Hot Wheels decided it was time to breathe new life into the Custom Camaro, Vance was part of a small group of designers tasked with cooking up new concepts. “We wanted a licensed vehicle but with an extreme custom,” says Staff Product Designer Fraser Campbell. “Knowing Dwayne’s work, I knew he’d create something wild.”

As pens hit paper in a flurry of ideas, the designers soon faced a challenge not uncommon for Hot Wheels: the ticking clock. Campbell explains that when putting together a year’s lineup for initial concept review (ICR), where the cars get evaluated and refined to ensure a good overall mix before things move along to production, the designers need to fill in any perceived gaps—quickly.

“Several of us designers were going to be working on the Camaro, but the other guys got so busy that it was up to me to finish the project,” says Vance. “So, I was like, ‘Okay, cool!’ I got to spend maybe two weeks on the design—it wasn’t a lot. One thing we don’t have here is the luxury of time.”

But just like race car drivers behind the wheels of the cars they’re inspired by, Hot Wheels designers thrive under pressure.

Vance began where he always begins—sketching. “I usually just go straight to Photoshop. I have a monitor on my desk, and I actually sketch right on the monitor,” he explains. But the motor muse can strike at any time and any place, and in the case of this redesign, it hit Vance at thirty thousand feet.

“I was on a plane and pulled out my sketchbook and put down some initial ideas,” he says. He typically has a sketchbook within reach, but any piece of paper will do. “Sometimes I’ll draw a little piece of a car on a sticky note,” he says.

Whenever the muse speaks, he listens—and gives it a soundtrack with the help of a little music and his headphones. “I listen to a lot of deep house when I’m drawing in my cube,” he says. “It’s got good energy and is easy to draw to.”

For the 2023 Custom ’68 Camaro reboot, Vance aimed to commemorate the past while bringing it into the future, inspired by what he saw happening in modern muscle-car culture. Instead of trying to restore vintage rides to their original settings, he saw customizers on a mission to “make muscle cars beautiful again” with new engines, new suspensions, and new brake systems—“they were just chopping them up.”

Vance studied the work of boundary-pushing, high-end car builders like Hoonigan, and when he saw a ’69 Mustang that a customizer had retrofitted with an LS1 Corvette engine, a vision began to crystallize.

“I thought, how fun would it be to do that to the Camaro?”

He broke out the chop saw in his mind and went to town, cutting out body panels to reveal the exhaust system sticking out of the side of the car. He lopped off the whole front bumper, exposing much of the car’s underpinnings. He added a recessed grille with an air intake, and in keeping with the Hot Wheelizing philosophy of pushing the limits while keeping it recognizable, he stayed true to the Camaro’s signature headlight shape.

Vance also created a hood bulge that hints at the powerful engine underneath and bolted on vertical fins in the back, inspired by the Le Mans Prototype (LMP) race cars used in endurance racing. “The fins help these race cars with cornering, giving them friction so they can stay grounded and accelerate. I thought, let’s add that to a muscle car!”

He then hacked off the rear bumpers to expose the roll cage, which he says, “really did something ultra-aggressive to the car.”

When it came time to create the 2026 Custom ’68 Camaro for this book, Vance again engaged in some role-playing—but this time he stepped into the shoes of someone with a very different perspective from a cyberpunk racer.

“I put myself in the Hot Wheels collector’s position—I wanted something that really celebrates the brand and yells, ‘Hot Wheels!’”

To that end, Vance gave his punked-up ’23 model a sleek new paint and decoration job. The base color is a rich Spectraflame red; the side panels are emblazoned with big Hot Wheels flames; the hood declares Hot Wheels loud and proud; and the side panels and roof feature the number 68, a nod to the year Elliot Handler started Hot Wheels. Vance also added classic race wheels typically found on 1960s stock cars to complete what he calls a modernized classic.

“I want a collector to see this and say, ‘Man, I want this book, but I really, really want the car!’”

Dan Bova is a writer/editor guy who was a producer at Jimmy Kimmel Live, wrote a weekly humor column for the USA Today Network, and was a writer at Spy and other humor magazines. He interviews amazing inventors and innovators for Entrepreneur.com and hosts the Get a Real Job podcast. He lives in New York with his wife, two sons, and a completely bonkers dog named Clark.

Freddie Holmes is the deputy editor of Car Design News, and automotive journalist with over a decade of experience. He explores everything from classic cars to electric and autonomous vehicles.

#4318. The Improbable Success of a ‘Poky Little Motoring Show’

Top Gear’s worldwide fame was a happy accident.

Through the lens of time, the early part of the Aughts can seem like a simpler age when phones were usually dumb, politicians were sometimes smart, and families gathered quaintly around one TV set to watch the same program at the same time. High-resolution internet video and the streaming revolution were distant spots on the horizon. But the changing landscape unwittingly created the perfect conditions for an accidental phenomenon: a TV show about cars with an estimated global audience of 350 million, a broadcasting triumph that would be impossible to replicate today. Because the Aughts was the decade that seeded the improbable success of a self-confessed “poky little motoring show” called Top Gear.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

In fact, Top Gear predated this century, debuting on BBC television in 1977 and plodding through the Eighties and Nineties with sensible car-buying advice and cozy trips to steam rallies. The series added Jeremy Clarkson to its hosting lineup in 1988 to bring a bit of wit to what was still a fundamentally earnest format. In 1999, he left the show, and two years later, the BBC announced that Top Gear was going to be “rested,” a polite British way of saying “canceled.”

At the same time, Jeremy and an old school friend, TV producer Andy Wilman, who had been a lesser Top Gear presenter, were working on plans for a bigger, more boisterous car show called Carmageddon. When the pair pitched it to the head of the BBC Two channel, she liked the idea and agreed to commission the show with one proviso: Carmageddon should become a reboot of Top Gear. The fuse had been lit, but free­wheeling global success wasn’t the master plan. In fact, there was no grand scheme, only a vague hope to make a halfway-­decent show for audiences in the U.K. I know this because from 2002 to 2015, I was Top Gear’s script editor.

This, like so much of the show, was something of an accident. I’d worked briefly with Jeremy on the old version of Top Gear, and he’d liked my satirical car website, Sniff Petrol, but if I hadn’t bumped into him in a restaurant and been invited to “come in for a chat,” perhaps the opportunity would have passed me by. As it is, I went to see Jeremy and Andy, and I listened to their ideas, many of which sounded strange. A racing driver who couldn’t tell you anything about a car because he never spoke? A segment forcing celebrities to drive around a track in a low-budget grocery getter? An indoor studio for a car show? Hmm. But Jeremy and Andy are persuasive people, and I agreed to join nonetheless.

We auditioned a lot of people to co-host and eventually found Richard Hammond, a car journalist who performed an unremarkable screen test but then reduced us to hysterics with self-deprecating stories as he was walking toward the exit.

We made a pilot episode, which was a disaster, then a second pilot episode, which was also a disaster, after which point there was no time to try again because we had a scheduled on-air date. We’d go to the pub after work and sit there making despairing sighs and ask, “What are we doing?” We were not plotting world domination. Our biggest goal was to get a show out on time so the BBC didn’t have to broadcast reruns instead.

But we were allowed to carry on, and our first season attracted modest viewing figures, just passing the low target the BBC had issued. Back then, some broadcasters were willing to nurture shows and let them grow gently rather than demanding instant success.

Top Gear needed this patience because it often felt like we were making it up as we went along. In the popular consciousness, the show is remembered for Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, and James May driving malfunctioning cars across harsh and distant lands. But it didn’t start like that at all. We didn’t have James in season one (BBC management thought he was too similar to Jeremy); instead, a car dealer called Jason Dawe was in the third spot. We didn’t go abroad because we were a British show and thought we should film in the U.K., no matter how gray and rainy it might be. We didn’t put the three hosts together in the field until the fourth season, an experiment that yielded nuggets of gold. We never planned to create epic road trips occupying entire shows, until a journey across the Southern United States generated too much material to squeeze into a 20-minute film and was allowed to roam free as an hour-long special.

What we did have from the start was a certain editorial rigor. Jeremy began his career as a local newspaper journalist. Richard had a background in live radio. James worked on car magazines for years. They’d grown up in worlds that demanded quick thinking and an endless supply of ideas. Sometimes Jeremy would stride into the office booming, “I’ve had a thought . . . .” Sometimes we’d sit around, batting stupid notions back and forth.

As part of my job, I’d scribble down what we said, then try to hack the best bits into something workable. After that came the important part. Any idea, no matter how brilliant it first seemed, was then poked and prodded and dismantled to make sure it was as good as it could be. When we had a full episode’s worth of vetted ideas, I’d sit down with one or all of the presenters, and we’d write a script. For a solo track test, this would be detailed and extensive. For a three-header out in the field, the introduction would be tightly written to make sure our mission was clear, in our minds and to the viewers, after which there would be rough scene headings and perhaps the odd one-liner. As a production team, we’d plan situations and challenges that we thought would allow the hosts to run free with ad-libs and arguing.

Jeremy, Richard, and James were very different people with a love of cars as their common ground. We never had to fake their on-screen personalities; that’s just who they were. Jeremy, bombastic and attention seeking. Richard, excitable and a verbal sniper with killer one-­liners. James, often giving the impression that he’d rather be at home dis­mantling a motorcycle than forced to hang out with these two morons. The dynamic worked.

That such a poorly planned piece of programming eventually found itself a global success is down to the decade in which it was born, a time when people still watched the same show at the same time. One inadvertent stroke of genius was the BBC’s decision to schedule Top Gear on a Sunday evening, traditionally a quiet night on TV in the U.K. Among straight-faced detective shows and florid costume dramas, the hijinks of Top Gear—a nun in a monster truck, a bus jumping motorcycles, a man trying to destroy a To­yota Hilux in increasingly elaborate ways—shone like a beacon of eccentricity. The next morning, everyone could go into work or school and talk about it.

Ratings grew steadily. Then, during filming in 2006 for the ninth season, Richard crashed a jet-­propelled dragster. The show was paused while he recovered from serious injuries. When we returned, viewing figures in the U.K. jumped dramatically.

Global success came later, especially with the growth of YouTube and other social media. ­Suddenly anyone could clip out their favorite bits of Top Gear and make them accessible all around the world. An American gearhead called Alex Mills founded a site called FinalGear, where fans could discuss Top Gear and share BitTorrent links so people everywhere could download the show, if not entirely legally. Top Gear became cult viewing in countries where car shows weren’t trying to turn pickup trucks into boats and a three-wheeled car into a space shuttle. Which was, of course, everywhere else.

Also, the car landscape of the Aughts gave the show great material upon which to build. It was the era of the hypercar, and at its peak was that stats-heavy poster child, the Bugatti Veyron. But it was also a time when Subaru and Mitsubishi were slugging it out to make the best roadgoing rally car. Countless manufacturers were serving up everything from high-powered wagons to hyperactive hot hatches. Best of all, in the U.K. at least, secondhand cars were fantastically cheap and accessible, even old supercars.

At the time, living hand to mouth simply trying to get the show done, we didn’t realize how lucky we were, though I hope we made the most of the luck that came our way. The reports of ever-­bigger audiences seemed abstract and unbelievable. Only when it became harder and harder to find any country in the world where our filming presence wouldn’t attract a large and excitable crowd did we start to realize that perhaps this stupid show of ours was catching on.

Nonetheless, we rarely had time to rest on our laurels. Indeed, Andy Wilman actively tried to stop us from becoming full of ourselves by, among other things, stridently discouraging attempts to make our disgustingly shabby offices nicer. He believed we had a job to do, and that job was to make an hour of entertainment for Sunday nights on BBC television. The rest was an implausible-­sounding bonus. And perhaps by dint of not trying too hard to be globally appealing, Top Gear became a worldwide phenomenon of the Aughts and beyond. It really couldn’t have happened at any other time.

#4317. Trump says he ‘protected’ Musk in first term after ‘a tough incident’ – what could it be?

President Trump says he “protected” Elon Musk during his first term, and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.” He tied it to “a certain incident” that he called “a tough incident,” but he didn’t say what it was.

Musk had plenty of run-ins with federal regulators between 2017 and 2021. One of them could have ended his career as a public company CEO, and it’s our best guess.

Trump called in to CNBC’s Squawk on the Street on Monday. That same morning, Nvidia’s board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, and in its press release it said it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” before concluding Huang posed no national security risk.

Trump argued that the US needs to “protect our geniuses.” Then he brought up Musk:

“You know, I protected Elon in my first term. Very big. Elon was protected. I talk about it, and I’m proud of Elon. I love Elon. I think he’s great. You know, 80% super genius, 20% he has other problems. But I tell him that. But Elon, I protected. You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me. And, you know, a certain incident took place, which was, you know, a tough incident.”

It’s not the first time he has hinted at it. Last week, in a Fox News interview from Shenzhen, Trump said: “I helped Elon a lot in my first term. I helped him a lot. He was in big trouble.” Back in 2024, he told CNBC he had helped Musk “when I was president,” again without details.

On August 7, 2018, Musk tweeted that he was “considering taking Tesla private at $420. Funding secured.” It wasn’t. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had shown interest, but no deal or price had been agreed, and the take-private plan was dead within three weeks.

The SEC sued Musk for securities fraud on September 27, 2018. The agency didn’t only ask for a fine. It asked the court to bar Musk from serving as an officer or director of any public company. That would have meant no more Elon at Tesla, which lines up with “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me” better than anything else on this list.

And then it went away fast. Two days later, the SEC announced a settlement: Musk stayed CEO, gave up the chairman title for three years, and he and Tesla each paid $20 million, $40 million in total. Tesla added two independent directors and agreed to have a lawyer pre-approve Musk’s material tweets, but the SEC never fully enforced it. Musk didn’t admit or deny anything.

The SEC was run at the time by Jay Clayton, a Trump appointee.

There was a criminal side too. In September 2018, federal prosecutors in San Francisco opened a fraud investigation over the same tweet. It never led to charges, and the Justice Department never said publicly why.

The SEC came back in February 2019 and asked a judge to hold Musk in contempt after he tweeted Tesla production guidance without pre-approval. That one ended in April with an amended deal listing the topics he needed approval for, and no new penalty.

In May 2020, Musk reopened the Fremont factory in defiance of Alameda County’s COVID orders and tweeted: “If anyone is arrested, I ask that it only be me.” Trump tweeted the next day that California “should let Tesla & @elonmusk open the plant, NOW.” But the county was already working toward a reopening date of May 18, and a president doesn’t control county health orders.

There’s also the September 2018 Joe Rogan episode, where Musk smoked a joint on camera. NASA followed with a workplace safety review of SpaceX and Boeing, and SpaceX lives on federal contracts.

For context, Musk sat on Trump’s business advisory councils early in that first term, and quit in June 2017 when Trump pulled out of the Paris Agreement. That feels like a lifetime ago now that xAI runs its data centers on natural gas turbines.

Musk announced a take-private deal at a specific price that the other side never agreed to, and the stock jumped. It’s textbook securities fraud. The SEC asked to remove him from public company leadership, and two days later he got a $20 million fine, an insignificant amount of money for him, and lost a mostly insignificant title. For someone who’s now worth hundreds of billions, that’s a slap on the wrist.

The main remedy was supposed to be independent oversight. Tesla gave the chair to Robyn Denholm, who had been on the board since 2014, and the board has done what Musk wanted ever since: it defended his pay packages, approved new ones, and stayed quiet while the brand took damage. Denholm herself has sold tens of millions of dollars in TSLA along the way. The SEC got a governance fix on paper and nothing in practice.

Just imagine where Tesla would be if a product oriented CEO had taken over from Elon in early 2018. The company would have spent the last 6 years developing new models instead of betting the farm on autonomy. The Cybertruck almost certainly does not happen, at least not in its current form. Instead, they would have developed a more conventional pickup. We'd have gotten 2nd generation models of the X and S instead of them being canceled. Instead of a Cybercab, there would be a model 2 compact car people could buy. And there would likely be a Tesla van and a full sized SUV, possibly developed on the same underlying platform. Also, the SEC was trying to ban him from running public companies. At the time, SpaceX was still private. So, Elon could have still run SpaceX.

Trump likes to take credit, and he could be inflating his role here. But if the White House leaned on the SEC or the Justice Department in 2018 to help a CEO facing fraud allegations, that’s a serious problem, and someone should look into it.

The timing doesn’t help. He said it the same day he appears to have intervened to reinstate Huang as CEO of Nvidia.

So what exactly did the administration do in 2018, and what does Musk owe for it?
