#4288. Carnegie Mellon’s Buggy Is the 100-Year-Old Race Series You Never Knew About, But Won’t Be Able to Stop Watching

Race pits teams against each other to engineer a new vehicle every year that balances aero, handling, and weight, while enabling a driver to somehow squeeze inside.

Ever heard of Buggy? With a capital B? Referring to a specific type of racing? Neither had we, until recently—but where there’s racing, count Road & Track intrigued. Buggy, so you know, is a unique form of racing only taking place at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), and it’s been happening for more than 100 years. Similar to Formula SAE, students engineer, build, and drive the vehicles that compete in the odd spectacle. And yes, in case you were questioning how the buggy is driven, someone is actually inside that tube of carbon fiber.

To understand how this sport works from the car design to the track, Road & Track spoke with Caroline Kiesnowski, the head mechanic and driver for a team. Currently a junior in mechanical engineering at CMU, she broke down what it takes to compete in Buggy.

“Basically, the easiest way to describe it is you put a person in a tube, and you use it as a baton in a relay race,” Kiesnowski says. “You get pushed up two hills, you do a free roll where the driver is completely in control—they're steering and everything—and then you get pushed back up three more hills to a finish line.”

It’s incredibly competitive, with lots of teams vying for the win. Just like professional motorsports, each team designs a new buggy every year using experience from years past and new digital tools to refine the vehicle. The priorities are fairly self explanatory: you want the smallest, lightest buggy possible for being pushed up the hill, then for the downhill sections, designing a buggy with the smallest coefficient of drag and wheels with minimal rolling resistance is paramount. Speeds top out around 40 miles per hour, so these little vehicles are positively cruising at their fastest pace—especially considering their pilots are a foot above the pavement.

The students who end up piloting them are highly recruited, Kiesnowski tells me. Each team wants the smallest possible buggy, which means you need a small person to design the buggy’s body around. If you watch how a driver load into their respective buggy, you’ll quickly understand how tight the squeeze is and how much the design is centered around the driver.

While most of the course is straight or mild curves, there’s one rather challenging turn called The Chute. It’s the source of many crashes and spins, and is something students need to design their buggy around every year. Two layouts are widely used: one is the standard trike that positions two wheels in the rear and one in the front; while the other is the reverse trike, which, logically, puts two wheels up front and one in the rear.

They each have their pros and cons, but in general, the standard trike is thought to be a bit dodgier in The Chute. With only one front wheel controlling steering and turning, it’s a simple design, but ergonomics and visibility for the driver can suffer. Meanwhile, the reverse trikes most often use Ackermann-style steering, which increases complexity, but Kiesnowski finds it to be a better design for steering and braking.

“The steering question is interesting because of the nature of buggy,” Kiesnowski said. “It's in a sense, proprietary information; it's historically been super-secret about people talking about their teams. Some teams even have blacked out windshields, like reflective windshields, so you can't see their steering.”

Another challenge for the track is that said track is actually just a road, and it’s mighty bumpy. Kiesnowski recalls that teams in the past even designed suspension to give the trike a better ride, but it’s a rare design choice that adds weight to a structure you’re trying to keep as light as possible. And yes, there is passing, especially in the downhill roll section, so you could end up doing some proper wheel-to-wheel racing. As you’d expect, though, safety is the number one goal in this whole competition, so drivers have helmets, and there are regulations teams have to follow in building their vehicles to ensure the sport is as safe as possible.

As with any good motorsports event, I asked Kiesnowski about teams trying to bend the rules and regulations for an advantage. She declined to offer details, but still said there have indeed been instances of teams looking for an advantage beyond the book. (After all, the grand prize of pride and bragging rights over your peers is a mighty tempting trophy in college.)

The competition takes place every April at Carnegie Mellon’s campus in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. And while the engines are essentially members of the team pushing, it’s still a form of racing we can get excited about.

#4285. The Acura Integra Type S Is Now on Sale in Japan—As an Acura, Not a Honda

It marks the first time an Acura-badged car has officially been sold in Japan.

While it may be the luxury offshoot of Honda, Acura’s cars have never actually been sold in Japan in any official capacity. The luxury automaker has been focused on North America for almost the entirety of its four decades of existence, meaning that any Acura cars in the brand’s would-be home country are either imported or modified cars initially sold as Hondas.

That finally changes today. As of Wednesday, the Acura Integra Type S is now on sale in Japan, fulfilling a promise made earlier this year. In addition to being the first Acura to reach that market, it is the first variant of the new Integra to be sold outside of North America in any form.

Acura has been teasing the possibility of the Integra Type S reaching the Japanese market all year, starting with a production model conspicuously on display among Honda’s Tokyo Auto Salon offerings in January. The Integra was shown again at another Japanese show in February before production plans were confirmed in March. Now, Japanese buyers will actually be able to get their hands on the Ohio-built Integra.

The Acura shares an engine and many other parts with the Honda Civic Type R, but the pair diverge in a few key ways. While the Integra is softer and more refined, the Honda is sharper and more harsh. American buyers could pick freely between the two, but other markets have not had the option to do so until now. It’s good news for Japanese enthusiasts looking for a slightly different flavor of performance Honda—a list that includes noted Integra Type S fan Yuki Tsunoda.

Fred Smith's love of cars comes from his fascination with auto racing. Unfortunately, that passion led him to daily drive a high-mileage, first-year Porsche Panamera. He is still thinking about the last lap of the 2011 Indianapolis 500.

#4283. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

#4281. NIO targets 10,000 battery swap stations and $52B in batteries by 2030

NIO says its energy arm, NIO Power, will operate more than 10,000 battery swap stations and manage over RMB 350 billion ($52 billion) worth of battery packs by 2030.

That’s more than double the swap network NIO runs in China today. And it comes from a company that already missed its last big swap station target.

NIO shared the targets today at NIO IN 2026, its annual technology event, held in Guangzhou to mark the company’s 12th anniversary. NIO Power also expects to deliver over 10 billion kWh of energy per year through charging and battery swapping by the end of the decade.

As of November 11, NIO had 4,252 battery swap stations in China, alongside 5,584 charging stations, according to the company’s latest network count.

Getting to 10,000 by 2030 means adding roughly 1,400 swap stations per year for four straight years. NIO added 679 in 2024 and 681 in 2025. So the new plan needs about double the company’s recent pace.

Even this year’s goal of “at least 1,000” new stations looks tight. NIO had 3,729 swap stations in February when it celebrated its 100 millionth swap, which means it has added just over 500 since then.

There’s also some history here. At its 2021 Power Day, NIO committed to more than 4,000 battery swap stations worldwide by the end of 2025, with about 1,000 of them outside China. By February 2026, it had about 3,700, almost all of them in China.

The energy target is just as aggressive. NIO’s swap network had delivered 5.28 billion kWh in total by February, after roughly eight years of operation. The 2030 goal is nearly twice that every year, although it also counts NIO’s charging stations.

NIO’s swap network is tied to its Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) model, where customers can buy the car without the pack and rent the battery instead. That means someone has to own a massive fleet of packs, both in customers’ cars and sitting charged in stations. NIO says it wants to manage more than $52 billion of them in four years.

For context, NIO reported total revenue of about $4.7 billion in Q2 2026.

NIO has been moving the heavy capital off its own books. Under deals like its agreement with Zhongan Energy to build 500 swap stations within a year, partners own the stations while NIO handles the technology and operations. NIO Power says it has now co-built more than 900 swap stations with partners.

The hardware is also getting better. NIO opened its first fifth-generation swap stations in August, and they’re the first to serve all three of its brands. That includes the compact firefly, which couldn’t use older stations because of its shorter wheelbase.

NIO CFO Stanley Qu, who also heads NIO Power, presented the unit as NIO’s showcase for running a business with AI agents, using them to manage battery value, station operations, and energy efficiency.

The swap targets were only part of the event; everything else focused on NIO’s AI-fication.

NIO also launched NIO WorldModel (NWM) 3.0, the latest version of its driver-assist AI, which starts rolling out in December to vehicles with the Banyan, Cedar, Cedar S, and Coconut+ systems, pending regulatory clearance.

NIO says NWM 3.0 needs 40% fewer driver interventions than the previous version. It didn’t say how many interventions it started from, which makes the number hard to evaluate. It also claims a roughly 60% boost in drivers’ “sense of reassurance,” whatever that means.

The more concrete claims are about speed: NIO says overall vehicle control latency is down 54% and chassis control latency is down 78%, while training is five times more efficient.

NIO also unveiled NOMI Intelligence 4.0, a rebuild of its in-car assistant around an AI agent framework that can plan and carry out tasks on its own instead of following set commands. The first release, Cedar 2.0.0, will be filed in early December. Cars on Cedar S and Banyan should get it in Q2 2027, followed later by ONVO models.

Finally, CEO William Li pitched NIO as an “AI-native organization.” He argued the global auto industry is worth $7 to $9 trillion and that AI could add more than $1.2 trillion in value to it. NIO says it has deployed over 7,500 AI agents internally, with more than 2.9 million executions so far.

NIO’s swap network is real, and it works. The company passed 130 million swaps this month, and nobody else has built anything close at this scale. Tesla sort of tried battery swapping and quietly dropped it. NIO kept going.

BYD charges in 5 to 9 minutes. a swap takes 5 minutes. I don't know man. It doesn't look good for NIO.

But 10,000 stations by 2030 requires a build pace NIO has never hit, and its last swap target slipped badly. So we’d treat that number as an ambition, not a forecast.

The $52 billion battery figure is the interesting part. It shows what NIO Power really is: a battery asset manager that also builds stations. That only works if partners keep putting up the capital and the batteries keep earning money over their lifetime. NIO has been trying to get other automakers on board for years, with limited results – though it appears to be starting to attract more players.

And the competition isn’t standing still. Chinese automakers like BYD are pushing megawatt-level charging that adds hundreds of kilometers of range in about the time it takes to swap a battery. If ultra-fast charging becomes common, NIO’s swap advantage gets a lot thinner.

Battery swapping is one way to recharge in minutes, but if you drive an EV, charging at home on solar power is still the cheapest way to fuel it. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4280. A Change of Tune: How the 2000s Changed How We Listen to Music in Cars

From the CD changer to the iPod and aux jack, the decade saw audio options shift—for better or for worse.

These days, each of us is in our own little world. We’ve forfeited a largely shared reality and replaced it with an almost infinite series of more private universes. And I’m going to be honest with you: Results have been mixed. The seeds of our collective solitude were planted in the decades before, and the worst of it wouldn’t hit us until the years after, but 2000–09 was the era when the monoculture really began to fracture and fragment into microcultures. The great American mainstream was dwindling in the Aughts, a narrative expressed through our music. New technology changed the way people across the world listened. And as Americans, we in particular experienced this historic shift through our car stereos.

This story originally appeared in Volume 38 of Road & Track.

Once we shook off Y2K anxiety, the new millennium began as normal. Fueled by boy bands, blockbuster hip-hop, and, somehow, Limp Bizkit, the recording industry was flush in 2000. What was big was huge, and whether you liked the songs or not, you knew them. My main musical memory of the year 2000 took place in a rental car, on a drive up to the mountains with my roommates. The mid-size sedan had a mere cassette player, so we made do with the radio. On that October afternoon, some station played the comeback single from a band that hadn’t released a studio album in three years: U2’s “Beautiful Day.” We turned it up, we nodded along, and we were impressed that a band could sound this good despite having members who were now 40. Best of all, we shared the experience with however many strangers were also tuned in to this frequency.

As the Aughts progressed, I found myself sliding into my car’s CD slot fewer store-bought discs and more homemade mixes I burned using my iBook after downloading music from iTunes. It was easy, it was cheap at 99 cents per song, and it was as frictionless as a click on the touchpad. I recently found a box of these discs in my garage, and each one is packed with music I have not thought about since I put them there. These early-­Aughts songs left me no physical album covers to remember them by; the playlists were not yet saved for posterity on streaming services. They vanished.

Then there was the iPod. Other MP3 players predated it, but the iPod was sleek and sexy and held up to 1000 songs, which I swear sounded like a lot in 2001. The forward-thinking among us might carry a special cord in our bag in case we found ourselves in a car with an auxiliary input. Traditional radio stations suffered as we ditched the DJs and did their job for free.

Satellite radio launched an effort to fill the void—XM in 2001, Sirius in 2002, then SiriusXM in 2008, with hundreds of hyperspecific-genre stations on the digital dial. Satellite radio broke us in to the concept of paying a monthly fee to listen to music we don’t own, and Spotify and Apple Music would run with that idea in the decades ahead. Now we all have access to virtually every piece of music ever recorded, but who is guiding us through it? It’s chaos. I find myself longing for those days before endless choices, before Bluetooth or aux cables, when I’d trust a stranger to play something for me while I was driving. When I’d be on a road trip and an unknown station would fuzz in and play a country song and a public service announcement, when a human being in a studio said something that streaked on radio waves across the desert air, and we were connected, until the station fuzzed out.

Of course, I can still do that. But the convenience culture that has continued to creep in since the Aughts has conditioned me to pull out my phone, wirelessly connect it to the car, and put on a mix or a podcast. I actually have to remind myself that those days were real, when the radio was once our go-to.

I miss those times. The new stuff from U2 is pretty good, though.

#4277. Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."

By revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

#4276. Tested: 2027 Audi SQ7 Is the Punchier 3-Row SUV

Audi's twin-turbo V-8 makes plenty of the right noises, and a deft chassis makes it fun on a twisting road as well.

Audi is slicing its bread thin when it comes to three-row performance SUVs. Below the flagship SQ9, there’s now a 2027 Audi SQ7. It’s the SQ9’s doppelgänger, minus a few inches of length and wearing what will be a more familiar badge for longtime Audi buyers. This is the third generation of Q7 and, like before, it straddles the space between a BMW X5 and X7, or a Mercedes-Benz GLE and GLS. And thankfully, the S model marches on with a bruiser of a V-8 engine. Audi pitched it as the SUV for the “performance family,” which is a concept that may have lost a little in translation. No matter the 0–60 of your family, though, this SQ7 is more than adept at moving lots of people around in a fast, fun manner.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

Every SQ7 comes with Audi’s familiar 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 under the hood, and this version makes 90 hp more than the outgoing model. The numbers come in at 590 hp and 591 lb-ft of torque, sent through the same new, rear-biased Quattro all-whee- drive system that debuted on the SQ9. Shifting is handled by a ZF eight-speed automatic transmission, and Audi claims a 3.7-second 0–60-mph time, one-tenth quicker than the bigger SQ9. When equipped with optional summer rubber, the SQ7 tops out at a limited 155 mph.

Transmission: Eight-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

EPA MPG: 15/20/17 mpg (city/highway/combined)

The TL;DR summary? Refer to my Audi SQ9 review from last month. The dynamic experience of both cars is overwhelmingly similar. But there are some small but significant differences which are worth exploring in more depth.

Like the SQ9, the SQ7 offers an optional Sport adaptive air suspension that lowers the ride height by 0.6 inch, fits more aggressive anti-roll bars, and tweaks the tune of the adaptive dampers and air suspension. While the SQ9 I drove was not fitted with this suspension, the SQ7 I tested was.

As advertised, this optional suspension is indeed more dynamic than the standard setup. The big SUV went from, sure, you can drive it hard if you want, to, this thing is actually kind of fun. Of course, the 5.5-inch shorter wheelbase, a near-nine-inch reduction in overall length, and the 100-pound diet compared to the SQ9 does some heavy lifting here too. On the Sport setup, the SQ7 turned in more quickly and benefited from notably improved body control. Plus, power distribution is clearly more pronounced from the back axle than it is in the standard Q7 on account of the heavily rear-biased Quattro system shared with the SQ9. It’s still not as rigid or as hardcore as an X7 M60 or an AMG GLE 63 S, but Audi is moving in that direction with its sportier tune.

The SQ7 makes its V-8 soundtrack known to a slightly more obvious degree than the SQ9 too. This could be down to my slightly closer proximity to the quad-tipped exhaust from the driver’s seat, or minor improvements in sound deadening, but whatever the reason, it’s improved. The V-8 rumble and meaty rip to its 7000-rpm redline were like a luxurious dessert I never tired of taking bites out of. The new SQ7’s raw pace is improved over the outgoing model, with the extra 90 horses over the previous SQ7 obvious whenever I pushed.

Fuel economy is the big loser here. I looked down after 100 miles of California canyon road driving and noticed the trip computer readout stating 11.4 mpg. More typical driving will be better at 17 mpg combined, per the EPA rating, but expect this big SUV to gulp down the premium stuff.

There’s little to no penalty in ride when you spec the firmer suspension. The difference is so minute that it took some deep concentration over similar stretches of road to discern any penalty to comfort versus the regular Q7. If anything, there’s a touch of additional flintiness to the biggest impacts, which could just as easily be the fault of the 23-inch wheels and summer tires fitted to the SQ7 compared to the 22-inch all-seasons on the Q7. Whatever the reduction in comfort may be, the drop in ride height is worth it purely from an appearance perspective. With the Midnight Green Metallic–painted body (I know, it looks black) hugging the black-painted multi-spoke wheels, the SQ7 would make for a perfect villain car in a spy thriller.

Here’s where you really need to make the tough decision between SQ7 and SQ9. Are you planning on using the third row frequently? If so, don’t pass go, head directly to the 9. If you’re just in the game for a larger SUV and might use the third row on occasion, then the SQ7 is the one to get. The big difference isn’t necessarily in the amount of space for third-row passengers, but in cargo room with the third row in place.

Surprisingly, legroom in the wayback is identical between the two. But clambering into said space was much tougher in the SQ7 thanks to a narrower crawl-through gap behind the second row (available with a standard bench or optional captain’s chairs). Once situated, life is pretty much the same in both three-row Audis. The 4.2 cubic feet of reduced cargo space in the SQ7 will make it so that you won’t be able to bring as many goodies to the picnic as an SQ9 can carry, though.

From a driver’s perspective, the SQ7’s cabin is about as good as it gets in a modern Audi. The whole layout, from the screens to the center console and feature set, is identical to the SQ9 flagship, so you could consider this a junior flagship. Optional auto-opening and -closing doors can be had. The Digital Matrix LED headlights that are so astoundingly cool in the SQ9 come standard here. Bang & Olufsen 4-D sound (also optional) with exciters in the seats makes for one hell of an audio experience.

And if you like screens, Audi’s got ’em. The 11.9-inch digital cluster blends into the 14.5-inch central infotainment system, and the 12.3-inch passenger display comes standard. I wish there were more physical controls, especially for the frustrating screen-controlled air vents, but at least Audi supplies some buttons and knobs both on the steering wheel and center console.

Luxury accoutrements by way of unexpected or interesting material usage are plentiful. The carbon-weave trim stands out versus traditional glossy carbon fiber. Funky fabrics on the doors and contrast stitching are appropriately nice touches. Audi claims it’s trying to do better with how it presents its interiors by doing away with piano-black plastic, and while this effort is a good start, there’s still plenty to go around on the dash, steering wheel, and center console.

The approximately $19,000 you’ll save on the SQ7 over the SQ9 sure is a motivating factor for picking the smaller three-row. Its slightly better driving dynamics are another good one, but again, it’s all about priorities here. An extra-large family would be better served by the larger option.

For now, BMW doesn’t offer an X5 M60 with a V-8, and the AMG price match is the inline-six PHEV GLE 53. In other words, this gas-powered V-8 performance SUV has a little niche of its own for the time being. A Porsche Cayenne S is considerably more expensive to start, and the gap only widens when the option book comes into play.

There’s a lot going for this latest generation of Audi’s smaller three-row, and outside of some small digital quirks you need to get over, it talks a persuasive game. Audi nailed the powertrain with this V-8 and its rear-biased Quattro system. And despite the SQ7’s sporty potential, there’s little compromise when it comes to usability here. The styling is arguably a bit soft in spots, but it has far more attitude than the brand’s electric offerings thanks to an upright face and pronounced fender flares.

The rear-wheel steering does an excellent job of making the SQ7 drive smaller than it should. It comes standard and can turn the rear wheels up to five degrees in the opposite direction to tighten the turning radius or make the SUV dive into corners with the eagerness you’d expect from a much smaller vehicle. This, combined with lighter-than-typical and progressive steering from Audi, removed that sensation of excessive size from the driver’s seat.

#4275. Volkswagen’s new affordable electric SUV gets a sporty upgrade with GTI DNA

Volkswagen gave its entry-level electric SUV a sporty makeover with GTI-inspired performance. The new ID. Cross R-Line tops the range with added power and style, but there’s more to it than meets the eye.

The new Volkswagen ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany, starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.

While VW’s R-Line is typically just a style and equipment upgrade rather than a true performance upgrade, the range-topping ID. Cross version borrows its electric motor, battery, and chassis from the ID. Polo GTI.

The flagship ID. Cross R-Line model, which will go on sale in March 2027, will use the same 222 hp (166 kW) front-mounted electric motor with up to 290 Nm of torque, which VW said enables it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.9 seconds.

It will also use the same 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 266 miles (428 km).

The range-topping version comes with VW’s custom chassis technology, also used in the ID. Polo GTI, which includes an electronically controlled front differential lock, DCC adaptive chassis control, and progressive steering.

As such, the flagship R-Line model is 15 mm lower than the standard ID. Cross. The lower ride height and front differential lock help to improve traction, driving stability, and control, while DCC automatically adjusts to road conditions.

The 222 hp (166 kW) version debuts with an exclusive new Traction profile with different drive modes, including Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual.

While pre-sales for the flagship version will open in March 2027, the entry-level ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.

The entry-level version uses a 132 hp (99 kW) electric motor and a 37 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 195 miles (314 km).

The entry-level version gains “extensive” R-Line standard equipment, including R-Line style bumpers, vertical daytime headlights, and 19″ alloy wheels.

Other standard features include Volkswagen’s interactive ID. Light with LED matrix headlights, Keyless Access, Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), and a rear-view camera.

0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.9 seconds. Not very sporty : )

Inside, all ID. Cross R-Line models feature sports comfort seats, R-Line trim, and progressive steering as standard. It also gains the Innovision Pro infotainment package with the “IDA” voice assistant.

Volkswagen has yet to reveal prices for the flagship ID. Cross R-Line with the 222 hp (166 kW) and 52 kWh battery, but it will likely be closer to €40,000 ($44,000) when it goes on sale next March. Volkswagen’s ID. Polo GTI electric hot hatch starts at €39,995.

The new R-Line trim comes after Volkswagen opened orders for the standard entry-level ID. Cross last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000).

What do you think of the new VW ID. Cross R-Line? Would you buy one in the US? Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the entry-level electric SUV to the US, but it will launch the ID. Tiguan in 2027, which will replace the ID.4 SUV.

#4273. One More Than GT40: The Ford GT41 Le Mans Hypercar Is Finally Here

Yes, it’s about 41 inches tall. But that’s not really why it bears that name.

Ford’s return to the top class of the 24 Hours of Le Mans was finally unveiled during the Thanksgiving Day NFL game between the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, along with an official name that clearly evokes the company’s past success: GT41.

Of course, there weren’t 39 cars before the GT40, as that name comes from the fact that the car was 40 inches tall. The GT41, for what it’s worth is 41 inches tall… almost. Technically, the car is 41.7 inches from the ground to the top of its air intake, a dimension dictated by the current FIA regulations for the LMDh class. But GT42 doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.

And while the GT41 is based off the same Oreca chassis as used by the Genesis GMR-001 and outgoing Alpine A424 and Acura ARX-06, the car and team is a wholly internal Ford effort. “Everything that we’re building, it’s in-house,” said Mark Rushbrook, global director of Ford Racing, “It's the design, the engineering, the development, all the technical elements of the car.”

That internal approach particularly applies to the engine, which Rushbrook calls the heart of the car. The naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V-8 is based off Ford’s production engines, so much so that the block is shared with the supercharged 5.2-liter in the Mustang Dark Horse SC and F-150 Raptor R and is pulled straight from the line at the Essex Engine Plant in Windsor, Ontario. Assembled inside Ford’s dyno lab at the company’s headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, every part inside the racing engine “is designed by a Ford engineer,” according to Joseph Hendrickson, motorsports powertrain calibration engineer. “The engines are also tested on a dynamometer inside the same building. It’s a huge point of pride for us,” he said.

The final livery of the GT41 that will race at Le Mans will be revealed closer to the start of the 2027 WEC calendar, which being at Qatar in March. The car seen here features a camouflage pattern made of the Ford Racing wordmark, with Easter eggs hidden throughout that reflect the team’s pride as an American and Detroit-based automaker; look closely, and you’ll see an American flag, a bald eagle head, the Statue of Liberty, the Spirit of Detroit, and a football.

Until then, testing of the GT41 continues at several tracks around the world (and, as a reminder, Ford has no plans to run in IMSA or the 24 Hours of Daytona in 2027), while its new “Go Like Hell” ad campaign—directed by Zac Snyder and narrated by Matt Damon—will make regular appearances on your various screens for the rest of the year. Including this one, if you click on the video below.

Prior to joining Road & Track he finally put his engineering degrees to use as an EV analyst. His personal cars skew slightly oddball, including a 1991 Honda Beat, 2001 Volkswagen Eurovan, 1987 Alfa Romeo Spider, and 2007 Saab 9-3 wagon.

#4271. EU pushes back Tesla ‘Full Self-Driving’ vote meeting again, now set for December 15

The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned. The meeting is now December 15.

A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the new date to Reuters. The Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) has already discussed Tesla’s file at two meetings without putting it to a vote.

Two weeks isn’t much on its own. But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.

In late 2025, Tesla told owners the Dutch regulator RDW had “committed” to approving FSD in February 2026. The RDW publicly corrected it. The Dutch approval came on April 10. Tesla then pointed owners to an EU-wide vote on October 6, and the TCMV agenda for that meeting had no vote on it.

Even the new date took a minute to settle. Belgium’s Flanders transport ministry first said the meeting had moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified it’s December 15. Nobody has given a reason for the change.

And a meeting isn’t a vote. The committee can discuss the file again and push the decision into 2027. Elon Musk said on Tesla’s Q3 call in October that he’d be surprised if EU-wide approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.

EU-wide approval needs at least 15 of the 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU’s population.

Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval so far: the Netherlands, Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, last week, Italy, where Tesla has started the rollout. Using Eurostat population figures, we count those 12 at roughly 29% of the EU’s population.

Germany is the obvious next yes. Berlin got Tesla to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe and then cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in exchange for its support. That would bring the yes camp to about 47%.

So Tesla still needs France, or both Spain and Poland, to get over 65%. Not a sure thing. Sweden asked the EU in June to reject the system unless Tesla removed the ability to drive above the posted limit at all.

There’s also a catch for owners. According to Reuters, an EU-level rejection would invalidate the national approvals already granted. If the vote fails, drivers in Italy, the Netherlands, and the 10 other countries who are paying for the system today could lose it.

A two-week slip in a Brussels committee calendar isn’t too bad, but the delays are adding up. It’s December, the committee has other files, and nothing Reuters reported points to a problem specific to Tesla.

Article and headline should consistently refer to it as Tesla Assisted Driving as that is the name which Tesla has agreed to use in the EU. I think the other big question for EU approval is how easily can the driver avoid paying attention to the road.

We also don’t think most owners realize what’s at stake. If this vote goes the wrong way, the national approvals go with it. Italian owners who just got the system would lose it a few weeks later.

What would help Tesla’s case more than a new name and a lower speed cap is data. The RDW still hasn’t published its test results, and Tesla has never released disengagement data in Europe or anywhere else. Governments on the fence, like Sweden, want to see evidence the system is safe, not a rebrand.

December 15 is the next date to watch. Does Tesla walk into that room with Germany, France, or Spain on board, or does this slide into 2027?

#4269. Driven: 2027 Audi Q7 and SQ7 SUVs Muscle Up

Over the past two decades, if you were looking for an upscale three-row German SUV, the Audi Q7 or its performance-oriented SQ7 sibling was likely on your shopping list. Both have long delivered on style, family-friendliness, and luxury.

The mid-size Audi SUVs are completely new for 2027, but the automaker has been careful not to stray too far from a blueprint that has proved so successful. With this latest generation, the Q7’s design has been brought up to speed with the rest of the Audi lineup. That means softer edges, a more muscular stance, and a lot more digital displays inside.

While the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch. If you need more space, there’s now a full-size Q9 model that’s larger inside and out.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 10400

The Q7 does gain a sought-after second-row feature: optional captain’s chairs. Choosing the two-seat second row reduces seat count from seven to six, but it also decreases the risk of sibling quarrels.

Speaking of the cabin, we’ve complained that Audi’s latest interiors haven’t lived up to the standard set by the company’s earlier efforts, but the new Q7 represents a reversal of that trend. Granted, the models we sampled were well-optioned examples, but the interior materials are premium, and even the $72,295 base model gets genuine leather upholstery and real wood inlays.

Upgrade to a higher Q7 trim, and you’ll enjoy luxuries such as soft-close doors, a Bang & Olufsen stereo, and massaging front seats. The SQ7 comes in just one trim level, starting at $100,095, and it’s comprehensively equipped with only a few available packages, most of them designed to improve performance and handling.

Special attention has been paid to the SUV’s exterior lighting elements. There are a lot of them, and some are genuinely useful, none more so than Audi’s digital matrix headlights.

Not only do these high-tech headlamps deliver a shockingly bright view of the road ahead, but they also sense oncoming vehicles and will temporarily deactivate some of their bulbs to avoid blinding other motorists. A set of OLED taillights illuminate in different ways depending on context, with the intent to help communicate with other drivers: For example, if another vehicle is too close to the Q7’s rear bumper in traffic, the lights will illuminate with additional brightness as a warning to back off.

Other flashy features push into gimmick territory. There’s a light-up grille, a customizable taillamp and daytime-running-light signature, and a system that projects arrows on the street surface to indicate which direction the driver is signaling. Are blinkers no longer enough? Luckily, if you don’t want your Audi lighting up like a Christmas tree, some of these features can be deactivated via the Q7’s infotainment system.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 10400

Speaking of infotainment, there are a lot of screens inside the Q7. A large infotainment touchscreen is expected, surely, but there’s also a digital gauge display, a passenger’s display, and an optional head-up display.

While the previous-generation Q7 offered a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four as standard with a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 as an upgrade, the 2027 model ditches the four-banger altogether, making a V-6 standard. This version’s six—a turbo 2.9-liter—packs 429 horsepower, a 94-hp advantage over the outgoing model.

A twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 has always powered the SQ7, and the new generation is no different. It also gets more power, jumping from 500 horsepower in 2026 to 591 horsepower in 2027.

Acceleration is plentiful in the Q7, which makes quick work of highway passing maneuvers and will beat most regular traffic off the line with a quick stab of the throttle. Audi estimates a 4.8-second 60-mph time.

The SQ7 is another animal altogether. While both SUVs have launch control, using it in the SQ7 results in a giggle-inducing run to highway speeds. Audi wagers a 60-mph run would take just 3.7 seconds. The V-8’s muted burble is a bonus.

Confident and predictable handling, an Audi touchstone, remains the default. While all Q7s come with Balanced, Dynamic, and Comfort drive modes, those with the optional air-spring suspension benefit most, with each mode delivering noticeably different ride qualities. SQ7s get air springs as standard but can be optioned with a sport-tuned version of the system, which lowers the ride height 1.2 inches in Dynamic mode and firms everything up to the max.

SQ7 models also feature a retuned all-wheel-drive system with more rear bias. Unlike previous Audi performance SUVs, which were short on driving drama, the new SQ7’s more fun-loving nature shines on twisty roads with that newfound rear-end boogie. Our test drive took us down some of northern California’s twistiest roads, and both SUVs proved entertaining and luxurious.

With this new generation, Audi has boosted the Q7 and SQ7’s swank factor. It has modernized their styling without introducing a new polarizing design language while adding options buyers want. Retaining the Q7’s just-right size and keeping the focus on refined, performance-oriented road manners is the hedge that will keep it near the top of the shopping list of enthusiast drivers who need family-sized space.

#4267. NASA's powerful Moon rocket engine roars through a dramatic 200-second test

NASA has successfully completed another powerful rocket engine test as the agency prepares for future Artemis missions that will return astronauts to the Moon and lay the groundwork for human exploration of Mars.

On November 18, engineers fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 at the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA's Stennis Space Center, located near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The developmental engine ran for its full scheduled duration of three minutes and 20 seconds (200 seconds).

Although this particular engine is not intended for spaceflight, the successful test will provide NASA and its primary contractor, L3Harris Technologies, with valuable performance data. Engineers will use the results to improve the power, efficiency, and reliability of RS-25 engines designed for upcoming Artemis missions.

Powerful RS-25 Engines Will Help Send Astronauts Back to the Moon

NASA is preparing for Artemis IV, a mission scheduled for 2028 that aims to land astronauts on the lunar surface. The mission will launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, using the massive Space Launch System (SLS) rocket to carry astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft.

Artemis IV represents an important step toward NASA's larger ambitions. The agency plans to explore the Moon's South Pole, establish a sustained human presence on the lunar surface, and develop the experience and technologies needed for the first crewed journey to Mars.

The RS-25 engines play a crucial role in making these missions possible. Each SLS rocket uses four of the engines, which together generate up to 2 million pounds of thrust to help propel the spacecraft off the launchpad and into space.

Before any RS-25 engine is cleared for flight, it must undergo testing at NASA's Stennis Space Center to verify that it can perform reliably under the extreme conditions of a rocket launch.

These tests are carried out by specialists from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions, working together to ensure the engines are ready to power future journeys beyond Earth.

#4265. Ford Has A Dedicated Battery Abuse Team. It Obsesses Over How Cells Fail

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Electric vehicle batteries live a harder life than the ones in your phone or laptop. They spend most of their time outdoors, deal with extreme heat and cold, and can take a beating from road debris and potholes.

That means for battery makers, engineering for durability is a priority right up there with energy density and charging speed. And to make sure its cells can handle the abuse of daily life as an EV, Ford has a team dedicated to understanding how batteries fail—and how to stop it.

“That team is 100% focused on battery abuse, design, and testing as a function,” Wesley Thibault, the global chief engineer of battery product development at Ford said last week during a media roundtable at the automaker’s new battery plant in Marshall, Michigan.

Ford is new to the EV battery business. Last week, it started cranking out lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, using technology licensed from China’s CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. The batteries will power the all-important Ford Fathom pickup, which the automaker says will enter production toward the end of next year and kick off a new generation of vastly better and more profitable EVs.

Despite the licensing deal, Ford officials said they were involved in developing the batteries from the outset, with a focus on durability.

The job is not as simple as it sounds. The battery abuse team isn’t tasked with destroying fully made cells and then finding ways to make them indestructible. Instead, Thibault said, it is involved in the design process from the start.

“They want to understand down to the physics level, how a cell fails and why, and when it does fail, how we can prevent it from creating harm to the occupants,” he said.

Quality operator at Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan.

For example, the team measures how cells vent, a crucial process that keeps batteries from catching fire or damaging themselves when they overheat. When temperatures inside a cell get too high, the electrolyte, the liquid chemical that shuttles electrons between the anode and cathode, gets hot and releases gases.

If those gases stay trapped, they can cause short circuits or thermal runaway, so they need to escape in a controlled way. Thibault said his team can measure all of this analytically—using computer models—before the cells are validated.

Production adds another layer of scrutiny. At various stages, the materials inside the cell, as well as the finished cell itself, go through thousands of quality checks, Ford engineers said. Those include CT scans, X-ray machines, lasers, camera inspections, and AI systems.

For example, when the anode slurry is coated onto a copper foil, every millimeter is scanned by lasers for wrinkles and other anomalies. All employees have the ability to pause production if they spot any problems.In case of any issues, they quarantine the cells affected during a specific time period. Ford also claimed that impacted components can be traced all the way from production to the vehicle they end up in.

To be sure, not all of this is unique to Ford. Strict quality checks like these are common among major battery makers, who all aim to minimize scrap rates for costly batteries and maximize the amount of material that actually gets sold.

Ford engineer operating a winding machine, which brings together the anode and cathode, adding a separator in between.

Ford continuously tests the manufacturing process in other ways, too. Engineers said they intentionally feed damaged components and cells—which they call “red rabbits”—into the production machinery to confirm the quality systems catch them and are working as intended.

When cells are almost ready, they’re blasted with helium gas to check for leaks. Once a pack is assembled, it’s mounted on a hydraulic shaker that mimics thousands of miles and years of real-world road use. The shaker can twist, dive, squat, contort, yaw, and replicate the other movements of a car, putting the pack through everything it would see on the road.

Ford’s EV batteries have fared well, by and large. High-mileage Mach-Es with 100,000 or even 200,000 miles on the odometer show little range loss compared to their original capacity, according to data the company released this month.

On the other hand, Ford’s emphasis on battery quality isn’t exactly surprising. The company has grappled with high warranty costs in recent years. And both the Mustang Mach-E and the F-150 Lightning have had issues linked to their high-voltage batteries. Some early Mach-Es were recalled because their battery contactors would overheat during DC fast-charging. A small number of Lightnings were recalled in 2023 due to defective battery cells.

Ford will want to avoid any similar quality issues as it rolls out the high-stakes Fathom, which it hopes will outsell its previous EVs and set the stage for an electric comeback. It will be years before we know how the Fathom's batteries hold up in the real world. For now, it looks like the company is pulling out all the stops to make sure things go off without a hitch.

#4264. The Suzuki Ignis is back, and this time it will be a low-cost EV sold globally [Images]

Suzuki offered a first look at the all-new Ignis, its first compact EV designed specifically for global markets.

The first-generation Ignis went on sale back in 2000 as a three- and five-door hatchback, and in 2016, Suzuki reintroduced it as a compact crossover.

After discontinuing the gas-powered version just last year, Suzuki is now bringing the Ignis back. This time, as a fully electric compact EV.

Suzuki revealed the all-new Ignis EV on Wednesday, deeming it the brand’s “first compact EV for global markets.”

The electric city car is based on the original Ignis and clearly draws inspiration from the e Sky, Suzuki’s first kei EV that debuted last month in Japan.

Unlike the e Sky, the new Ignis EV is designed for global markets, including Europe. Suzuki said the Ignis was developed under the concept of “Easy to Switch,” which, as you can guess, means it’s designed to make it easy for drivers to switch from a gas-powered car to electric.

To ensure it can handle urban areas and winding roads in Europe and other regions, Suzuki put the electric city car through “extensive testing” on public roads.

Suzuki fine-tuned the chassis and power delivery specifically for the different road conditions and needs of drivers in major global markets.

The global Ignis EV is also slightly larger than the e Sky, measuring 3,570 mm long, 1,565 mm wide, and 1,635 mm tall, with a 2,460 mm wheelbase.

It’s built on the same dedicated “HEARTECT-e” EV platform as the e Sky, with a single electric motor that delivers 90 hp (67 kW) and 98 lb-ft (133 Nm) of torque.

The Ignis also uses the same 26 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery as the e SKY. However, Suzuki hasn’t revealed driving range figures yet. Suzuki didn’t specify, but the LFP battery pack used in the e SKY is supplied by BYD’s battery unit to keep costs down.

According to Suzuki, the e SKY for Japan offers a WLTC driving range of up to 310 km (192 miles) and a “class-leading” AC energy consumption rating of 97 Wh/km.

Inside, the new Suzuki Ignis EV adopts a similar setup to the e Sky with a space-maximizing four-seat layout and a wide infotainment display.

Great to have a small car option like this. Let us hope it reaches open global markets at a price similar to the e SKY. That is about the price of the BYD Seagull in Australia today (US13-14k). Unfortunately the Seagull is growing in size so it would be good to have the option of this small Suzuki.

It seems likely it will be much more expensive in Europe as all EVs are.

Suzuki will launch the Ignis in Europe and other markets starting in summer 2027. Prices have yet to be announced, but the Ignis will enter an increasingly competitive segment of entry-level compact EVs, including the Renault Twingo, BYD Dolphin Surf, and Honda Super-N.

In Japan, Suzuki’s e SKY undercuts much of the competition with prices starting at just ¥2,120,000 ($13,500).

For context, the Renault Twingo E-Tech starts at under €19,490 ($21,500) in Europe and £14,745 in the UK. BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at around €22,990 ($25,500) and £18,675 ($24,500) in the UK, while the Honda Super-N starts at £18,995 ($25,000) in the UK.

Which compact EV would you drive? Let us know in the comments. Unfortunately, none of them will be coming to the US.

#4262. VW’s Cheap EVs Are So Popular, Buyers Face Wait Times Of Nearly Two Years

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volkswagen, along with its group siblings, Skoda and Seat, are facing huge demand for their small electric cars, which in turn is leading to wait times that are nearing two years in some cases.

With over 50,000 orders on tap already, the Volkswagen ID. Polo hatchback is one of the most successful models from the Volkswagen Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family, with the most affordable trim having wait times of up to 21 months in Germany, according to Spanish outlet Motor.es. That’s double compared to the 10-month wait times reported earlier this year.

Cupra Raval and Volkswagen ID. Polo production in Martorell, Spain

It’s a similar story when it comes to the technically similar Skoda Epiq, with over 80,000 orders since its introduction and wait times of up to 17 months for the most popular versions. The Cupra Raval, meanwhile, has amassed roughly 50,000 orders and has faced a multi-day production halt at the Martorell plant in Spain, where it shares an assembly line with the ID. Polo.

Together, the four models that make up the group’s affordable EV family, namely the Volkswagen ID. Polo, the Cupra Raval, the Skoda Epiq, and the Volkswagen ID. Cross, have attracted approximately 150,000 orders in Europe since their debut through the end of September.

It’s worth noting that while the cheap trims of all these cars, which start at around €24,995 ($27,300) in Germany, have put the Volkswagen Group in an unfavorable position, the more expensive versions are scheduled to ship a lot faster. The ID. Polo Sportline currently has a five-month wait time, while customers of the ID. Polo GTI have to wait roughly seven months.

The higher-than-expected demand has put all automakers at the mercy of battery cell suppliers. Currently, the Martorell factory that assembles the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval is working double shifts and has a daily output of up to 1,000 vehicles, but work has already begun to add a third shift, which would increase output to 1,200 vehicles daily.

The expansion is tied to battery production, and while there’s a factory nearby that can build up to 1,200 packs per day, it relies on cells that come from an external supplier. The same goes for the Pamplona plant that assembles the Volkswagen ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq electric crossovers. The two EVs share the same assembly line as VW’s combustion-powered T-Cross and Taigo, both of which bring in more money than their battery-powered counterparts.

A Volkswagen spokesperson told Germany's Automobilwoche that demand has increased “significantly more dynamically than originally expected” and that ramping up production “cannot be adjusted short-term to the same extent as this dynamically increasing demand.”

More employees are being added to the workforce, and Gotion’s new cell factory in Spain is expected to be fully operational early next year, which should help the automaker boost production without relying on outside help.

#4259. Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

The research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

"These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease."

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's

More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

Two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an important role in how the disease develops.

Microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is important for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role

"Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology."

The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

One of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the new research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

That distinction could be important for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments

"We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential."

The findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an important opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

However, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

The work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (BIG Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration."

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal

The research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.

"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he said. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science."

Funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.
