#4232. Electric Porsche Boxster Prototype Reviews Are Out. Here's What Critics Think

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

This is a big moment for the auto industry. Whether you're an EV fan, an EV doubter, or just a car enthusiast in general, the electric Porsche Boxster is a big deal. It marks the first time that a true, enthusiast-based roadster switches from piston to electric power. Its public reception will make a huge impact on the future of electric sports cars. Yesterday, that reception began. The review embargo lifted for the Boxster on Tuesday, so we can finally hear the thoughts of genuine gearheads and EV enthusiasts alike.

Before we dig into what critics think, it's important to note the tumultuous journey the electric Boxster has had. The will they/won't they discussion of whether Porsche would even build the damn thing, and whether an electric Boxster would be any good, seemed endless. There was also discussion of whether Porsche would build a gasoline Boxster alongside it, as that seemed to originally be the plan. But for now this is electric-only. So now that the electric Boxster is finally here, and Porsche has no gas-powered version to hide it behind, how is it?

The overall consensus is this: It's a proper Porsche Boxster. The Boxster might actually be the perfect sports car to electrify because its engine has always been secondary to its handling. A Boxster is supposed to be sharp, nimble, and thrilling on a twisty road. According to early reviews, this new "983" generation Boxster is all of those things.

"Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle," said Dave VanderWerp said for Car and Driver.

"The steering in the electric 718 Boxster is Carrera GTS good, obviously, since that’s where it’s from. Perfect weight, razor-sharp, with quick turn-in; it’s easy to place the car in and through a corner," Joel Feder wrote for The Drive. "It’s also extremely easy to kick the rear end of the electric 718 Boxster out and then control the slide through a corner. I imagine this thing will be a drift machine when given the opportunity without Porsche’s handlers watching my every move."

Autocar's Illya Verpraet had similar things to say: "The classic Porsche driving position and round wheel immediately sets the mood. At the lower speeds on our sighting lap, I didn’t immediately gel with the steering, which seems a bit too eager to bring the rear-steer into play, but as soon as we picked up the pace, it came alive in the way that the best 911 steering tends to: not crazy fast or heavy, but lightning-accurate and full of feedback."

Most reviewers also seem to note the Boxster's similarity to its gas-powered predecessor. It supposedly looks familiar inside (Porsche didn't allow photos of it, so we have to just take every reviewer's word for it), handles like a Boxster, and it feels as expensive as one.

"If you put a Boxster GTS 4.0 owner into this EV with the fake noise turned on, all they’d notice would be the slightly different interior and how much quicker the car is when they drop the hammer," said MotorTrend's Jonny Lieberman.

And it's said to be quick. Porsche didn't reveal exactly how much power the car has, nor which model it was. It could have been a regular Boxster, Boxster S, or even something spicier, like a Boxster GTS. Either way, this Boxster impressed with its performance, despite being a single-motor, rear-wheel drive car. That single motor pairs to a limited-slip differential, too, so it should feel pretty natural through corners for current Boxster owners.

Porsche didn't say what sort of battery powered the prototype Boxster, but we do know where the battery is. Rather than having a skateboard battery pack in the floor, Porsche stuffed it behind the driver, where the engine normally would be. That does two things. It gives the 983 the same sort of weight distribution as every other Boxster, while also allowing passengers to sit lower than a normal EV. The result is that the electric Boxster has a lower center of gravity than previous generations.

Overall, this new Boxster seems incredibly promising. It's fast, it's apparently very fun to drive, and it feels like a Boxster should. I can't wait to see what it's like when Porsche finally reveals it.

#4231. Can Pirelli’s Cyber Tyre Technology Replace Drive Modes?

The Cyber Tyre’s sensor gathers data in real time to influence a vehicle’s traction, stability, and braking systems. We trialed it at Las Vegas Motor Speedway.

After roughly 25 years of development, Pirelli's Cyber Tyre technology is preparing for a wider rollout. The tires use a sensor that looks a lot like a Dexcom G7 to feed temperature, air pressure, acceleration, and identification data to a vehicle's computers.

That information, combined with software help from Bosch, allows a vehicle to adjust its ABS and traction-control calibrations based on tire data. For example, swap your summer tires for squishier winter rubber, and a compatible car could recognize the change and automatically adjust how its electronic controls intervene, leaving you free to imagine a world where maybe we all just drove better.

See all results for used cars for sale near 06010

"This is one of the worst environments for electronics," explained Pirelli chief technical officer Piero Misani. The sensor, weighing just 13 grams, is bonded to the tire's inner liner beneath the tread using a specially developed adhesive and rubber housing. The process was developed using learnings from Pirelli's Noise Cancelling System, which uses foam inside the tire to absorb sound waves and reduce cabin vibration. The sensor must survive extreme temperatures, constant flexing, and the insane lateral g-forces that tires are susceptible to at over 200 mph. Engineers explained that its battery is designed to outlast the tire and enters a low-power sleep mode during extended storage.

The more inspiring part is what the car does with the information it gathers. As we found in our recent all-weather tire comparison test, summer, winter, and all-season tires perform dramatically differently. Yet a vehicle's electronic controls are generally calibrated around its original equipment, using things like wheel speed sensors that aren’t as close to the road surface as the Cyber Tyre. Instead, it identifies the specific tire installed at each corner, allowing it to use different wheel-slip targets. And with the sensor attached to the inside of the tire, the data informing those systems is closer to the road surface than ever.

We sampled the technology at Las Vegas Motor Speedway in two Mercedes-AMG GT63 S four-doors wearing Cyber Tyre-equipped P Zero MS all-season tires.

The first exercise had us pin the throttle through a corner from 40 mph using three different traction-control calibrations, all on the same P Zero MS all-season tires. The first, intended for ultra-high-performance summer tires, was overly restrictive, cutting power before the tires could deliver much acceleration. The second, calibrated for winter tires, permitted considerably more wheelspin, making the AMG easy to slide. Despite that setting being the most fun (and our favorite), Cyber Tyre delivered a happy medium, allowing more controlled acceleration without either extreme.

See all results for used cars for sale near 06010

This is where Cyber Tyre begins to make the case against selectable drive modes. The same car, wearing the same tires, just behaved three different ways without any mechanical changes. It's not going to replace the button that stiffens your dampers or changes your exhaust note, but it could eventually make some traction-related settings redundant.

The second AMG demonstrated ABS braking from 65 mph. With Cyber Tyre integration active, our stopping distance improved by 0.9 meter, or about three feet, according to Pirelli's instrumentation. That's not dramatically different, but still a measurable improvement.

Of course, these demonstrations weren't proof that Cyber Tyre can outperform a conventional system already calibrated for the correct tires. And the technology isn't smart enough to know it's snowing just because the tires are cold. But the distinction is that Cyber Tyre can give the car information about its tires without the driver doing anything. That could be super useful as tires wear, temperatures change, or owners swap between summer and winter sets. Pirelli is also developing tire-wear estimates using its sensor data, which could prove useful for fleet operators managing hundreds of vehicles.

Pirelli and Bosch announced their development partnership in 2024, and the technology has already appeared in vehicles from McLaren and Pagani. Pirelli executives say a substantially higher-volume application should be announced in the first half of 2027, with production expected in 2028. So it's possible this tech could arrive in models as common as a Ford pickup.

Pirelli is also investing approximately $1.2 billion to expand its Rome, Georgia, manufacturing facility, where Cyber Tyre-equipped products will be produced alongside conventional tires. By 2033, the company expects annual production capacity to reach six million tires and plans to add up to 1000 engineering jobs.

They also recently announced that China's state-owned Sinochem, formerly Pirelli's largest shareholder, reduced its ownership to 13.6 percent in November. The Italian government has restricted Sinochem's influence and specifically prohibited sharing Cyber Tyre data with entities connected to the Chinese government. Following those governance changes, Pirelli received U.S. authorization to market the technology here. Not that anyone was worried about a Pagani Utopia Roadster being a boon of classified information.

Cyber Tyre isn't about to take the Ford Bronco's G.O.A.T. modes out back to shoot them. There are plenty of reasons to let drivers decide how their cars behave. But after experiencing three dramatically different calibrations in the same AMG, it's easy to see why some of those decisions might eventually be better left to the car. Just make sure we’re able to fully disable them.

Austin Irwin has worked for Car and Driver for over 10 years in various roles. He's steadily worked his way from an entry-level data entry position into driving vehicles for photography and video, and is now reviewing and testing cars. What will he do next? Who knows, but he better be fast.

Volkswagen is moving back to more physical buttons, after suffering some backlash from its touch-button-heavy design. Mercedes also publicly recognized that maybe the world went too far with touchscreens. Audi, too, seems to be eyeing more physical controls. But it isn't giving up its touchscreen ones to do so. The company just patented a technology that lets it have its cake and eat it, too, but creating a physical button panel that can hide behind a touchscreen.

Unearthed by CarMoses, this patent shows off a little button bar, which is just a strip of physical buttons and possibly one knob that lives below the touchscreen. At the press of a button, or even with voice control, the button bar can hide away behind the touchscreen, for anyone who prefers a simpler looking cabin. Once the buttons are hidden, the touchscreen creates a duplicate set of icons at the bottom, so button functionality isn't lost while hidden.

What sort of physical buttons will occupy such a button bar? There seems to be a circular knob in the center of the buttons, so that will likely be volume. The flanking buttons could be for climate control, maybe heated seats, or perhaps even some drive mode buttons. Whatever they end up being, it will be nice to see Audi's with high-quality physical buttons again.

In the '90s, 2000s, and 2010s, Audi had some of the best buttons, switches, and knobs in the industry, all with satisfying, high-quality clicks. The current crop of piano-black plastic touch buttons in most modern Audis feels like a slap in the face for fans of the brand. So to see the return of some buttons in places where they can be easily memorized and adjusted without looking would be wonderful.

Obviously, Audi can't use physical buttons for everything. There are far too many controls and features in modern cars for that to work. There'd be hundreds of buttons on the dashboard if that were the case. But the main buttons, the ones you use everyday, should be physical. And the beauty of this patent is that it, if you like a more high-tech vibe, you can hide them away. With this patent, Audi gets to make both camps happy.

#4228. Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi said.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

#4227. Europe Gets This Tiny New Suzuki EV. It Makes A Mini Look Big

Suzuki left the U.S. car market in 2012, but it still builds the kind of small hatchbacks European buyers have long favored, now also powered by electricity. Its latest is the Ignis EV, a city car that measures just 11 feet 9 inches long (3.57 meters). It’s due in Europe in summer 2027, when it will face a new generation of small EVs from both European and Chinese automakers.

The Ignis is Suzuki’s first subcompact electric car developed for global markets, but its roots are in Japan. The company recently launched the e Sky there, an electric kei car that supplies the basis for the Ignis’s body and powertrain. The Ignis still has the typical kei proportions (it's tall and narrow), but Suzuki says it took the car onto European city streets and winding roads to tune the suspension and power delivery, making it more appealing to the people it hopes will buy one.

A 26-kilowatt-hour lithium iron phosphate battery sits under the floor of Suzuki’s dedicated Heartect-e electric platform. Yes, that really is what it's called. Up front, the motor, inverter, and reduction gears share a single compact assembly that sends 90 horsepower and 98 pound-feet (133 Nm) to the front wheels. Suzuki says it chose LFP for safety and longevity, but it hasn’t given the European car a range or charging figure yet.

The Ignis EV has a very tight 29.5-foot (9-meter) turning circle. Its overhangs are tiny, giving it a wheel-at-each-corner stance that looks unique while maximizing available interior room. The LED signatures at both ends take their shape from digital numerals, and the dark pillars give the roof a floating look.

Inside, a curve runs from the dashboard into the doors, with a wide display and a ceramic-inspired storage tray across the dash. Suzuki President Toshihiro Suzuki credits the company’s decades of building Japanese mini vehicles for its ability to provide a genuinely usable cabin in such a small footprint.

For decades, European brands had most of this business to themselves. If you wanted an inexpensive car that could squeeze down a narrow street, Fiat would happily sell you a Panda, Renault a Twingo and Volkswagen an Up. Chinese automakers see an opening as those buyers go electric.

Leapmotor brought the T03 to Europe through its partnership with Stellantis, while BYD adapted its Chinese-market Seagull for Europe and called it the Dolphin Surf. Driving the latter, what stood out to me was how well it drove, how little felt cheap, and how much kit it had for its sub-€20,000 starting price.

By the time the Ignis arrives next year, European buyers will have had plenty of practice shopping for small EVs. Renault has revived both the 5 and the Twingo as electric cars, and there’s also the related Dacia Spring. Volkswagen has the ID. Polo, Cupra has the Raval, and Skoda has the Epiq, and there definitely seems to be demand for them. In September, a major VW dealer group reported more than 30,000 orders for the ID. Polo and a waiting list stretching to ten months.

That leaves one big question for the little Suzuki. What will it cost? Consider the redesigned Dacia Spring. Dacia moved production from China to Slovenia, shared the electric Twingo’s underpinnings, and produced a car that starts at €17,900 in Italy. It gets up to 155 miles (250 kilometers) of WLTP range from a battery only slightly larger than the one in the Ignis.

#4226. Tesla’s Driver-Assistance Software Now Looks Like a Video Game

It’s called Reality View, in which the system’s new ‘follow’ camera angle records the real world around your Tesla and re-creates it onscreen.

Tesla is rolling out the 15th iteration of its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, and the update comes with some pretty impressive graphics. It’s called Tesla Reality View, and it’s exactly that, using the vehicle’s cameras to record what’s going on around you, then re-create the scene on the central screen accurately.

The intent is to show a visual representation of what the latest FSD driver assistance is going to do, as represented by onscreen arrows. Turns are represented, and the screen shows what parking spot the vehicle has selected when using auto park.

It all looks extremely slick, just like the real world rendered into a video game in real time. Tesla says the actual driving assistance has also been greatly improved, with an increased ability to spot and react to potholes, small animals, and road debris. The system also uses fleet learning from the trips other Teslas take on the same route, something Tesla has been doing for several iterations of FSD.

See all results for used Tesla for sale near ?

Although Tesla claims that this new iteration is 25 times safer in critical interventions, this claim isn’t backed up with provided data such as miles driven; it’s just Tesla’s claim thus far.

Users’ experiences since the rollout have indicated that V15 appears to be more cautious in certain situations, and in some cases a little overcautious. Posts on Reddit’s Tesla forum report a vehicle aggressively avoiding random items in the road and reacting to a road repair site as if it was a pothole. Other forum users point out that early FSD updates often are a little shaky right at rollout but more polished by the time the release goes out more broadly.

Our own experience with Tesla’s FSD is that it works flawlessly—right up until it doesn’t and the driver needs to take over. Tesla’s own literature notes that drivers are expected to keep their attention on the road. The pretty new graphics look attractive, but if you’re staring at the screen instead of out the windshield, FSD should theoretically automatically disconnect.

#4225. If I could only use one bike lock, it’d be this: FoldyLock Elite 110 review

I ride e-bikes professionally, regularly testing new bikes and biking gear. I don’t even own a car – I get around almost exclusively on two wheels. So when it comes to important gear like bike locks for my fleet of e-bikes, I’ve become pretty well-versed out of necessity. And after testing out the world’s strongest folding lock, the FoldyLock Elite 110, I’m more than impressed. If I could only have one lock for my e-bikes, it’d be this one.

Of course, the name of the game in bike theft prevention is to use more than just one lock, and I’m going to return to that idea at the end of this article.

But for now, believe me when I say that this lock is seriously good, to the point that it has become my new primary.

The FoldyLock Elite 110cm is identical in strength and security to the FoldyLock Forever 90cm that I tested a few years ago, yet is 20 cm (8 inches) longer, reaching 110 cm (43 inches).

The FoldyLock Forever 90 and FoldyLock Elite 110 are the strongest folding locks in the world, confirmed by the premier international lock certification organization ART. These are the only folding locks that have ever achieved a 3-star ART certification. The scale goes up to 5, but 4-star and 5-star certifications are motorcycle-level locks.

To make things even more impressive, the FoldyLock line achieved that ART 3-star rating three years ago, and no other lock company has matched it on a folding lock since.

If one independent and international lock testing association isn’t enough for you, the lock is also Sold Secure GOLD rated, which is just one step below Sold Secure’s highest ever rating for bike locks.

Again, more on that at the end of this article to get you to that last step for top security.

There are a lot of different styles of locks out there, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. But as someone who rides e-bikes every day as his job, I’ve come to the opinion that a strong folding lock has the best combination of maximizing advantages and minimizing disadvantages.

For starters, folding locks allow you to lock to larger diameter anchors that would be impossible for U-locks (trees, telephone poles, multiple fence bars, etc). They’re more compact than chain locks of comparable security, both in size and weight. They’re significantly stronger than cable locks (when made with quality materials). And they mount more easily to a bike frame than nearly any other lock style, as they fold tightly and usually come with a holster.

Yes, there are disadvantages too. The segments mean they can’t form as close to a circle as a chain, meaning the maximum size of the tree or telephone pole you’re locking to is slightly smaller than for an equal length chain. And they usually aren’t quite as strong as U-Locks made with angle-grinder-resistant materials. But for their size and convenience, they make perhaps the best single style of lock for the best pairing of strength and convenience.

Since I began testing the FoldyLock Elite 110, I’ve been living with it as my main e-bike lock. I test a lot of locks, and most go onto the shelf when I’m done as backups or to give to friends/family. But the FoldyLock Elite 110 has stayed as my new primary lock, and here’s why.

First of all, as I mentioned, it’s the strongest folding lock in the world, as confirmed by multiple independent testing organizations. So if you want the advantages of a folding lock, there’s simply none more secure than this.

But beyond that, the FoldyLock Elite 110 is covered by multiple patents, including the specialized protected rivets that prevent nut splitter attacks and that take out any squeaks or rattles that are common in other folding locks. The lock also physically locks into its holster, which keeps it both secure (no bounce-outs) and helps keep it silent during the ride. There’s even a coating on the hardened steel segments to protect my bike frame from scratches and resist corrosion during winter use (plus a shutter on the locking mechanism for additional winter corrosion resistance).

Basically, it seems like the company has taken pretty much all of the learnings from previous locks in their lineup, and applied those lessons to the FoldyLock Elite, making it a perfect combination of strength, security, and convenience.

As I mentioned, after my time testing the FoldyLock Elite, I can say for sure that if I could only use one bike lock, it would be this one.

But I don’t just use one bike lock. And I recommend you don’t either, if you can swing it.

We’ve long known that the best way to keep your bike safe from thieves is to use two bike locks. It’s partly for the extra security, and partly for the extra time it takes a thief to work on defeating two locks, meaning they’re more likely to choose a different sucker’s bike to steal.

I always recommend using two different styles of bike locks. Think: folding lock plus U-lock, or U-lock plus chain lock, or chain lock plus cable lock, or cable lock plus folding lock, etc. You get the idea.

My FoldyLock Elite is now my primary lock, and it allows me to lock onto just about everything on the street, from official bike racks to chunky utility poles. For my secondary, I use a SeatyLock Mason 220. This U-lock is actually one step higher-rated by Sold Secure, reaching that testing organization’s Diamond level – its highest level of security rating.

When I can lock both the folding lock and U-lock to an anchor, I do it. But sometimes, when I’m forced to lock to something wide like a lamppost, I lock the frame and rear wheel with the FoldyLock Elite 110, then lock the front wheel to the frame with the Mason 220 U-lock, as seen in the photo above.

That keeps both of my wheels and my bike locked. Despite there only being one lock keeping the bike in place to the anchor (lamppost), the second lock adds an extra layer of frustration for a thief and is likely to convince them to just choose the next bike on the sidewalk.

That’s why I always recommend using two different locks, and ideally of different styles. I believe the FoldyLock Elite 110 offers the most advantages, but its few disadvantages are offset by a secondary lock, such as a strong U-lock.

When it comes to mounting, I’ve got the holster mounted onto my fork using the supplied flexible mounting straps.

Normally you’d mount it to one of your bottle mounts, but I only have a single set of bottle bosses on my e-bike’s frame, and they are currently taken up by a water bottle holder (surprise!).

I found that despite adding 1.9 kg or 4.1 lb to the side of my fork, my bike still rides just fine. The advantage of a rigid frame is that there’s not really much change to the unsprung mass since everything is unsprung!

I love riding hands-free in the city, and it did take me a day or two to get used to the slightly altered steering moment, but I can still ride my bike hands-free even with the extra weight there on the side of the fork.

At some point I might shift the holster onto the rear rack or swap it out for my bottle holder in favor of a new bottle spot, but so far it’s working great there and hasn’t caused me any handling issues.

When it comes to value, I think the FoldyLock Elite 110 takes the cake here, too. It’s normally priced at an MSRP of $145, though it’s currently on sale for $119 as part of the Black Friday promotions.

As I said, I test hundreds of bikes and dozens of locks as my day job. I live and breathe bikes. The fact that this lock has become my go-to everyday lock is pretty much all you need to know about how impressive it truly is. It’s a pleasure to live with and use, which means that I actually end up using it.

#4224. Ionna Slashes EV Charging Prices For Thanksgiving

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Ionna, the EV charging network that ranked first in J.D. Power’s latest public charging satisfaction survey, has slashed prices at its stations across the country for Thanksgiving weekend.

The company, which usually charges an average of $0.40/kilowatt-hour, is now asking for $0.20/kWh plus tax at all its DC fast charging stations in the United States. That’s a 50% discount, and drivers don’t have to do anything special to get it—just plug in and pay, either through the automaker’s official smartphone app, the on-site payment terminals, or the Presto app for Tesla owners who want to enjoy the Autocharge function.

For long-distance travel, the slashed charging rates can make a big difference. A single 50-kilowatt-hour session that used to cost $20 will now be just $10 plus tax, but seeing how many people are traveling across the country these days, multiple sessions will be necessary, driving the cost savings even further.

And it’s not like the cost reduction comes with any strings attached. Ionna uses 400-kilowatt chargers from Alpitronic exclusively, so there’s plenty of wiggle room for even the most power-hungry EVs out there. What’s more, many stalls have dual cords for each port, with a CCS2 connector and a NACS connector, so charging adapters aren’t needed at most locations.

Separately, Ionna has discounts for several automakers, including Mercedes-Benz, BMW, General Motors, and Stellantis.

The charging operator installed its first stalls in 2024, and it has wasted no time expanding its footprint quickly. On its second anniversary, Ionna celebrated by opening its 100th site, and the company now has 229 sites and nearly 1,900 ports nationwide, according to the Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center (AFDC). Still, the charging network is not slowing down, with dozens of locations under construction and plans to introduce 500-kW chargers in the near future.

Most EV brands support Plug & Charge at Ionna, with Tesla recently getting Autocharge functionality through a third-party smartphone application. Ionna itself doesn’t have a smartphone app, instead relying on automakers and third-party apps to integrate its locations. So far, this approach has turned out to be quite successful, with J.D. Power’s latest public charging survey putting the operator first, ahead of Tesla and the rest of the competition.

#4223. BYD Barred from Selling Ti7 SUV in EU Because of a Copycat Design

A Dutch court barred BYD from selling the SUV in the European Union, ruling that the company copied the design of the Land Rover Defender too closely.

A Dutch court has ruled that BYD cannot sell the Ti7 mid-size three-row SUV in the European Union, according to a report from Automotive News. According to the report, a preliminary ruling from the Dutch court found BYD guilty of copyright infringement, with the Ti7 ruled to be a dupe of the Land Rover Defender.

Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) brought the case against BYD earlier this year after the Chinese automaker announced that it would launch the car in the United Kingdom in 2027. The preliminary ruling marks a significant setback in BYD’s recent explosive expansion into Europe.

See all results for used cars for sale near 06010

“In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover,” the court said in its November 20 ruling, AN reported. “The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7.”

The Defender is JLR’s best-selling vehicle globally, with the automaker shipping more than 100,000 units last year. Both vehicles have boxy designs with flat rooflights, squared wheel arches, and, notably, body-colored panels in place of the rear side windows.

Unfortunately for JLR, the judge also ruled that the court does not have authority over BYD’s U.K. arm. To that end, JLR is reportedly planning to bring the same claim to the courts in England.

According to AN, BYD “strongly disagrees” with the ruling and has plans to appeal the result. “The BYD Ti7 is the result of BYD’s own independent design work and infringes none of JLR’s rights,” the company said. “We will pursue every legal avenue to demonstrate that this decision is incorrect.”

While the final ruling will likely take some time before it is announced, the Dutch court has prohibited BYD from producing the Ti7 at its new factory in Hungary, where it was due to begin mass production early next year.

#4222. Volvo Is Bringing Humanoid Robots Into Its Factories. Here's When They'll Start Working

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo, the maker of the EX60 electric crossover, wants to replace some factory workers with humanoid robots that are capable of doing repetitive tasks without complaining about back pain.

To make that happen, the car manufacturer has brought in the first Aeon units at its factory in Ghent, Belgium, where humans are currently training them to do various tasks. Volvo said that it aims to support employees in repetitive and “ergonomically challenging work,” and it’s not the only car company that’s leaning towards replacing humans with robots.

Volvo Cars is training AEON humanoid robots for future work in factories

While fixed robotic arms have been a staple of automotive factories for decades, some brands are now investing a lot of time and money in artificial intelligence-powered robots that can do tasks where components don’t always land in the same exact spot. So-called pick-and-place jobs are gradually being taken over by robots, with Tesla, General Motors, Ford, and Rivian slowly but surely filling their factories with complex robots.

Volvo is no different, and while the first humanoids shipped to the company’s plant in Ghent are only being trained right now, they’ll gradually start going to work in real conditions starting in mid 2027, the Swedish manufacturer said.

Currently, Volvo Cars is using imitation learning to teach the robot how to pick up and place certain components into two fixtures with high precision. Through the learning process, the team will gradually make the work more challenging, adding multiple parts, moving around the production area, and interacting with the plant’s automated systems.

“Aeon’s humanoid design means it can fit into our production as it is today, alongside our teams and existing automation,” says Magnus Nilsson, Chief Manufacturing Officer at Volvo Cars. “Our aim is for humanoid robots to take on some of the most physically demanding tasks and help make work more ergonomic for our people.”

The robot chosen by Volvo looks like a human, but it doesn’t have feet. Instead, the 5.4-foot (1.65-meter) robot moves on wheels and is capable of reaching up to 5.3 miles per hour (8.6 kilometers per hour). It weighs 132 pounds (60 kilograms) and can carry up to 22 lbs (10 kg). Several cameras and sensors are used to capture its surroundings and handle parts with precision.

#4221. Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A new study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged.

The findings, published in Radiology, a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized.

Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain.

Using AI to Investigate Bone Density and Brain Health

To explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance.

The researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine.

Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group.

The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia.

Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time.

Lower Bone Density Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline

The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance.

The researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are important for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention.

Another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density showed a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity.

"This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri said. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration."

Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia.

Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging.

"This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri said. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect."

These findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health.

Routine CT Scans Could Reveal Hidden Signs of Brain Aging

One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons.

"Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh said. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function."

By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together.

Dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms."

The study highlights a potentially important connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain.

The study, "Deep Learning-derived Bone Mineral Density and Longitudinal White Matter Microstructure and Cognitive Decline: Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis," also included Quincy A. Hathaway, M.D., Ph.D., Michael P. Bancks, Ph.D., M.P.H., David A. Bluemke, M.D., M.S.B., Ph.D., R. Graham Barr, M.D., Dr.P.H., Wendy S. Post, M.D., M.S., Mohamad Habes, Ph.D., Ilya Nasrallah, M.D., Ph.D., Susan R. Heckbert, M.D., Ph.D., R. Nick Bryan, M.D., Ph.D., Jose A. Luchsinger, M.D., M.P.H., Mei Wan, Ph.D., Matthew Budoff, M.D., João A. C. Lima, M.D., M.B.A., Timothy M. Hughes, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Christos Davatzikos, Ph.D., who collaborated with Drs. Demehri and Momtazmanesh.

#4220. Lucid Gravity Robotaxis Begin Driverless Testing for Future Uber Service

A collaboration between Lucid, Uber, and Nuro enters the next testing stage, ditching the human safety net for test drives in the San Francisco Bay Area.

The San Francisco Bay Area has become an unofficial proving ground for robotaxis, with companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Tesla running supervised road tests on San Francisco’s streets. A fleet of specially equipped Lucid Gravity SUVs has also been on the prowl in the Bay Area this year, testing a self-driving ride-hailing experience for Uber. While these tests have been run with a safety driver ready to take over, the Gravity SUVs are now going fully driverless.

The modified Gravity SUVs are the product of a collaboration between Lucid, Uber, and Nuro, a company that builds autonomous driving software. The robotaxis feature an Uber-designed cabin interface and are operated by Nuro’s autonomous driving system. High-resolution cameras, lidar sensors, and radar sensors are integrated into the Gravity’s body and mounted to a rooftop “halo” that doubles as a way for riders to identify the correct vehicle through LED lights.

See all results for new 2027 Lucid Motors Gravity for sale near 06010

Testing first began with human supervision in the Bay Area in December 2025. Since then, Nuro has continued to conduct supervised round-the-clock testing in San Francisco and Houston. The company now says it’s ready to begin its next phase, which involves driving on public roads without a safety operator inside.

Lucid built and delivered over 100 autonomous vehicles to complete this next stage. The California Department of Motor Vehicles has issued two permits this year that allow the vehicles to test on public roads without a safety operator inside and allow for passenger rides when a safety driver is present.

As part of the collaboration’s terms, Uber has committed to owning and operating at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles equipped with Nuro’s autonomous technology. The service is expected to launch to the public in the Bay Area by early 2027, followed by launches in dozens of global markets over the next few years.

#4219. A Used Cybertruck Is Selling A Month Faster Than A Ford F-150

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you had to guess which used pickup found a buyer fastest in October, the Toyota Tacoma would be a sensible bet. It’s America’s best-selling midsize truck and has a reputation for holding its value. Or you might pick the super frugal Ford Maverick Hybrid. But the truck that beat them both was the Tesla Cybertruck.

The data from the new iSeeCars study covers 1.1 million used vehicles that changed hands in October, so this was before Tesla announced it would discontinue the Cybertruck in 2027. The study looked at one- to five-year-old vehicles and ranked models by how long they’d been listed before selling.

The Cybertruck surpassed all other pickups, averaging 39.1 days, compared to 65.5 days for used pickups overall. The Maverick Hybrid came closest at 43.3 days, followed by the Rivian R1T at 45.2 and the F-150 Lightning at 47.4. The Tacoma came in fifth position.

The gap between the two electric pickups at either end of the list was even more striking. A used Chevrolet Silverado EV took 107.5 days to sell, putting it last among the 24 trucks in the study. That’s a 68-day difference between two American electric pickups. Across the wider used market, EVs averaged about 46 days to find a buyer, around nine fewer than hybrids and 15 fewer than gas vehicles.

How quickly a used Cybertruck sold seems to have changed a lot since May 2024, when some sellers were cutting as much as $30,000 from their asking prices after listing their trucks for close to $200,000. By December of that year, we reported that used Cybertrucks were piling up on dealer lots, with data at the time showing they stayed for 75 days, up from 27 in May.

Then owners got a look at what Tesla itself would pay for a used Cybertruck trade-in. One year later, in May 2025, one owner of a $99,990 dual-motor Foundation Series truck got a trade-in estimate of $65,400 after driving it just 6,211 miles.

So even though the Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used pickup in iSeeCars’ new study, it didn’t report what buyers paid, so we don’t know whether owners got their asking price or had to lower it to sell.

Tesla will build the last Cybertrucks at the end of summer 2027, and this will reshape their used market. Elon Musk originally announced production would end around the middle of the year, but then extended the run to fill more orders. And if you order a Cybertruck now, the only one you can get is the $110,000 tri-motor Cyberbeast, so anyone who wants a less expensive dual-motor truck has to look for a used example.

Once the last new Cybertruck is sold, I’d expect collectors and everyday truck buyers to look at used ones differently. Someone after a clean Foundation Series truck with low miles might pay a little extra for one close to home, especially since it could be months before another comes up for sale nearby.

At the same time, someone who just needs an electric pickup to tow a trailer has more options. If a used dual-motor Cybertruck costs about the same as a Ford F-150 Lightning or a Rivian R1T, I suspect that buyer will care more about mileage, condition, and how much battery warranty is left than when Tesla built its last truck.

#4218. These are the e-bike sales you should really care about this Black Friday

It’s that time of year again; Black Friday approaches! And while the e-bike sales have been pretty good all month, there’s no better day than today to find an amazing deal on a new way around your city (or a fitness e-bike, leisure e-bike, cargo e-bike, etc…)!

A lot of sites will throw a lot of affiliate links at you today for anything they can hawk for a few bucks (this site included from our deals team, probably). But this isn’t that. I’m a professional e-bike rider and tester, and the deals below are only for bikes I actually ride, and for companies I would actually recommend to my own family and friends. Basically, this is the good stuff.

Let’s start with Lectric eBikes, since, as the largest e-bike company in North America, they have long been setting the standard for incredible deals and value in the e-bike industry. I’ve long said that you can’t get better value than here. Sure, you can find lower-priced e-bikes out there, but not at this quality level and with this level of customer support.

Lectric’s sales are usually defined by huge collections of free accessories added to their already low-priced e-bikes, further increasing the value. But this year there are also some legit price drops as well. See all of their Black Friday Sales packages here.

The major standouts for me have always been the XP and XP Lite lines.

The latest of each, the XP4 and the XP Lite3, offer bundle deals with savings of up to $731 and $257, respectively. For price drops, you’ll find that both the Lectrix XPLite 2 and the XPTrike2 are marked down to new record-low prices.

I’m also a huge fan of their cargo bike, the Lectric XPedition2, which has savings of up to $405 thanks to those impressive bundles.

But you should also explore the rest of their deals because just about everything is either marked down or comes with a crazy amount of free accessories that you can’t get for this price any other time of the year!

Ride1Up is another major value leader in the space, and in fact, I’ve been using the Ride1Up Roadster V3 as my everyday commuter e-bike since the summer.

I’m set to surpass 1,000 miles on it (1,600 km) by the end of the month!

That bike is marked down $100 to just $1,295 right now, making it a major deal for a lightweight, 40 lb (18 kg) commuter e-bike that doubles as a gravel bike. Ask me how I know that it can handle hard off-roading, too!

You can also save $150 on the Vorsa, which is an awesome all-around e-bike with multiple levels for riders who want higher or lower performance.

The new Portola 02 folder is a killer deal at $100 off for just $795 (that’s a crazy price!). If you want to go big and powerful, the Revv1 will crush Super73 and is doing so for $500 off!

Last but not least, the Prodigy V2 Eco is just $1,295 after the $100 deal, which is literally the most affordable Bosch-powered electric bike in the world. The only thing stopping me from buying that bike is that I already have one, though at this price, part of me wonders if I should get a spare for friends to use!

Basically, Ride1Up has a ton of Black Friday Sales going on now, and you can check them all out here.

If you want to go a bit further up the quality ladder to get a more premium e-bike, but you still don’t want to spend $2k+, then you should check out Monarc Bikes. It was founded by Lectric eBikes as an offshoot that could focus on building higher-end models while still leveraging Lectric’s industry heavyweight status to get better pricing. That means the company can offer higher-end e-bikes that rival some of the bike shop brands, while still offering direct-to-consumer pricing, 5-year warranties, and industry-leading local customer support by phone and email.

The two models they’ve launched so far are the urban-focused Tracer and the off-road-optimized Marker, though you better believe they’ve got more interesting stuff coming, likely next year. For now, though, these two models cover most folks’ needs and come with higher-end parts like quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, reverse arch forks, Bafang’s powerful motors, large batteries, and impressive add-ons like rear-facing radar to keep tabs on approaching cars.

The company started by selling e-bikes that came with a free spare battery, but has recently opened up options for single or even no-battery bikes, meaning if you previously bought a Monarc model and already have that free spare battery, you can save a bunch of money by buying only the bike and using your spare battery across the line. Yep, it’s like the power drill model!

You can see all of the sales and deals here!

JackRabbit may be a bit of a divisive brand due to how different the bikes look, but I freakin’ love these things! My JackRabbit OG is one of my prized possessions, and I just love how much performance and convenience JackRabbit has been able to pack into small-format two-wheelers that start at barely 25 lb (11 kg).

Literally every one of their micro e-bikes is 20% off, meaning you’re saving hundreds of dollars. But then the rest of their gear is up to 50% off, such as 30% off their big RangeBuster batteries.

The awesomeness of JackRabbit’s Micro-bikes is a micro-hill I’m prepared to die on, and I definitely recommend these models to anyone who wants a compact electric two-wheeler that rides as stable as a typical Class 2 e-bike but can fold flat to fit in a tiny space like behind a couch or under a dorm room bed.

I’m never parting with my own JackRabbit, and I love seeing new riders discover just how much fun these awesomely strange bikes are!

Austin, Texas-based Mod Bikes doesn’t get as much press as some of the larger players, but I think they deserve a second look for several reasons. Not only are they continuously pushing out new and impressive bikes as well as cool technology alongside them (don’t forget about their locking streetside charging stands for e-bikes!), but they also have cool rides that no one else has managed to create.

Case in point: The Mod Easy Sidecar e-bike that looks like a million bucks, but costs just $3,495 after the $400 deal for Black Friday. I love this e-bike for riding around with my nephews as well as the family dog, which you can see below.

There’s even a Sahara version of it that looks like it just got back from an incredible desert expedition!

Juiced Bikes was revived this year, and the company is back with a vengeance! The high-performance bikes are better than ever, and the prices are better, too!

The recently launched Scrambler Mini leads the pack in pricing, starting at just $949 thanks to its Black Friday promotional price. That’d be an awesome model for any young riders this season. But the larger versions are also pushing the value war forward with their own great sales.

There’s a lot to like here, from higher-end parts to 5-year warranties to the backing of the nation’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes. Basically, it’s hard to imagine finding a better deal on a moto-style electric bike these days than from Juiced.

Sure, e-bikes are my first love, but electric scooters absolutely deserve their place in the micromobility ecosystem thanks to their extreme portability and compact, space-saving size.

VMAX is my favorite electric scooter company, which brings its Swiss design to the US and European scooter markets. When it came to putting my nephew on a scooter to get to school, I made sure he had a VMAX VX2 Lite to cruise around safely and securely. That scooter is marked down to just $639 for Black Friday, despite offering impressive performance of 25 mph (40 km/h) and over 50 miles (80 km) of range! The new VX4 is a 37 mph (60 km/h) model that is on sale for just $1,199, though you can get the previous version of that scooter with slightly more muted performance for an even better price of $889!

There are a lot of great deals to be had, and you can see all of VMAX’s sales here.

These are the major sales that jumped out at me, but let me know what other sales you’ve seen on e-bikes you recommend.

I’ll take a look too and update if I see something I know I can stand behind. There are a lot of great e-bikes out there, and having ridden so many by now, I love being able to share my experiences, especially when there’s a good deal to be had at the end!

#4217. BYD Just Put a Fold-Away Steering Wheel in a Car People Can Buy

One touch of a button and you instantly get extra cabin space to relax.

Anyone who has ever tried to eat lunch sitting in the driver’s seat while parked—or worse yet, flip open a laptop to catch up on emails—knows that a steering wheel takes up a surprisingly large amount of real estate. Thus, manufacturers of all kinds have come up with various steering solutions that have largely remained conceptual, cool show-off pieces for the auto show circuit but little more. Chinese manufacturer BYD just stuck one in a mainstream SUV.

The Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 is a large six-seater SUV that’s about the size of an Infiniti QX80, with prices starting at the equivalent of $41K in the Chinese market. It’s not a pure EV, but rather a series plug-in hybrid with a 150-hp 1.5-liter turbo four-cylinder acting as a generator to power the 66-kWh battery pack; the dual electric motors combine for 536 hp.Fang Cheng Bao is one of BYD’s subbrands, aimed at delivering an off-road-ready flair. The Tai 9 is certainly a chunky-looking thing, but what’s perhaps most interesting about the top trim level is how it behaves when parked.

See all results for used cars for sale near l9y 2h5

Spend the equivalent of $49K for the highest-grade Tai 9, and you get a folding steering wheel that disappears into the dash. Because the vehicle is entirely steer-by-wire, a technology that only became legal in China less than six months ago, the Tai 9 has no steering column geometry to worry about. The rim splits in half, folds back over the column, and the whole thing retracts, airbag still facing forward.Paired with a driver’s seat that reclines almost completely flat, the appeal here is to provide a more spacious place to relax or work while you charge. Again, this feature is only available when parked, so you can’t retract the wheel while using the Tai 9’s driver-assistance functions.

However, this folding steering wheel does show how car interiors might look for vehicles with Level 4-or-higher autonomy, ones that can operate completely without human intervention in certain cases. On a geofenced section of highway, with automated cruise control activated, you could simply pack your steering wheel away for extra room.

Obviously, driving enthusiasts who obsess over steering feel aren’t going to be too happy about the proliferation of steering-by-wire, never mind having the steering wheel fold away entirely. However, it’s not like a three-ton, three-row PHEV SUV is going to feel like piloting a Caterham anyway.

What’s perhaps most impressive of all is the speed at which BYD managed to get its folding steering wheel technology into the hands of the public, considering the regulatory requirements only came into being months ago. Combined with the company’s production-car speed record under its Yangwang performance brand, and the sub-$10K price of its Seagull entry-level EV, BYD is certainly active in all segments of the market. Watch this space to see what it gets up to next.

#4216. Arc Raiders just keeps breaking its own Steam player records

Word of mouth has done wonders for the popularity of Arc Raiders, clearly more than all the pre-launch marketing and hype.

Arc Raiders just cannot be stopped. The extraction shooter from Embark Studios has once again attracted more players over the weekend than it has in its launch week, and over its first weekend on the market.

The positive reception the PvPvE game has garnered from players has clearly caused many of them to convince their friends to jump into this unique gem of a game.

The day Arc Raiders launched, it peaked at 264,673 concurrent players on Steam. Although not massive, it was quite a bit more than the game’s most popular - free - beta test managed to attract.

That figure was broken yet again over the game’s first weekend, with Arc Raiders having reached 354,836 concurrent players on Steam. This is where many thought it would settle, as we start to see the gradual - and expected - decline of player numbers.

To everyone’s surprise, however, Arc Raiders shattered even that record yet again on Sunday, November 9. According to SteamDB, the game peaked at 462,488 concurrent players on Steam, which is a sizeable increase on its launch day numbers. Indeed, should this trend continue, Arc Raiders is going to be well on its way to doubling its initial launch record.

While a few games have broken their launch Steam player records in the past, it’s incredibly rare to see it happen - especially twice in such a short period after launch. Embark clearly has a winner on its hands here.

Arc Raiders’ next big moment is the game’s first post-launch map, which is set to arrive at some point this month, alongside new Quests and other gameplay items. Seeing as how the Steam concurrent record has been broken twice, there’s every chance the arrival of the new map will bring another boost to player numbers.

If you’re among the millions of players who have been exploring the Rust Belt, you’re probably wondering where to find prickly pears, where to find lemons and apricots, and where to find olives - and those links will answer all of those questions. And, if you just jumped in over the weekend, you’re definitely going to find these Arc Raiders tips very helpful.

#4214. Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease

Changes in mood later in life may offer important clues about what is happening inside the brain, even before problems with memory or thinking become noticeable. New research suggests that the buildup of tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, may contribute to worsening depressive symptoms in older adults.

The study, published in JNeurosci, was conducted by Teodora Markova of Brandeis University and her colleagues. The team investigated how tau levels relate to depression during normal aging and in people experiencing the cognitive (memory, attention, and thinking) difficulties associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Worsening Depression

To investigate this connection, researchers analyzed information from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, a research project that tracks changes in brain health over time. The data included older men and women, some with cognitive difficulties and others whose memory and thinking abilities remained intact.

Participants underwent multiple brain scans designed to detect tau accumulation and completed questionnaires assessing depressive symptoms at different points during the study. This allowed researchers to examine how changes in tau levels corresponded with changes in mood over time.

Among participants with normal cognitive abilities, the researchers discovered a striking pattern. Those whose tau levels increased more rapidly also tended to experience a faster rise in depressive symptoms. Higher tau levels also helped predict more severe depressive symptoms in these individuals.

The results suggest that tau may begin influencing mood before measurable cognitive problems emerge. However, the same relationships were not observed among participants who already had mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease.

Could Depression Reveal Early Brain Changes?

The findings suggest that tau accumulation during the early stages of brain aging may contribute to the development or worsening of depression. They also raise the possibility that changes in mood could provide useful information about brain health before memory loss becomes apparent.

Researchers believe that following depressive symptoms over time, alongside other assessments, could eventually help identify older adults who may be at greater risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases. However, additional research is needed to establish whether these early changes in mood can reliably predict future cognitive decline.

Markova emphasized the importance of studying these relationships over longer periods, particularly as some participants develop more noticeable depression or begin experiencing cognitive difficulties.

"Future work can continue to track how participants' tau levels and depression symptoms evolve over longer periods of time, particularly as some develop cognitive impairment or more clinically significant levels of depression. Continuing to follow these trajectories, observing how early mood changes relate to later clinical outcomes, and establishing relationships with other methods tracking the development of Alzheimer's disease will provide more clarity on methods to determine which individuals may be at an increased risk."

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4213. View Photos of the 2028 Porsche 718 Boxster EV Prototype

See the exterior of the 2028 Porsche 718 Boxster EV Prototype from every angle.

Porsche won’t unveil its electric 718 Boxster until 2027, but we were able to slide behind the wheel of a camouflaged prototype for a quick track spin.

Whereas most EVs shove their batteries under the floor, the Boxster EV puts its battery pack behind the seats, where the gas engine used to be.

This gives the electric Boxster a 60 percent rear weight distribution, not far off the gas-fed 718’s 55 percent rear bias.

After a few laps at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles, we can confirm this EV handles like a Boxster should.

We don’t know any other details, really: Porsche won’t say anything about range, power, price—any of that.

#4212. Battlefield 6 patch finally ends the menace of the Lock-Guided Missile, shuts down the Recon Drone Sledgehammer exploit and more

Today's Battlefield 6 patch is laser-focused on taking care of some of the more infuriating bugs while also taking out a couple of exploits.

The next Battlefield 6 update is here. Having gone live just moments ago, update 1.1.1.5 is something of a midseason update, bringing a few quality of life tweaks to the game alongside some key fixes for a few of the issues that cropped up since the launch of Season 1 in late October.

This latest release is also the first to tackle some of the problems players have been running into playing Redsec battle royale, the free-to-play component that also came out recently.

Patch 1.1.1.5 is fairly limited in scope. The biggest fix in this one comes to the Lock-Guided Missiles going through flares, and generally being annoying enough to stop players from using air vehicles altogether.

The Lock-Guided Missiles were mainly used by AA vehicles, but they could also be equipped by IFVs, which made it even more of a nightmare to pilots. It got so bad that Battlefield Studios disabled it entirely while the team worked on a proper fix.

Another exploit the patch fixes is the one that allowed players to stand on the Recon Drone and reach areas they’re not supposed to. This was done by… repeatedly hitting it with a Sledgehammer. The long-running issue of vehicles not spawning for certain teams in Conquest and Breakthrough appears to have finally been fixed, too.

In terms of battle royale, the patch has a few fixes that should help make the experience more consistent, as well as improve the flow of matches. One of the more interesting addresses an issue that could eliminate the entire squad instead of reviving dead teammates when using a Mobile Spawn.

Patch 1.1.1.5 also has yet more adjustments to weapon dispersion (bloom). Some of the casses it addresses include transitioning from sprint to firing in ADS, and others where it apparently scaled with player movement speed.

#4211. Driven: 2028 Porsche 718 Boxster EV Prototype Wags Its Tail Like a Mid-Engine Sports Car

The Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution, which is unusual for an EV, makes it handle like a sports car should.

There’s still a lot that Porsche won’t divulge about its forthcoming 2028 718 Boxster EV, including horsepower, battery capacity, range, pricing, or even its final, un-camouflaged looks. But after some seat time around the handling course at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles, we now know what it feels like at—and a little bit beyond—its cornering limits.

Whether you’re welcoming the Boxster’s EV transition or bemoaning the loss of its internal-combustion engines, particularly the iconic flat-six, we think anyone who drives the next-generation 983 Boxster will agree it’s fantastic. The steering, inherited from the 992.2 911 Carrera GTS, is eager and sharp, and rear-axle steering will also be available. You can feel the Boxster’s rear-biased weight distribution in the way its rear end steps out when lifting off the throttle.

In other words, this new EV feels like a mid-engine Boxster, because that’s where the weight is concentrated. Other than some hypercars, such as the Rimac Nevera, the forthcoming electric Boxster rides atop one of the first EV platforms built around a two-seat sports car. The 800-volt battery pack lives entirely behind the passenger cabin, in the place the engine used to reside, which leads to a 40/60 front/rear weight distribution, similar to the gas-powered Boxster’s 45/55 split. And since there’s no battery under the floor, you sit as low as you would in any other sports car.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 10400

We drove what will become the top Boxster model when it goes on sale after its formal debut in early 2027, but Porsche wouldn’t confirm what it will be called. S? GTS? These models wear Pirelli P Zero R Elect tires—and for the first time—mount on staggered-diameter wheels just like the latest 911. The tires measure 255/35ZR-20 up front and 305/30ZR-21 in back, which is more meat than even the last 718 Spyder RS. The company isn’t saying how much power this Boxster’s single rear motor will make—all electric Boxsters will be rear-drive only—but they do claim the sprint to 60 mph will require less than 3.0 seconds. After experiencing being pinned to the seat by a few launch-control starts, the new Boxster feels every bit that quick.

Porsche says this will be the quickest, most powerful Boxster with the highest cornering and braking performance, with a center of gravity that’s—no surprise—much lower than before. We can attest to feeling tons of grip, but can we feel the EV’s added weight? As the Boxster slithered through transitions and dove into apexes, we can’t say it felt heavy, although the squealing from its wide tires sounded at times more tortured than those we recall from the just-over-3000-pound gas-powered Boxster. Porsche says the Boxster EV’s curb weight will fall somewhere within that of the 911 lineup, which ranges from the 3350-pound Carrera to the 4000-pound Turbo S Cabriolet. Here’s hoping it’s toward the lower end of that range, which would be very light for an EV.

See all results for new 2028 Porsche 718 EV for sale near 10400

While this new electric version looks like a Boxster and the low seating position feels like a Boxster, with a forward view of a quickly disappearing hood, Porsche wanted to add some more nostalgic tie-ins by way of fabricated engine noises and simulated shifts. The Taycan got a similar E-Shift feature earlier this year, but while the Taycan’s engine noises weren’t modeled after a specific engine, the Boxster’s very much pays homage to its past. The Boxster’s E-Shift, which is controlled by a knob on the steering wheel and can shift automatically or be controlled by steering wheel paddles, mimics the 981 Boxster GTS’s 3.4-liter flat-six, which Porsche engineers say is the high-water mark for flat-six wails. They told us emissions compromises to the most recent flat-sixes made them choose that one from circa 2015. That said, there’s a bit of revisionist history going on with the electric Boxster’s 8000-rpm “redline” versus the actual 7600-rpm redline in its 981 muse. Either way, the noise emanating from the two speakers—one inside the cabin, one outside—absolutely sounds like a flat-six.

Although the synthesized sound is a solid re-creation, we do think it would be easy to identify the real from the facsimile in a blindfolded test. There’s a lot of nuance going on in the sounds of a flat-six belting to redline—intake and exhaust noise, valve and other mechanical clatter—and it’s hard to generate all of that from a couple speakers. That said, after doing a few hot laps with the system on, we believe it adds to the experience, and it felt weird to switch over to silent and shift-free lapping. We think we’d use this more in a sports car like the Boxster than in the four-door Taycan sedan.

What else did we learn? As before, the 983 Boxster has both front and rear trunks, and its NACS charge port, which is hidden behind a powered door in the middle of the rear bumper, is the first from Porsche to accommodate both AC and DC charging. Today’s Cayenne and Taycan electrics have separate ports for AC and DC with the NACS only handling DC charging.

Officially, there won’t be any gas-powered Boxster variants, but who knows what the lifecycle might hold, especially if early sales disappoint. After all, remember when the previous generation went four-cylinder only, but then the flat-six made a reappearance a few years later? While we’re as sad as anyone to see the flat-six and manual transmission leave the Boxster lineup, we think that anyone who drives the new one will agree it’s a great-handling sports car.
